ground.summary: Researched what South African permaculture, agroecology and indigenous-food practitioners actually plant, by function, prioritising SA primary sources (SANBI PlantZAfrica and SANBI bee-forage infosheets, the DFFE national Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline, ARC-VOPI's indigenous crops programme, Agribook, Vetiver SA, and SA farming press). Headline finding: the genuinely SA-specific, repeatedly-documented species set is much narrower than global permaculture lists suggest, and two staples of international permaculture practice — Tithonia diversifolia and Leucaena leucocephala — are NEMBA-listed invasives in South Africa and should not be recommended. Note also that SA permaculture organisations publish surprisingly little species-level guidance: Permaculture South Africa's own food-forest page names no species at all, which is why most "SA permaculture plant list" content circulating online is recycled temperate/tropical material. Several sources refused fetch (Food & Trees for Africa's site now redirects to trees.africa; Random Harvest, Mahlathini and Farmer's Weekly returned 403), so a few functions below rest on search-level evidence rather than a fetched primary document — flagged individually.
points: NITROGEN FIXING — the strongest SA-documented pair is pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and Sesbania sesban. The DFFE national Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline names these two specifically as "the woody legumes that have been used as improved fallows in South Africa", with a photo captioned 'Pigeon pea being grown as an improved fallow in KwaZulu-Natal', plus pigeon pea hedgerows cut at 90 cm and maize established directly into Sesbania prunings. This is the only SA government document I found that commits to named species for this function. Indigenous option: Vachellia karroo (sweet thorn) — SANBI PlantZAfrica states its nitrogen fixation leads to "grasses and other plants thriving in its shade". Herbaceous/cover-crop layer (search-level, ECHO + southern African CA literature): cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), lablab (Lablab purpureus), velvet bean (Mucuna pruriens), sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea), jack bean (Canavalia ensiformis) — ECHO trials in South Africa reported over 100 kg N/ha accumulated in above-ground biomass of cowpea, horse gram, sunn hemp and velvet bean.

FODDER / BROWSE — Portulacaria afra (spekboom) is the standout, and it is used at landscape scale, not just talked about: it is planted on riplines across degraded thicket in the Baviaanskloof and Camdeboo (350–500 mm rainfall zones), is browsed by goats, cattle and kudu, and restored plots reportedly provide cattle fodder from about year three. Vachellia karroo — SANBI: "stock and game feed on the leaves, flowers and pods". Dovyalis caffra — SANBI: "The leaves are used as fodder (bulk feed for livestock)." Pigeon pea and Sesbania sesban again, explicitly for cut-and-carry protein fodder in the DFFE guideline. Moringa oleifera is actively promoted to Limpopo smallholders partly as livestock feed supplement (search-level: SA Journal of Science review and NW Dept of Agriculture production guide). Tagasaste/tree lucerne (Chamaecytisus palmensis) appears in SA regenerative circles for the Karoo and Eastern Cape but I could not confirm it against an SA institutional source — treat as weaker.

LIVING FENCE AND STOCK BARRIER — this is one of the best-evidenced functions. Dovyalis caffra (kei apple) is the classic: SANBI states it can be "used to form an impenetrable hedge around a garden to keep unwanted animals and people out", and it was ranked among priority indigenous fruit trees for KZN domestication, so it doubles as fruit. Erythrina lysistemon (coral tree) is the traditional one and the mechanism matters: SANBI states the trees "were planted as living fences around kraals, homesteads and waterholes", and truncheons (whole dried branch sections) are planted directly and root in place — so the fence post literally becomes the fence. Vachellia karroo is used for live fencing and brushwood fencing. Portulacaria afra prunes into a dense long-lived hedge. Documented Eastern Cape live-fence practice also includes Agave americana, Opuntia ficus-indica and Phoenix reclinata (Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine, EC survey) — note the first two are aliens and Opuntia is invasive-listed in SA, so they are what people use, not what should be recommended.

CHOP-AND-DROP MULCH — the SA-documented practice is pigeon pea and Sesbania sesban prunings in alley cropping (DFFE guideline: 'Establishing maize into the mulch from Sesbania prunings'; tree prunings used for nutrient cycling in the wet season and forage in the dry). Vetiver is cut back to 20–30 cm after 3–4 months and the cut grass used as mulch and bedding, though Vetiver SA is explicit that mulch is a by-product, not the primary purpose. CRITICAL CORRECTION: Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — the single most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture literature — is a NEMBA Category 1b invasive in South Africa. It may not be owned, grown, moved, sold or given away, and it is already invading Lowveld Mpumalanga, Limpopo and coastal KZN. Do not put it in an SA plant list. Mahlathini Development Foundation's KZN/EC work found mulching uptake was low (32%) specifically because farmers lacked mulching material — which is the real-world argument for growing a dedicated biomass species rather than a design nicety.

POLLINATOR AND BENEFICIAL-INSECT FORAGE — best-sourced function of the lot. SANBI's own infosheet names the indigenous forage that "stands out" for SA beekeepers: fynbos species (ericas, proteas, mesembs), several aloes including mountain aloe and Aloe greatheadii var. davyana (the key winter-flowering species for migratory beekeepers), wild asparagus, buchus (Agathosma), and the trees Vachellia karroo and Ziziphus mucronata (buffalo thorn). SANBI notes V. karroo's long flowering season makes it particularly valuable. The Kirstenbosch list (built on Kirstenbosch observations plus Johannsmeier's ARC handbook 'Beeplants of the South-Western Cape', PPRI Handbook No. 17) is a large explicit species list; repeatedly-named practitioner staples in it include Leonotis leonurus (wild dagga), Tecomaria capensis (Cape honeysuckle), Buddleja salviifolia and B. saligna, Salvia africana-lutea and S. africana-caerulea, Searsia spp., Polygala myrtifolia, Eriocephalus africanus, Helichrysum spp., Euryops spp., Felicia spp., Grewia occidentalis, Lessertia frutescens (=Sutherlandia), Artemisia afra, Mentha longifolia, Agathosma spp. and Dovyalis caffra (bees again). Caveat SANBI gives: plant locally-occurring subspecies to avoid hybridisation with local veld.

SHADE — SANBI on Searsia lancea (karee): "an excellent shade tree especially in hot regions such as the Karoo and Kalahari since it is evergreen and drought resistant", and it has a non-aggressive root system so it can go near paving. Vachellia karroo provides shade under which grasses thrive (nitrogen effect). Erythrina lysistemon is named in SA farming press for shade over crops and livestock. Celtis africana (white stinkwood), Harpephyllum caffrum (wild plum), Kiggelaria africana (wild peach) and Syzygium cordatum (waterberry) appear on SANBI's regional recommended-tree lists (compiled by Alice Notten from Van Jaarsveld's 'Wonderful Waterwise Gardening' plus Kirstenbosch horticulturists' experience) — that list is organised by region (Cape Flats/west coast, fynbos, subtropical forest, arid Karoo/Namaqualand, bushveld/savanna, highveld grassland, thicket/noorsveld) and is the single most useful SA document for matching a shade tree to a bioregion.

WINDBREAK — Searsia lancea is the one that recurs across sources: SANBI says "the density of the plant makes it suitable for use as a screen or barrier against wind". SA farming press (Farmers Magazine, Oct 2025) lists for windbreak plus soil stability: Searsia lancea, Vachellia karroo, Olea europaea subsp. africana (wild olive — also stabilises slopes and riverbanks), Podocarpus latifolius, and Erythrina lysistemon. Casuarina cunninghamiana is used commercially in SA to protect citrus orchards from wind scar, and macadamia industry guidance specifies 40–60% porosity as the design target — that porosity figure is the practical detail most plant lists omit. The DFFE guideline treats shelterbelts as one of the three main agrisilvicultural systems practised in SA but does not name species for them. Dovyalis caffra and Portulacaria afra double as low windbreak/hedge.

EROSION CONTROL AND BANK STABILISATION — vetiver (Chrysopogon zizanioides) is unambiguously the practitioner default, and it is a commercial reality in SA, not a theory: Vetiver SA gives operational spec — slips 10–15 cm apart in a single row across the slope, plant in the rainy season, establishment 3–6 weeks, visible hedgerow within 3 months, trim to 20–30 cm at 3–4 months then once or twice yearly. Documented SA applications: mine rehabilitation in Mpumalanga and North West, roadside slope stabilisation, and small-farm/rural homestead erosion control; Hydromulch (Pty) Ltd introduced the system to SA road and environmental engineers. For gullies, vetiver hedges planted on contour above the gully head stop head advance. For riverbanks specifically the indigenous choices are Combretum erythrophyllum (river bushwillow — found in all nine provinces, almost exclusively on riverbanks and floodplains, tolerates black loam through riverine alluvium) and Salix mucronata (Cape silver willow); Food & Trees for Africa's 'Respect the River' programme does exactly this work. Portulacaria afra on riplines for runoff and soil-loss reduction in thicket. Mahlathini's KZN/EC farmers use stone bunds (61% uptake) alongside planting.

GROUNDCOVER — be honest that this function splits in two in SA, and only one half is real permaculture practice. (a) Field-scale living mulch / cover crop, which is what practitioners actually do: cowpea, lablab, velvet bean, sunn hemp, jack bean, pigeon pea and groundnut, cited in the southern African conservation-agriculture literature as delivering 5–50 t/ha extra biomass for groundcover and/or fodder and 50–350 kg/ha residual N; sweet potato is used as an edible running groundcover. (b) Water-wise ornamental groundcover, which is nursery-trade rather than food-system practice: Bulbine frutescens, Gazania spp., Dymondia margaretae, Delosperma, Aptenia cordifolia, Plectranthus neochilus, Carpobrotus, prostrate Portulacaria afra. Category (b) is genuinely widely planted in SA but I found no SA permaculture or agroecology source recommending it for a productive system — if the target is a farm rather than a garden, category (a) is the honest answer. This is the weakest-evidenced of the eleven functions.

INDIGENOUS FRUIT — a KZN prioritisation study (Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution, 2020) ranked species by domestication and commercialisation potential, with Strychnos spinosa (spiny/green monkey orange) first, alongside Sclerocarya birrea (marula), Dovyalis caffra (kei apple) and Vangueria infausta (wild medlar). Agribook's indigenous food crops page lists the working set as: marula, red milkwood (Mimusops zeyheri), Mobola plum (Parinari curatellifolia), wild medlar, num-num (Carissa macrocarpa), kei apple, monkey orange, wild apricot, wild plum (Harpephyllum caffrum), raisin bush (Grewia spp.) and sour plum (Ximenia). Marula is the most productive per tree by fruit quantity and has a real commercial chain (Marula Natural Products); Vangueria infausta has poor handling qualities because of its thin papery skin, which is why it stays subsistence. Syzygium cordatum (waterberry) appears on SANBI's regional lists. Note the overlap that makes these efficient in a design: Dovyalis caffra is simultaneously fruit, stock-proof hedge, fodder and bee forage.

TRADITIONAL LEAFY GREENS (imifino / morogo / muhuro) — ARC-VOPI's indigenous crops programme names the working set it researches and promotes: Amaranthus spp., Cleome gynandra (spider plant), Corchorus spp. (jute mallow/Jew's mallow), Brassica carinata (Ethiopian kale), Solanum retroflexum (nightshade), plus Cucurbita spp. (traditional pumpkin, leaves eaten), Citrullus lanatus, Vigna unguiculata (cowpea, leaves eaten) and Colocasia esculenta (amadumbe). ARC frames them as tolerant of harsh conditions, nutrient-dense (vitamin A, iron) and part of cultural heritage. Add Bidens pilosa (blackjack / uqadolo / mushijeje), which Agribook lists among indigenous vegetable crops and which SA food writing treats as a core imifino. Vernacular pairing matters for an app: imifino (isiZulu/isiXhosa), morogo (Sesotho/Sepedi), muhuro or muroho (Tshivenda); imbuya/utyuthu = Amaranthus, umsobo = Solanum retroflexum, uqadolo = Bidens pilosa. Over 100 edible species have been recorded in SA. Practical detail from SA practitioners: harvest at 4–6 weeks and 15–30 cm, roughly half adult height, and take only young Bidens leaves as they turn bitter with age. Key point for a design tool: several of these are volunteers in disturbed ground — the practice is often managed encouragement rather than sowing.

REGULATORY CAVEAT WORTH BUILDING INTO ANY SA PLANT PICKER — two standard global permaculture species are NEMBA-listed in South Africa. Tithonia diversifolia is Category 1b (may not be owned, grown, moved, sold, gifted or dumped; requires containment). Leucaena leucocephala is Category 1a in the Western Cape and Category 2 in the rest of the country (Category 2 = permit required). Opuntia ficus-indica and Agave americana, both genuinely used as live fences in the Eastern Cape, are also alien/listed. SA's 2020 NEMBA list covers 383 plant species. Any species recommendation engine aimed at SA users should carry a NEMBA status field, because the international permaculture canon will actively lead users into illegal plantings.

METHOD AND CONFIDENCE NOTES — Fetched and text-extracted as primary documents: the DFFE Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline (via curl + pdftotext; the site has a broken TLS chain so WebFetch fails on it), both SANBI bee-forage PDFs, SANBI's regional recommended-trees PDF, ARC-VOPI indigenous crops, three PlantZAfrica species pages, Vetiver SA, Agribook, and SA farming press. Blocked (403) and therefore search-level only: Random Harvest nursery, Mahlathini Development Foundation, Farmer's Weekly, Living Earth wiki. Food & Trees for Africa's trees.org.za now 301-redirects to trees.africa, so their food-forest guidance could not be captured — worth a manual look since EduPlant is SA's largest school-garden programme and their species guidance would be the most practitioner-representative source available. Permaculture South Africa's food-forest design page was fetched and names zero species, only layers and functions, explicitly deferring to bio-region — a real finding, not a fetch failure, and the reason this research had to lean on government, SANBI and ARC rather than on permaculture organisations themselves.

STRONGEST OVERLAP CANDIDATES IF YOU WANT A SHORT DEFENSIBLE CORE LIST — species that showed up repeatedly across independent SA sources and serve multiple functions: Vachellia karroo (N-fix, fodder, bee forage, live/brushwood fence, shade, dryland rehab, dune stabilisation), Dovyalis caffra (stock-proof hedge, fruit, fodder, bee forage), Portulacaria afra (fodder, hedge, erosion/riplines, restoration, groundcover form), Searsia lancea (windbreak, shade, erosion, drought-hardy, non-invasive roots), Cajanus cajan (N-fix, chop-and-drop, fodder, grain), Sesbania sesban (N-fix, chop-and-drop, fodder), Chrysopogon zizanioides (erosion, gully control, mulch by-product), Erythrina lysistemon (live fence from truncheons, shade, erosion), and the ARC leafy-green set (Amaranthus, Cleome gynandra, Corchorus, Solanum retroflexum, Vigna unguiculata, Cucurbita). Everything beyond that list starts shading into 'could work' rather than 'is used'.

ground.summary: Researched from primary gazette texts (downloaded and parsed locally, not from memory). The instrument in force is the **Alien and Invasive Species Lists, 2020** (GN 1003, GG 43726, 18 Sept 2020) read with the **Alien and Invasive Species Regulations, 2020** (GN R.1020, GG 43735, 25 Sept 2020), both commenced **1 March 2021** by GN 115, GG 44182 (which also suspended the trout listings indefinitely). These repealed the 2014 regs and the 2016 lists. As of DFFE's own October 2025 briefing, **no amendment to the lists has been gazetted since 2020** — a Risk Analysis Review Committee has been working through ~140 taxa since March 2023 but nothing has been published. 383 plant taxa are listed. The single most dangerous naive assumption for a permaculture app is that "Category 3 / Category 2 = fine": Category 2 possession requires a **permit**, and without one the plant is legally treated as Category 1b; Category 3 permits **nothing new** — planting, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are all outright prohibited (s71A), only keeping what already stands is exempt. Many staple permaculture species are listed: Leucaena (2), old man saltbush (2), Napier grass (2), black locust (1b), honey locust (1b), Tithonia/Mexican sunflower (1b), elderberry (1b), Azolla (1b), watercress (2), white mulberry (3), silky oak (3). Working files: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-roryclark-Claude/ac3bcb04-4f79-45ce-8605-7e2434d68f3e/scratchpad/nemba/ (list1.txt = parsed 383-taxa plant list, regs2020.txt, lists2020.txt, nisw2025.txt, act.txt).
points: **WHAT IS IN FORCE (verify this before anything else).** Alien and Invasive Species Lists, 2020 — Government Notice 1003, Government Gazette 43726, 18 September 2020, signed by Minister B.D. Creecy under NEM:BA ss 66(1), 67(1), 70(1)(a), 71(3) and 71A. Alien and Invasive Species Regulations, 2020 — GN R.1020, GG 43735, 25 September 2020. Commencement was deferred twice (GN 1100, GG 43818, 16 Oct 2020) and both finally took effect **1 March 2021** per GN 115, GG 44182, 24 Feb 2021 — with the sole exception of Rainbow Trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) and Brown Trout (Salmo trutta), List 7 items 20 and 29, which 'shall not come into effect until further notice'. The 2020 Lists expressly 'replace and repeal any Alien and Invasive Species lists published under the Act including Government Gazette 40166 Notice 864 of 29 July 2016'; regulation 37 of the 2020 Regulations repeals the 2014 Regulations (GN R.598, GG 37885). The lists comprise Notice 1 (the restricted-activity/category matrix), Notice 2 (exempted alien species, s66(1)) and Notice 3 (the 11 national species lists, s70(1)). List 1 — terrestrial and fresh-water plants — has 383 numbered taxa. DFFE's own National Invasive Species Week briefing of 21 October 2025 still cites 'Alien and Invasive Species Regulations and Lists, 2020' as the operative framework, so **there is no post-2020 amendment to the lists**. A standardised Risk Analysis for Alien Taxa process has completed analyses for ~140 taxa and an inter-departmental Risk Analysis Review Committee first met 1 March 2023, with 54 of 123 analyses recommending substantive listing changes — so amendments are coming, and any app must treat the list as versioned data with a 'gazette version' stamp, not hardcoded.

**CATEGORY MEANINGS — the operative text, not the folklore.** Regulations 2–5 define the categories; **Notice 1 of the Lists is what actually determines legality per activity**, and 'species-specific exemptions and prohibitions in Notice 3 take precedence over Notice 1, in the event of any conflict'. Reg 2(1): Category 1a = species 'which must be combatted or eradicated'; a person in control must *immediately* take steps to combat or eradicate and must allow officials onto the property. Reg 3(1): Category 1b = species 'which must be controlled'; the Minister may require a written Category 1b Control Plan (species ID, extent of invasion, control measures, clearing schedule, biomass potential). Reg 4(1)–(2): Category 2 = species 'which require a permit to carry out a restricted activity within an area specified in the Notice or an area specified in the permit'; 'no person may carry out a restricted activity in respect of a Category 2 Listed Invasive Species without a permit'; reg 4(3) the holder must ensure specimens do not spread beyond the permitted land; **reg 4(4): a Category 2 species occurring outside the specified/permitted area 'must … be considered to be a Category 1b Listed Invasive Species'**. Reg 5(1): Category 3 = species subject to s71(3) exemptions and s71A prohibitions as specified in the Notice; **reg 5(2): any Category 3 plant occurring in a riparian area is deemed Category 1b**. Reg 7(1) applies across 1a, 1b and 3: any landowner, occupier, person in control of land or of the species 'must prevent the escape and spread of the species, including its growth or spread of propagules, and must control any specimen that escapes or spreads.'

**WHAT IT MEANS FOR A SMALLHOLDER WHO PLANTS ONE — activity by activity, straight from the Notice 1 matrix.** Notice 1 tabulates each restricted activity against each category. For **Category 1a, 1b and 3** the results are identical on the activities a grower cares about: importing = Prohibited; **growing, breeding or in any other way propagating, or causing it to multiply = PROHIBITED**; conveying/moving/translocating = Prohibited; selling, buying, receiving, giving, donating, accepting as a gift, or in any way acquiring or disposing of = Prohibited; spreading or allowing the spread = Prohibited; releasing = Prohibited. The one difference from Category 2 is that for 1a, 1b and 3, **'having in possession or exercising physical control over any specimen' is EXEMPTED** — you do not need a permit merely to have the plant standing on your land. For **Category 2, every one of those activities including possession 'Permit Required'.** So: (a) *Planting a Cat 1a, 1b or 3 species is a prohibited act under s71A — there is no permit route, it is simply an offence.* (b) *Planting a Cat 2 species without a permit is an offence under s71(1); with a permit it is lawful within the permitted area.* (c) *Having an inherited Cat 1a/1b/3 plant is not itself an offence, but failing to eradicate (1a) / control (1b) / prevent spread (1a, 1b, 3) is.* (d) *Having a Cat 2 plant without a permit is an offence, and reg 4(4) then converts it into a Cat 1b obligation to control it.* DFFE's October 2025 briefing states this bluntly: 'Category 2 species require a permit to remain in place. Without a permit, they become Category 1b species.' Practical short version for app copy: **1a = kill it now; 1b = you must control it, never plant/move/sell it; 2 = permit or it is illegal; 3 = what stands may stand, but you may never plant, propagate, move, sell or give away another one — and if it is in a riparian area it is 1b anyway.**

**IS A PERMIT POSSIBLE?** Only for Category 2 (and for a handful of species-specific Category 2 carve-outs inside 1b/3 listings, e.g. nursery breeding of Duranta erecta, Murraya paniculata and Syngonium podophyllum in named provinces). NEM:BA s71(1): no restricted activity involving a listed invasive species without a permit issued under Chapter 7; s71(2): such a permit 'may be issued only after a prescribed assessment of risks and potential impacts on biodiversity is carried out'. Regulations Chapter 6 (regs 16–19) sets the risk-assessment framework and requires a qualified risk assessment practitioner; Chapter 7 (regs 20–31) governs issuing, conditions, validity, amendment and transfer. Permits are issued by DFFE's Biosecurity issuing authority (application form: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/forms/biodviersity/permitapplication_invasivespeciesregulations.pdf, submissions to AISpermits@environment.gov.za), with provinces consulted. Reg 31: a permit attaches to the land — a landowner may transfer the permit to a new landowner/occupier of the same land, who must notify the issuing authority within 30 days; but a buyer of a *specimen* must obtain their own permit before acquiring it. Reg 32 allows emergency suspension. For a smallholder the honest framing is: a Cat 2 permit is a real but non-trivial process involving a paid risk-assessment practitioner and DFFE turnaround — it is not a form you tick. Between Oct 2014 and Dec 2022 only ~2,906 permits were issued nationally across 268 taxa.

**OFFENCES AND PENALTIES — cite these exactly.** NEM:BA s101(1)(a) makes it an offence to contravene s71(1) (restricted activity without a permit); s101(1)(c) makes it an offence to contravene a directive issued under s73(3). NEM:BA s73(2) imposes three duties on **the owner of land on which a listed invasive species occurs**: (a) notify the relevant competent authority *in writing* of the listed invasive species occurring on that land; (b) take steps to control and eradicate it and prevent it spreading; (c) take all required steps to prevent or minimise harm to biodiversity. s73(3)–(4): a competent authority may issue a written directive and, on failure to comply, implement it and **recover all reasonable costs from the owner**. s74: any person may request the authority to issue such a directive, and may go to court if it refuses — i.e. a neighbour or NGO can force enforcement. s75(1)–(3): control must use methods appropriate to the species and environment, cause least possible harm, and be directed at offspring, propagating material and re-growth. Penalties: regulation 36(1) applies s102 to s101 offences; **regulation 36(2) makes contravention of regs 2(2)–(3), 3(2)–(5), 4(2)–(5), 5(2), 6, 7(1), 7(3), 8, 9, 12(1), 12(4), 17, 18, 24(1), 29, 31(1) and 31(3) an offence carrying a fine not exceeding R5 million (R10 million on a second or subsequent conviction), or imprisonment not exceeding 5 years (10 years on a second conviction), or both.** DFFE reported 114 enforcement notices and R517,000 in fines from 1 April 2024 to Oct 2025, most transgressions being illegal possession, trade, transport and import, concentrated in North West, KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng.

**TWO GENERAL EXEMPTIONS WORTH BUILDING INTO THE APP.** Notice 1 carries five general exemptions, of which two matter to a farm: (1) 'All dead specimens of any listed invasive species are exempted from requiring a Permit for any restricted activity' — so felled wattle, chipped material and dry biomass are outside the permit system. (2) Any person in possession of a listed invasive **plant** being **utilised as biomass** is exempted from needing a permit to convey/move/translocate it and to sell, trade, buy, give, donate or acquire it — conditional on complying with any norms and standards on biomass published under the Act; and a separate exemption covers moving listed invasive plant material for disposal or treatment as waste, subject to disposal norms and standards. This is the legal hook that makes 'clear the wattle, use it for firewood/charcoal/biochar/mulch' lawful. Separately, Notice 2 (s66(1) exempted alien species) exempts alien species legally introduced for **agricultural purposes** and new cultivars/varieties/hybrids of such species — **but expressly 'excluding those which are already listed as invasive'**, so it does not rescue anything on List 1.

**CATEGORY 2 — SPECIES A PERMACULTURE LIST WOULD NAIVELY RECOMMEND (permit required to possess, grow, move or sell; unpermitted = treated as 1b).** *Nitrogen-fixers and fodder:* **Leucaena leucocephala (leucaena) — Category 2, nationwide, no area qualifier** (the single most likely trap in any tropical-permaculture species list); **Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia (old man saltbush) — Category 2** (the standard Karoo/dryland fodder shrub); Acacia mearnsii (black wattle) — 2, exempted for an existing plantation; Acacia decurrens (green wattle) — 2, exempted for an existing plantation; Acacia melanoxylon (Australian blackwood) — 2, exempted for an existing plantation; Acacia dealbata (silver wattle) — 2, no exemption stated. *Fodder/biomass grasses:* **Pennisetum purpureum (elephant/Napier grass) — Category 2** (huge in cut-and-carry fodder and biomass designs); Sorghum halepense (Johnson grass) — 2. *Fruit:* **Rubus fruticosus agg. (European blackberry) — Category 2**, with 'the fruit of the European blackberry is not listed if used for human consumption'; **Psidium guajava (guava) — 2 for plantations in Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West; 3 elsewhere in those same provinces; fruit not listed if used for human consumption; not listed elsewhere**; **Passiflora edulis (purple granadilla) — 2 in Eastern Cape, Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and North-West; not listed in urban areas in those provinces; not listed elsewhere; fruit not listed if used for human consumption**; Hylocereus undatus (dragon fruit / pitahaya) — 2, fruit not listed if used for human consumption. *Other:* **Nasturtium officinale (watercress) — Category 2** (matters for aquaponics/greywater beds); Ricinus communis (castor-oil plant) — 2; Jatropha curcas (physic nut) — 2; Agave sisalana (sisal) — 2; Hypericum perforatum (St John's wort) — 2; Ammophila arenaria (marram grass) — 2 in Western Cape only, not listed elsewhere; Casuarina equisetifolia (horsetail tree) — 2; **Casuarina cunninghamiana (beefwood) — 2, but Category 1b within 100 metres of riparian areas or untransformed land**; Populus alba (white poplar) and Populus × canescens (grey poplar) — 2.

**CATEGORY 2/1b — THE PINE AND EUCALYPT RULES (windbreaks, woodlots, bee forage).** Six Eucalyptus taxa are listed and share one merged rule: **E. camaldulensis, E. cladocalyx, E. conferruminata, E. diversicolor, E. grandis, E. tereticornis.** Rule: (a) **Category 1b within riparian areas, a Protected Area under the Protected Areas Act, or a Listed Ecosystem / ecosystem identified for conservation in a Bioregional Plan or Biodiversity Management Plan**; (b) **not listed within the Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes**, excluding any area in (a); (c) **Category 1b in the Fynbos, Grassland, Savanna, Albany Thicket, Forest and Indian Ocean Coastal Belt biomes, BUT (i) Category 2 for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and the lining of avenues; (ii) not listed within cultivated land at least 50 metres away from untransformed land; (iii) not listed within 50 metres of the main house on a farm; (iv) not listed in urban areas for trees with a diameter over 400 mm at 1000 mm height at the time of publication** — (ii)–(iv) all excluding areas in (a). Exempted for an existing plantation. Pines: Pinus elliottii — 2, exempted for an existing plantation of sterile specimens; P. patula — 2, exempted for an existing plantation; P. roxburghii — 2, exempted for existing plantation; P. taeda — 2, exempted for existing plantation; **P. pinaster and P. radiata — Category 2 for plantations and wind-rows, Category 1b elsewhere**, with a large-tree urban exemption in Cape Town, Overberg and Winelands district councils (circumference over 1.256 m at 1000 mm height as at August 2014) that falls away in riparian areas, in or abutting protected areas, or where ruled a wildfire risk; all smaller specimens are Category 1b. P. canariensis — 3. P. halepensis — 3 in Eastern Cape, Free State and Western Cape; not listed elsewhere. Design consequence: an app can legitimately suggest a eucalypt wind-row or bee-forage block in the right biome *with a Cat 2 permit*, but must hard-block it in riparian zones and protected/listed ecosystems.

**CATEGORY 1b — SPECIES A PERMACULTURE LIST WOULD NAIVELY RECOMMEND (compulsory control; planting/propagating/moving/selling/giving all prohibited, no permit route).** *Nitrogen-fixers and support species:* **Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) — 1b**; **Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust) — 1b**; Albizia lebbeck — 1b; Albizia procera — 1b; **Paraserianthes lophantha (= Albizia lophantha, stink bean) — 1b**; Sesbania punicea (red sesbania) — 1b; Crotalaria agatiflora — 1b; Senna didymobotrya (peanut butter cassia) — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP, WC, not listed elsewhere; Senna septemtrionalis, S. hirsuta, S. occidentalis, S. bicapsularis, S. pendula var. glabrata — all 1b; Calotropis procera — 1b; Mimosa pigra — 1b; Parkinsonia aculeata — 1b; Acacia cyclops (rooikrans), A. saligna (Port Jackson), A. longifolia, A. elata, A. podalyriifolia, A. pycnantha — all 1b. **Prosopis glandulosa var. torreyana and P. velutina (mesquite) — 1b in Eastern Cape, Free State, North-West and Western Cape; Category 3 in Northern Cape; 'the utilisation of the pods for fodder is not listed' in NC, EC, FS, NW and WC; not listed elsewhere.** *Chop-and-drop / biomass:* **Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — 1b** and Tithonia rotundifolia — 1b (Tithonia is a canonical permaculture green-manure plant and is flatly illegal to plant here); **Arundo donax (giant reed) — 1b**; **Canna indica — 1b** (common in greywater reed beds); Solanum mauritianum (bugweed) — 1b; Chromolaena odorata — 1b; Ageratina adenophora and A. riparia — 1b; Montanoa hibiscifolia — 1b; Plectranthus barbatus var. grandis — 1b.

**CATEGORY 1b — FRUIT, HEDGE AND POND SPECIES (continued).** *Fruit and edibles:* **Sambucus nigra (European elder) — 1b** and Sambucus canadensis — 1b (elderflower/elderberry hedgerows are illegal to plant); **Eriobotrya japonica (loquat) — 1b in the Western Cape and the Forest biome; not listed in urban areas in the Western Cape; not listed elsewhere; the fruit is not listed if used for human consumption**; **Opuntia ficus-indica (sweet prickly pear) — 1b, BUT 'spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed', and the fruit is not listed if used for human consumption** (so spineless fodder cactus is lawful — a critical distinction for Karoo systems); Opuntia robusta — 1a, but spineless cultivars and selections not listed; Psidium cattleianum (strawberry guava), P. guineense, P. × durbanensis — 1b; Syzygium cumini (jambolan) — 1b, fruit not listed if used for human consumption; Eugenia uniflora (Surinam cherry) — 1b; Pereskia aculeata (Barbados gooseberry) — 1b; Rubus cuneifolius, R. flagellaris, R. immixtus, R. niveus — 1b (R. ellipticus is 1a); Passiflora caerulea, P. suberosa, P. subpeltata, P. tripartita var. mollissima (banana passionfruit) — 1b; Prunus serotina (black cherry) — 1b; Duchesnea indica — 1b; Malva verticillata — 1b. *Hedges, windbreaks, shade:* **Ligustrum japonicum, L. lucidum, L. ovalifolium, L. sinense, L. vulgare (privets) — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP, NW and WC; Category 3 in Free State, Gauteng and Northern Cape** (sterile cultivars/hybrids of L. ovalifolium not listed); **Pyracantha angustifolia, coccinea, crenatoserrata, crenulata, koidzumii — all 1b**; Cotoneaster franchetii, glaucophyllus, pannosus, salicifolius, simonsii — 1b; **Lantana — 'all seed-producing species or seed-producing hybrids that are non-indigenous to South Africa' — 1b**; **Melia azedarach (syringa) — 1b, Category 3 in urban areas**; **Jacaranda mimosifolia — 1b in Gauteng, KZN, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West, with exemptions for urban areas, for trees over 400 mm diameter within 50 m of the main farmhouse outside riparian areas; not listed elsewhere**; Cinnamomum camphora — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP; 3 in WC; not listed elsewhere; Schinus terebinthifolius (Brazilian pepper) — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP; 3 in FS, GP, NW, NC, WC; Caesalpinia decapetala (Mauritius thorn, a classic living fence) — 1b; Nerium oleander — 1b; Thevetia peruviana — 1b; Tecoma stans — 1b; Ailanthus altissima — 1b; Leptospermum laevigatum — 1b; Pittosporum undulatum — 1b; Melaleuca quinquenervia — 1b; Grevillea banksii — 1b; Hakea drupacea, gibbosa, sericea — 1b, H. salicifolia 1b in WC only; Tamarix aphylla, chinensis, gallica, ramosissima — 1b (explicitly 'not to be confused with indigenous Tamarix usneoides'); Rosa rubiginosa — 1b; Bauhinia purpurea and B. variegata — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP; 3 in FS, GP, NW, NC, WC; Callistemon rigidus — 1b in EC and WC, 3 elsewhere; C. viminalis — 1b in EC, KZN, LP, MP, 3 elsewhere, sterile cultivars not listed. *Ponds, dams and aquaponics — all 1b:* **Azolla filiculoides, A. cristata, A. pinnata subsp. asiatica** (Azolla is widely promoted as duck/fish feed and a nitrogen source), Eichhornia crassipes (water hyacinth), Pistia stratiotes (water lettuce), Salvinia molesta 'and other species of the Family Salviniaceae', S. minima, Myriophyllum aquaticum (parrot's feather), M. spicatum, Egeria densa, Elodea canadensis, Nymphaea mexicana, Pontederia cordata, Echinodorus cordifolius and E. tenellus, Alisma plantago-aquatica. *Ornamental/bee forage that sneaks in:* Verbena bonariensis, V. brasiliensis, V. rigida — 1b; Echium plantagineum and E. vulgare — 1b; Cortaderia jubata and C. selloana (pampas) — 1b; Pennisetum setaceum (fountain grass) — 1b (sterile cultivars not listed); P. villosum — 1b; Vinca major — 1b, V. minor — 1b (sterile cultivars not listed); Tradescantia fluminensis and T. zebrina — 1b; Hedychium coccineum, coronarium, flavescens, gardnerianum (ginger lilies) — 1b; Catharanthus roseus — 1b (sterile cultivars not listed); Nephrolepis cordifolia and N. exaltata — 1b in EC, KZN, MP, LP, WC; 3 in FS, GP, NW, NC.

**CATEGORY 1a — 'eradicate immediately', including several fast-growth/biomass darlings.** **Paulownia tomentosa (empress tree) — 1a** (marketed everywhere as the world's fastest-growing timber/biomass tree); **Pueraria montana var. lobata (kudzu) — 1a** (still recommended as fodder/N-fixer in older permaculture literature); **Equisetum hyemale (rough horsetail / scouring rush) — 1a** (a standard biodynamic preparation and herbal ingredient); Cytisus scoparius (Scotch broom) — 1a; Genista monspessulana (Montpellier broom) — 1a; Ulex europaeus (European gorse) — 1a; Rubus ellipticus (yellow Himalayan raspberry) — 1a; Kunzea ericoides — 1a; Furcraea foetida (Mauritian hemp) — 1a; Triplaris americana — 1a; Fallopia sachalinensis (giant knotweed) — 1a; Acacia adunca, A. fimbriata, A. implexa, A. paradoxa, A. stricta — 1a; Metrosideros excelsa — 1a in the Overstrand District only, not listed elsewhere. Pond species at 1a: Cabomba caroliniana, Hydrilla verticillata, Iris pseudacorus, Lythrum salicaria, Ludwigia peruviana, Nuphar lutea, Nymphoides peltata, Sagittaria platyphylla, Hydrocleys nymphoides, Marsilea mutica. Note the paper record: 'Category 1a taxa are not more invasive than Category 1b taxa' — the split reflects management strategy (national eradication target vs compulsory control), not relative danger, so never present 1a as merely 'worse 1b' in UI copy.

**CATEGORY 3 — the one most likely to be mis-implemented as 'allowed'.** Category 3 means: possession of what already exists is exempted from permit, **but growing/propagating, conveying/moving, selling/buying/giving/donating/accepting, spreading and releasing are all PROHIBITED under s71A(1)** — there is no permit that unlocks them, and reg 5(2) converts any Category 3 plant in a riparian area into Category 1b. Species a permaculture list would plausibly suggest: **Morus alba (white mulberry) — Category 3, with 'the fruit of the white mulberry is not listed if used for human consumption'** (mulberry is a staple of chicken-forage and silvopasture designs — existing trees may stay, but you may not plant, propagate, move or give away another one); **Grevillea robusta (Australian silky oak) — 3**; Grevillea rosmarinifolia — 3; **Tipuana tipu — 3**; Toona ciliata (toon tree) — 3; **Syzygium jambos (rose apple) — 3**; **Solanum betaceum (tree tomato / tamarillo) — 3 in EC, KZN, LP and MP, fruit not listed if used for human consumption in those provinces, not listed elsewhere**; Acacia baileyana — 3; Acer negundo (box elder) — 3, sterile cultivars/hybrids not listed; Acer buergerianum — 3 in EC, KZN, LP, MP, NW, NC, WC but not listed in urban areas there, not listed elsewhere; Celtis australis and C. occidentalis — 3; Fraxinus americana and F. angustifolia — 3 in EC, KZN, LP, MP, WC, not listed elsewhere; Juniperus virginiana — 3 in EC and FS only; Buddleja davidii — 3 (sterile cultivars not listed); B. madagascariensis — 3; Callistemon citrinus — 3; Hedera helix and H. canariensis (ivy) — 3, sterile cultivars not listed; Lonicera japonica 'Halliana' — 3; **Houttuynia cordata (chameleon plant, an edible/medicinal herb) — 3**; Berberis thunbergii — 3, sterile cultivars not listed; Cardiospermum halicacabum — 3; **'Cestrum species not specifically listed' — 3** (a catch-all clause worth encoding); Sasa ramosa (dwarf yellow-striped bamboo) — 3; Rhus glabra — 3; Phytolacca dioica — 3; Pittosporum crassifolium — 3; Myoporum insulare, M. laetum, M. montanum — 3; Alpinia zerumbet — 3; Spathodea campanulata — 3 in EC, KZN, LP, MP; Schefflera arboricola — 3 in EC, KZN, LP, MP; Stachytarpheta cayennensis and S. mutabilis — 3; Tropaeolum speciosum — 3; Wigandia urens var. caracasana — 3; Oenothera sinuosa — 3; Polypodium aureum — 3 in EC, KZN, LP, MP; Agave americana subsp. americana var. expansa — 3 in Western Cape only, not listed elsewhere; Prosopis in the Northern Cape — 3.

**COMMON PERMACULTURE SPECIES THAT ARE *NOT* ON THE 2020 PLANT LIST (verified by alphabetical position in List 1, so these are true absences, not parsing gaps).** Azadirachta indica (neem), Moringa oleifera, Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea), Gliricidia sepium, Chamaecytisus/tagasaste (tree lucerne), Symphytum (comfrey), Helianthus tuberosus (Jerusalem artichoke), Chrysopogon zizanioides (vetiver), Ficus carica (fig), Prunus persica and all Prunus except P. serotina, Citrus, Mangifera, Persea americana (avocado), Carica papaya, Annona, Olea europaea (olive), Bambusa and Phyllostachys (only Sasa ramosa is listed, at Cat 3), and **Salix — no willow of any species appears in the 2020 List 1**. Also important: **Pennisetum clandestinum (kikuyu grass) is Category 1b only 'in Protected Areas and wetlands in which it does not already occur', and is 'not listed elsewhere'** — so the country's most common pasture grass is legal on ordinary farmland. Two cautions before an app declares any of these 'safe': (1) not being NEM:BA-listed is not the same as being non-invasive or lawful — the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 (CARA) declared-weed regime, the National Water Act s22 authorisation regime for plantations/stream-flow-reduction activities, and municipal by-laws all still bite; and (2) DFFE's own 2025 briefing flags unlisted species as risks on other grounds, e.g. weeping willow, English oak, box elder and castor bean as Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer amplifier hosts, and palms and cypresses as unlisted-but-severe fire risks.

**FIVE STRUCTURAL GOTCHAS TO ENCODE, or the app will give wrong answers.** (1) **Category is a function of place, not just species.** Dozens of entries are province-scoped (Ligustrum, Jacaranda, Prosopis, Psidium guajava, Passiflora edulis, Bauhinia, Schinus, Cinnamomum, Callistemon, Nephrolepis, Fraxinus, Juniperus, Acer buergerianum, Senna didymobotrya, Agave americana, Ammophila, Centranthus, Limonium, Hakea salicifolia, Metrosideros, Spathodea, Schefflera, Polypodium, Murraya, Duranta, Syngonium) and several are biome-scoped or feature-scoped (Eucalyptus and Pinus by biome; Casuarina cunninghamiana by distance to riparian/untransformed land; Eriobotrya by Forest biome; Glyceria by protected areas and wetlands). A species-only lookup will be wrong a large fraction of the time. (2) **Riparian override:** reg 5(2) makes any Category 3 plant in a riparian area a Category 1b plant. A design tool that knows where the watercourses are must apply this automatically. (3) **Urban-edge override:** several entries turn on 'urban area', defined in Notice 3 as 'the area within the proclaimed urban edge, as delineated in the Municipal Spatial Development Framework in terms of the Spatial Land Use Management Act, 2013'. (4) **Cultivar-level carve-outs:** 'sterile cultivars or hybrids are not listed' appears against Acer negundo, Ageratum houstonianum, Berberis thunbergii, Callistemon viminalis, Catharanthus roseus, Duranta erecta, Hedera spp., Ligustrum ovalifolium, Murraya paniculata, Nephrolepis exaltata, Pennisetum setaceum and Vinca minor; and 'spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed' for Opuntia ficus-indica and O. robusta; Duranta's 'Sheena's Gold' cultivar is named as not listed. A cultivar-blind lookup will over-flag. (5) **The fruit-for-human-consumption carve-out** exists for white mulberry, loquat, guava, purple granadilla, European blackberry, sweet prickly pear, jambolan, tree tomato and dragon fruit — it exempts *the fruit*, not the tree, so it never makes planting lawful. Finally, a naming rule from Notice 1 itself: 'Where the scientific name of any listed species changes or there is a spelling error in the scientific name, the common name of the species takes precedence and determines whether a particular species is listed or not' — so synonym-matching on binomials alone is legally insufficient.

**ONE WIDELY-REPEATED CLAIM THAT IS NOW WRONG.** Conveyancing and property sites still state that a seller of immovable property must notify the purchaser in writing of listed invasive species on the property. That duty was **regulation 29(3) of the Alien and Invasive Species Regulations, 2014** ('The seller of any immovable property must, prior to the conclusion of the relevant sale agreement, notify the purchaser of that property in writing of the presence of listed invasive species on that property.') — I downloaded and confirmed that text in GN R.598/GG 37885. **Regulation 37 of the 2020 Regulations repealed the 2014 Regulations, and the 2020 Regulations contain no equivalent seller-notification duty** (reg 29 is now 'Return of cancelled permits'; reg 31 covers sale/transfer of specimens and permits only). The surviving statutory duty is NEM:BA s73(2)(a), which runs to the *competent authority*, not the purchaser. Do not reproduce the seller-declaration claim without that caveat. Also worth noting for the app's disclaimer: DFFE's 2025 briefing tells landowners to 'Develop a Control Plan for listed invasive species on properties over one hectare in size' — but there is **no one-hectare threshold anywhere in the 2020 Regulations or Lists** (I grepped both); reg 3(5) makes a Category 1b Control Plan something the Minister *may* require. Present it as departmental guidance, not as a legal threshold.

**AUTHORITATIVE PLACES TO CHECK A SPECIES (all URLs verified live, HTTP 200, on 31 July 2026).** *Legal status — these are the only sources that determine category:* Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726 — https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf (DFFE mirror: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/legislations/nemba_invasivespecieslist_g43726gon1003.pdf). Alien and Invasive Species Regulations 2020, GN R.1020 GG 43735 — https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43735rg11176gon1020.pdf. Commencement/trout-suspension notice GN 115 GG 44182 — https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202102/44182gon115.pdf. NEM:BA Act 10 of 2004 itself (ss 65–77, 101–102) — https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/201409/a10-04.pdf. Watch for amendments at DFFE's gazetted-notices index — https://www.dffe.gov.za/legislation/gazetted_notices — and DFFE acts & regulations — https://www.dffe.gov.za/legislation/actsregulations. Permit application form — https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/forms/biodviersity/permitapplication_invasivespeciesregulations.pdf (AISpermits@environment.gov.za). DFFE's plain-language enforcement briefing, 21 Oct 2025 — https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/nisw25_21Oct25_ais.pdf. *Taxonomy, identity and synonyms:* SANBI Biodiversity Advisor (integrates BODATSA/POSA, ZODATSA, BGIS) — https://biodiversityadvisor.sanbi.org/ ; POSA / BODATSA on BRAHMS Online (names, specimens, distribution) — https://posa.sanbi.org/ ; PlantZAfrica species profiles — https://pza.sanbi.org/ ; SANBI Red List of South African Plants (indigenous conservation status — use this to check whether a *replacement* species is threatened, not to check invasiveness) — https://redlist.sanbi.org/. *Invasion ecology and distribution:* SANBI Invasive Species programme — https://www.sanbi.org/biodiversity/foundations/biodiversity-monitoring-assessment/invasive-species/ ; SAPIA, the Southern African Plant Invaders Atlas at ARC-PPRI — https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/weeds/Pages/Geographical-Distribution-of-IAPs-in-Southern-Africa-%28SAPIA%29.aspx. *Plain-language reference:* Invasive Species South Africa — https://invasives.org.za/ — normally the best lay explainer of the categories, but as of this check the site is displaying a re-launch/maintenance notice and its NEM:BA regulations page returns no content, so it cannot currently be cited or scraped. **Rule for the app: the gazette PDFs are the only authority on category; SANBI/POSA is the authority on identity and synonyms; SAPIA is evidence of spread; nothing else is authoritative.**

ground.summary: Fetched the full primary source — Mucina & Rutherford (eds) 2006, *The Vegetation of South Africa, Lesotho and Swaziland*, Strelitzia 19 (SANBI) — as complete book text plus four individual chapter PDFs (Fynbos, Succulent Karoo, Nama-Karoo, Grassland, Albany Thicket), supplemented by SANBI's PlantZAfrica biome accounts. Every biome chapter in Strelitzia 19 carries a standard climate section and per-vegetation-unit climate diagrams reporting MAP (mean annual precipitation), APCV (annual precipitation coefficient of variation), MAT (mean annual temperature), MFD (mean frost days — days when screen temperature was below 0°C), MAPE (mean annual potential evaporation) and MASMS (mean annual soil moisture stress). I extracted those envelopes for all nine biomes below, with the MFD/MAP ranges computed across all vegetation units where the chapter PDF text layer allowed it. Critical framing caveat from Chapter 3 (Rutherford, Mucina & Powrie): biome-level climate figures are "averaged over the entire area of the biome and, therefore, representing only a central tendency" — they are not per-site filters, and the authors explicitly note that climate alone does not determine biome boundaries (fire and soils do a lot of the work, particularly at the Fynbos/Succulent Karoo and Savanna/Grassland interfaces). The single most farm-relevant divergence is Fynbos: Strelitzia 19 states outright that "the low nutrient status of fynbos makes the soils unsuitable for agriculture."
points: METHODOLOGY / WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN. Strelitzia 19 defines its climate-diagram abbreviations identically in every chapter: MAP = Mean Annual Precipitation; APCV = Annual Precipitation Coefficient of Variation; MAT = Mean Annual Temperature; MFD = Mean Frost Days, defined precisely as 'days when screen temperature was below 0°C'; MAPE = Mean Annual Potential Evaporation; MASMS = Mean Annual Soil Moisture Stress, '% of days when evaporative demand was more than double the soil moisture supply'. MFD is therefore a screen-temperature statistic, NOT a ground-frost or radiation-frost count — real ground frost in a valley bottom will exceed the MFD figure, which matters for siting frost-tender crops. The climatic variables the authors found most diagnostic when they ran a CART classification of the biomes were: mean minimum temperature of the coldest month (Tmin), heat units (HtUnt), annual mean evaporation (Evap), and soil moisture days in winter (SMDW) and summer (SMDS) — note that raw annual rainfall is NOT among them. Forests were excluded from that analysis 'owing to their highly fragmented and widely dispersed nature', and Albany Thicket was the worst-predicted biome (<66% of its area predicted correctly from climate), which is the authors' own admission that thicket is a fire/substrate phenomenon more than a climate one.

SAVANNA. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.9 — 'MAP varies from less than 200 mm in the west in southern Gordonia Duneveld to about 1 350 mm at the highest altitude parts of Swaziland Sour Bushveld in the east. Outside the Kalahari areas, most of the savanna experiences a MAP of between 500 mm and 750 mm.' SANBI PlantZAfrica gives 235–1 000 mm. Season: strong summer / summer rainfall (Bailey 1979), sharply unimodal — 'most of the area in South Africa receiving less than 5 mm of rain in each of the months of June, July and August'. Rainfall concentration index peaks above 65% in Kalahari Duneveld and northern Central Bushveld/Mopane. APCV: >35% in the dry west, <25% in the mesic east. FROST — this is the hard internal split: 'Only lower-lying parts of the Mopane, Lowveld and Sub-Escarpment Savanna Bioregions can be regarded as frost-free.' At the other extreme, 'the Ghaap Plateau shows the longest period in the year when frosts can occur (>120 days)', with mean daily July minimum dropping below 0°C on the highveld (southern edge of Central Bushveld) and high-altitude Eastern Kalahari Bushveld; average heavy-frost dates run earliest (May) to latest (September) in those two areas. PlantZAfrica: 'frost may occur from 0 to 120 days per year.' Temperature: MAT ~16°C on parts of the highveld to >22°C in lower Lowveld; mean daily max for February rarely below 26°C, >32°C in Kalahari; summer heat units mostly >2 200 degree-days (Oct–Mar, base 10°C). Altitude mostly below 1 500 m, extending to 1 800 m. OTHER HARD FILTERS: soils split the biome into Huntley's (1982) moist/dystrophic (broad-leaved) vs arid/eutrophic (fine-leaved) savanna. Fire is near-annual and structural — PlantZAfrica notes 'less than 10% of plants... killed by fire' with resprouting from stem bases. Soil physical properties dominate in the dry west: 'Under extreme conditions of a high evapotranspiration and low annual rainfall (e.g. Kalahari), deep soils are needed for the trees and shrubs to survive'; duplex soils with a prismacutanic B-horizon and swelling clays both flip the system to grass dominance regardless of climate. FARM DIVERGENCE: the 0-to-120-frost-day span means 'Savanna' is useless as a single crop-palette unit — a frost-free Lowveld site takes bananas, mango, papaya and cassava, while a Ghaap Plateau or highveld-margin savanna site at >120 frost days takes none of them. Split any farm palette by bioregion, not biome. Second divergence: dystrophic broad-leaved savanna soils are genuinely nutrient-poor (the Nylsvley literature) and will need P and N for annual crops, whereas eutrophic fine-leaved savanna on basalt/dolerite is naturally fertile but often on cracking clays with seasonal root pruning — bad for perennials, fine for annual grains.

GRASSLAND. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.8 — 'The rainfall may vary spatially from 400–2 500 mm per year' (the 2 500 mm figure is the high-altitude Drakensberg; the chapter elsewhere notes 'MAP as high as 2 500 mm in places!'). Across the individual vegetation-unit climate diagrams I extracted, MAP runs 391–1 451 mm. Season: 'summer to strong summer rainfall and winter drought' — winter is the dry season, unlike Fynbos. FROST: 'Frost is a common phenomenon; the coldest periods (June–August) are exacerbated by aridity or along an increasing elevation gradient.' Across the unit climate diagrams, MFD runs 11–158 days depending on which units you count (2–158 including outliers); Gd 8 Lesotho Highland Basalt Grassland is the cold extreme at MAP 707 mm, MAT 9.6°C, MFD 96 days; Gd 7 uKhahlamba Basalt Grassland at MAP 1 234 mm, MAT 11.6°C, MFD 55 days; Gd 1 Amathole Montane Grassland at MAP 672 mm, MAT 14.7°C, MFD 25 days. Elevation 300–3 482 m (Thabana Ntlenyana). Snow-bound in winter at the top end. The chapter is explicit that the Grassland/Savanna boundary is partly a cold boundary: sub-escarpment grasslands persist because 'streams of cold air that descend from the Drakensberg... create severe climatic conditions that support frost-tolerant grasslands rather than savanna vegetation'. OTHER HARD FILTERS: the sourveld/sweetveld split is the single most useful farm variable. 'The division between dry and moist grassland can be made on the basis of annual rainfall, with 500–700 mm rainfall marking the boundary... Above 600 mm of rainfall, sour andropogonoid grasses predominate, whereas below 600 mm sweet chloridoid grasses are more common.' Crucially the chapter ties this to soil chemistry, not just rain: 'plant growth in moist grasslands with dystrophic soils is mostly macronutrient-limited and in dry grasslands with eutrophic soils it is mostly water-limited.' Moist grassland = sour grasses, leached dystrophic soils, high fire frequency; dry grassland = sweet palatable grasses, less leached eutrophic soils, lower fire frequency. Fire is obligatory for structure — 'without fire most of the eastern half of South Africa would be covered in trees' — and the biome has high lightning flash density. FARM DIVERGENCE: above ~600 mm you are on acid, leached, macronutrient-poor soil and must lime and fertilise; below ~600 mm you have decent base status but are water-limited, so irrigation and water harvesting outrank soil amendment. The frost regime (up to 158 days, MAT down to 9.6°C) rules out essentially the whole subtropical fruit list at altitude — this is deciduous/temperate territory (apples, pears, stone fruit, brassicas, potatoes, cold-hardy alliums), the opposite of the Savanna palette despite both being summer-rainfall.

FYNBOS. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.4 — 'Mean annual precipitation (MAP) averaged over the total area of the Fynbos Biome is about 480 mm. This is highest for the fynbos (FF units) at about 540 mm, followed by 370 mm for renosterveld (FR units), and 350 mm for strandveld (FS units).' Across individual vegetation-unit climate diagrams, MAP runs 106–1 384 mm; APCV 18–39%; MAT 10.1–17.6°C. PlantZAfrica: 'Below 200 mm Fynbos is replaced by Succulent Karoo.' The chapter's own boundary statement for the renosterveld component: at drier extremes 'usually below 250–300 mm' it is replaced by succulent karoo shrublands, and in wetter areas 'usually over 500–800 mm' by fynbos. Season: winter or even (non-seasonal) rainfall on the Bailey (1979) scheme. 'Strong winter rainfall' (≥80% Apr–Sep) is limited to a West Coast section around Saldanha and St Helena Bay; the 'winter' class is 60–79%; 'even' 40–59% covers much of the southern Cape; a few easternmost fynbos islands sit marginally in the 'summer' class (20–39%). Coefficient of variation <20% on southwestern mountains to >35% in the northern western coastal belt. FOG is a real and under-counted water source: 'Over 500 mm of water may be precipitated per year from wet stratus cloud without being recorded in standard rain gauges', and Schulze reports >600 mm p.a. of orographic fog moisture in the Jonkershoek Mountains. FROST: 'The lowlands near the coast are generally frost-free. However, frost does occur on higher-lying regions and towards the interior. Thus, for example, the average number of days with heavy frost (screen minimum temperature < 0°C) is 0.3 for Paarl, 3 for Riversdale, 12 for Grabouw, 14 for Ceres and 93 for Sutherland.' Unit-level MFD across the chapter's climate diagrams runs 1–62 days. Snowfalls on higher southwestern mountains at ~5.4 falls/year peaking late July; snowline seldom below 1 000 m; drifts >1 m on high plateaus with cover persisting two weeks or more; snow can fall into December. Extrapolated summit minima: −8.9°C (Matroosberg, 2 249 m) and −12.2°C (Seweweekspoort Peak, 2 325 m) for July. Heat extreme: 46.1°C recorded at Clanwilliam. SOILS — THE DEFINING FILTER: quartzitic mountain sandstones (Peninsula, Nardouw, Witteberg) 'weather slowly and generally give rise to stony, very sandy soils with a clay content of less than 5% and extremely low levels of free iron oxides.' Podzol B-horizon soils are 'usually extremely acid with pH values as low as 3.5–4.0'; Witfontein-form wet soils are 'extremely acid with pH(CaCl2) values usually of < 4.0 and base saturation of ≤ 20% at pH 8'; Fernwood/Clovelly soils in the Redelinghuys area at 250 mm rainfall are 'extremely acid (pH of < 4.5) with a low base status'. FIRE: 'Fire in fynbos burns on a 5–50-year rotation, usually in the order of 15–25 years' with natural fires in late summer/early autumn; renosterveld burns far more often (2–10 years, or 3–5 years per Moll et al.). Below a ~5-year interval serotinous species fail ('Serotiny requires predictable fire-return times at greater than 5-year fire intervals'); above 30–50 years 'fynbos cannot exist'. PlantZAfrica gives the management window as 6–45 years. SALT/WIND: soils near the West Coast are less leached than equivalents inland partly because of 'the salty sea mist which is common along the West Coast'; strandveld sits on the coastal hinterland but 'never in habitats under direct influence of sea spray'. FARM DIVERGENCE — THIS IS THE BIG ONE. Strelitzia 19 says it flatly: 'The low nutrient status of fynbos makes the soils unsuitable for agriculture, although with modern methods of fertilisation via watering this is no longer true. A characteristic of fynbos is the low number and biomass of animals... Carrying capacity for fynbos is generally lower than 1 small stock unit per 8 ha.' A food-crop palette on fynbos sandstone soils is not a plant-selection problem, it is a soil-construction problem: <5% clay, pH 3.5–4.5, near-zero base saturation, no nutrient buffer. You are building beds (imported topsoil, compost, lime, rock phosphate) rather than amending in place. The reciprocal risk is equally hard: the dominant wild families (Proteaceae, Restionaceae, Cyperaceae) 'are characterised by not having fungal associates to extract nutrients from the soil. Instead they have, respectively, proteoid and caudiform rootlets' — cluster roots evolved for extreme P scarcity, which are killed by phosphate fertilisation. So a fynbos-site farm plan must physically separate fertilised production beds from any retained indigenous vegetation, and keep fertiliser runoff off it (the chapter flags 'Fertiliser runoff also has a major influence'). Note also the near-total absence of annuals in fynbos, attributed by Wisheu et al. (2000) to soils too infertile for an annual to complete its life cycle and set seed in one season — an unusually direct warning about annual vegetable cropping. Renosterveld and strandveld soils (clay-rich, granite/dolerite-derived, more base-rich) are the exception and are where the historical agriculture actually went — 'converted to vineyards, fruit orchards'.

SUCCULENT KAROO. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.5 — 'The Mean Annual Precipitation (MAP) for most of the units is between 100 and 200 mm... The overall biome average is about 170 mm.' Richtersveld units adjoining the Namib/Gariep, part of Tanqua Karoo and some west coast units fall below 100 mm; most Little Karoo rainshadow valley units exceed 200 mm, with Robertson Karoo (SKv 7) the wettest at 'almost 300 mm'. PlantZAfrica gives 20–290 mm. Bioregion examples: Namaqualand Hardeveld MAP 150 mm / APCV 38% / MAT 16.7°C / MFD 9 d / MAPE 2 544 mm / MASMS 81%; Trans-Escarpment Succulent Karoo MAP 191 mm / MAT 15.9°C / MFD 35 d; Rainshadow Valley Karoo MAP 209 mm / MAT 16.6°C / MFD 19 d. Season: 'a typical unimodal winter-rainfall region' for Namaqualand and the western Great Escarpment; the greater Little Karoo shows all-year (SKv 8–11) or bimodal equinoctial (SKv 12–14) regimes. Summer Aridity Index >4.8 (Rutherford & Westfall 1986). Rainfall is cyclonic, 'mostly gentle showers' with low kinetic energy, and notably RELIABLE — 'relatively high predictability' and 'prolonged droughts are very rare', which the authors credit for the biome's species richness. Hailstorms are rare (relevant: succulents are 'extremely sensitive to mechanical damage'). FOG AND DEW are a real water input: coastal fog along the Namaqualand coast and west-facing escarpment, plus 'copious dewfalls which may occur all year round'. FROST: 'The occurrence of frost is apparently a function of the distance from the sea (continentality) and altitude. In the low-lying coastal regions (Sandveld, western Richtersveld and Knersvlakte) frost is a rare phenomenon, while along the Namaqualand escarpment frost may occur 7 to 13 days per year. The vegetation units found in deep valleys surrounded by high mountain ranges can have frost most often (mainly due to thermal inversion)—15 to 30 days per year. The units found on the continental plateau beyond the escarpment also have a high incidence of frost (20–25 days per year), with SKt 3 Roggeveld Karoo again a notable exception reaching almost 60 frost days per year.' HEAT: MAT 16.8°C biome-wide (most units 16–18°C; high-elevation Roggeveld only 14.5°C); 'Absolute temperature values greater than 44°C have been recorded in low-lying coastal regions' during catabatic berg winds, an autumn phenomenon that 'can persist for several days'. PlantZAfrica adds temperatures 'in excess of 40°C are common' in summer. Shortest summers of any biome (<198 days). Highest summer incoming radiation of any biome (270–280 J m⁻² day⁻¹). Soils: 'lime-rich, weakly developed soils on rock' (PlantZAfrica). Fire: effectively absent (insufficient fuel; succulent-dominated). FARM DIVERGENCE: the wild flora is a WINTER-growing, summer-dormant succulent flora — exactly inverted from the summer-cropping rhythm most South African farm advice assumes. A rain-fed food palette here is close to impossible at 100–200 mm; the honest farm design is winter-season cropping under irrigation or heavy water harvesting, with the rainfall's high predictability (unusual for an arid zone) being the one genuine asset to exploit. MAPE ~2 400–2 550 mm against MAP ~170 mm is a ~15:1 evaporation-to-rainfall ratio — shade, mulch and windbreaks are not aesthetic choices. The 44°C berg-wind events and the 60-frost-day Roggeveld exception both fall outside what 'mild maritime semi-desert' would lead you to plan for.

NAMA-KAROO. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.7 — 'MAP ranges from around 70 mm bordering the Desert Biome in the northwest to around 500 mm in the southeast.' PlantZAfrica gives 100–520 mm. Across the unit climate diagrams I extracted, MAP runs 103–384 mm. Season: 'Most rain falls in late summer (December to April)', with rainfall peaking in MARCH in all vegetation types. 'The low rainfall is unreliable (coefficient of variation of annual rainfall up to 40%) and droughts are unpredictable and sometimes prolonged.' Unit APCV values 35–38%. Rain is convective — 'highly localised, intense and short thunderstorms' — which is why erosion is the standing problem: 'Although less than 5% of rain reaches the rivers, the high erodibility of soils poses a major problem where overgrazing occurs' (PlantZAfrica). FROST: 'Frost occurs in all areas except in the extreme southeast of the biome (Albany Broken Veld) in winter.' Unit-level MFD runs 5–52 days (examples: NKb 2 Blouputs MFD 48 d, NKu 2 Upper Karoo Hardeveld MFD 46 d, NKu 3 Northern Upper Karoo MFD 37 d, NKu 4 Eastern Upper Karoo MFD 52 d, NKl 1 Gamka Karoo MFD 27 d). 'Winters cold (mean July minimum close to zero in the Upper Karoo vegetation types). Temperature extremes range from −5°C in winter to 43°C in summer.' MAT of units ~14.7–16.5°C; MAPE 2 360–2 615 mm; MASMS 82–84%. THE DECISIVE FARM CONSTRAINT is stated explicitly and is easy to miss: 'Rainfall peaks in March in all the vegetation types of Nama-Karoo, and this, together with the onset of frost soon afterwards in the higher-altitude areas, can provide a very short growth season for frost-sensitive species. For example, in the Western Upper Karoo, where very little rainfall is expected in the warm season before March, the average first date of heavy frost is in the first half of May (or even late April in the extreme south). The shortness of the growing season is further exacerbated in some years when rains arrive even later than usual or frost occurs earlier than average or, most seriously, when both of these occur in the same year.' Soils: 'over 80% of the area is covered by a lime-rich, weakly developed soil over rock'; 'generally base-rich, weakly structured and skeletal'; most soils south/north of the Great Escarpment 'shallow (<300 mm)'; duplex soils dominant around Hanover eastwards; dune sands in the Koa River Valley are 'deep, uniform, coarse-textured sand poor in plant nutrients' while interdune Bushmanland soils on dorbanks/calcretes are 'of high nutrient status'; Bushmanland-to-Prieska duribank soils 'may be high in most plant nutrients, especially potassium'. Fire: essentially absent — 'The amount and nature of the fuel load is insufficient to carry fires and fires are rare within the biome' (PlantZAfrica). Altitude 600–2 000 m (most 1 000–1 400 m). FARM DIVERGENCE: the wild vegetation is a drought-deciduous dwarf shrubland whose C4 grasses and shrubs simply go dormant between rain events — a strategy no annual crop can copy. The rain-then-frost pinch means the effective frost-free growing window barely overlaps the wet window: you get moisture in March and killing frost by late April/early May. Any Nama-Karoo food palette therefore needs either (a) very short-season frost-sensitive crops planted precisely, (b) frost-hardy winter crops with supplementary irrigation, or (c) perennial deep-rooted stock, and the base-rich shallow soils mean the limitation is water and rooting depth, not fertility — the opposite prescription to Fynbos. Soil erodibility under overgrazing is the primary degradation risk, so ground cover and stocking discipline outrank soil amendment.

DESERT. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.6 — 'By definition, the area is one of extreme aridity with a MAP generally below 70 mm.' PlantZAfrica: 'Mean annual rainfall is from approximately 10 mm in the west, to 70 or 80 mm on the inland margin of the desert', and 'The rainfall is highly variable from year to year.' Season — the biome is internally SPLIT: the western Southern Namib gets winter cyclonic rain (Alexander Bay: MAP ~50 mm, winter peak, MAT 17.2°C, CV 43%) while the eastern Gariep Desert gets late-summer convective rain (Goodhouse: MAP ~50 mm, late-summer peak, MAT 23.3°C, CV >65%). The authors stress the qualitative difference: 'the softer rain and drizzle of the cyclonic precipitation are much more effective for plant growth, when compared to the intense rainstorms which often generate runoff and formation of sheet washes. Also, the lower temperatures that prevail during the rain season greatly reduce evaporation compared to the high evaporation in the high temperature rain season in the east.' Temperature: 'The Gariep Desert is the hottest area within the whole of southern Africa'; summer-maximum difference between the two stations is about 15°C. FROST: 'Frost is not of any importance for the desert units close to the coast and at low altitudes further inland, while some frost occurs on higher mountain peaks, especially in the eastern units.' FOG: advective Benguela fog is 'the most important additional source of water for plants in the coastal Namib Desert', felt 'as deep as 100 km inland'; wind-driven low cloud on seaward hills 'can also significantly precipitate water directly on to plants'. Perennial plants concentrate 'in specialized habitats associated with local concentrations of water' — drainage lines and washes. FARM DIVERGENCE: there is no rain-fed farm palette at 10–70 mm MAP. The wild vegetation's strategies — fog harvesting, ephemeral annual grass flushes after wet years, seed banks that sit dormant through dry years, and perennials restricted to washes — are none of them croppable. A Desert-biome farm design is an irrigation-and-microcatchment design sited on drainage lines, and the west/east split matters: the winter-rain western half is far more forgiving of cool-season production than the summer-rain Gariep half, where a 23.3°C MAT and extreme evaporation during the rain season means almost all incident rain is lost.

ALBANY THICKET. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.10 — 'Albany Thicket is found in semi-arid areas of the Eastern and Western Cape, with 200–950 mm MAP (Vlok & Euston-Brown 2002).' Across the unit climate diagrams, MAP runs 259–677 mm (examples: AT 1 Southern Cape Valley Thicket 399 mm, AT 2 Gamka Thicket 267 mm, AT 3 Groot Thicket 299 mm, AT 5 Sundays Noorsveld 267 mm, AT 9 Albany Coastal Belt 677 mm, AT 10 Great Fish Noorsveld 420 mm, AT 11 Great Fish Thicket 449 mm, AT 12 Buffels Thicket 655 mm, AT 13 Eastern Cape Escarpment Thicket 520 mm, AT 14 Camdebo Escarpment Thicket 352 mm). SEASON — the distinguishing feature: 'Two prevailing climate systems (all-year rainfall to the southwest and summer rainfall to the northeast) converge in the region, resulting in all-year rainfall, with spring and autumn maxima. All the Thicket vegetation units have nonseasonal rainfall.' MAP overall ~400 mm with a west-to-east gradient from ~340 mm (Swellendam) to ~940 mm (Wilderness), and driest months December–February. APCV 27–36% inland, 'usually lower than 30%' near the coast. FROST: 'the region experiences high temperatures in summer (exceeding 40°C on occasion) and low temperatures with frost (0 to 64 days) in winter' inland; near the coast 'the number of days of frost fewer than 10 per year'. Unit-mean MFD across the diagrams runs 2–25 days (AT 1: 3 d, AT 2: 3 d, AT 9: 2 d, AT 10: 3 d, AT 11: 7 d, AT 12: 2 d, AT 3: 19 d). Individual unit descriptions in the chapter give the within-unit spread, e.g. 'the incidence of frost is only 3 days, but ranges from 0 days at the coast to more than 17 days of frost per year inland'. MAT ~17°C, i.e. warm-temperate (unit values 16.7–18.2°C). MAPE 1 695–2 396 mm; MASMS 72–81%. FIRE — the defining non-climatic filter: thicket 'does not support a regular or widespread fire regime' and a 'high degree of succulence has largely excluded fire from Albany Thicket (Kerley et al. 1995)'. Chapter 10 argues explicitly that 'the climate in itself is not the primary selective force for thicket patterns, but rather the fire regimes that are determined by seasonal precipitation', with the evidence being thicket outliers surviving in fire refugia inside both the winter- and summer-rainfall zones. Growth strategy: 'slow growth', 'low annual production, thus giving a false impression of the amount of forage available for animal production'. Geology is Cape Fold Belt sandstone/quartzite plus Karoo Supergroup sediments, Enon conglomerate and dolerite. FARM DIVERGENCE: this is the most farm-friendly rainfall regime in the semi-arid half of the country, because non-seasonal rain with spring and autumn maxima gives two planting windows rather than one, and low coastal frost (<10 days) plus a 17°C MAT means a genuinely long season. Two cautions. First, the 'low annual production / false impression of forage' line is the chapter's own warning that thicket biomass massively overstates carrying capacity — stocking rates set by eyeballing standing biomass will degrade the system, which is exactly the mechanism behind historical spekboom-thicket collapse. Second, being a fire-free system, thicket has no fire-adapted regeneration to fall back on; a farm palette here should not import fire as a management tool, and the fire-free status is itself an asset (no burn cycles to plan around) that distinguishes farm planning here from Fynbos, Grassland and Savanna.

INDIAN OCEAN COASTAL BELT. Rainfall: Strelitzia 19 Ch.11 — 'In the KwaZulu-Natal part of the IOCB the mean annual rainfall ranges between 1 272 and 819 mm (Camp 1999b), while on the Eastern Cape coast the mean annual rainfall reaches 1 120 mm at Cape Hermes (Port St Johns) and 1 128 mm at Bashee Lighthouse.' Unit MAPs: CB 1 Maputaland Coastal Belt 933 mm, CB 2 Maputaland Wooded Grassland 964 mm, CB 3 KwaZulu-Natal Coastal Belt 989 mm, CB 4 Pondoland-Ugu Sandstone Coastal Sourveld 1 075 mm, CB 5 Transkei Coastal Belt 1 015 mm. The inland gradient is brutally steep: 'especially in Maputaland, with around 1 200 mm on the coast, while about 60 km inland (Ndumo in the Savanna Biome) only about 60% of this amount occurs.' Season: 'The northern regions of the IOCB, close to the coast, have marginally nonseasonal (even) rainfall, with precipitation concentrated in summer. Richards Bay and St Lucia both have 41.6% of their annual mean rainfall in winter. There are approximately 14 rain days in June and July.' Winter-rainfall proportions run 27.6–36.6% down the coast (Empangeni 35.6%, Mount Edgecombe 30.9%, Pinetown 27.6%, Port Shepstone 31.8%, Cape Hermes 32.7%, Bashee 36.6%) — i.e. NO real dry season. RELIABILITY: APCV 18–21% across units, the LOWEST of any South African biome — Chapter 3 confirms 'The coefficient of variation in annual precipitation is the lowest in the IOCB'. FROST: effectively zero. Unit MFD values are 0 d (CB 1, CB 2, CB 3) and 1 d (CB 4). The chapter: 'Summers are hot to very hot, while winters are mild, with hardly any frost (higher in the southernmost parts and then only mild).' Chapter 3: 'The number of frost days per year varies from zero in the IOCB to a maximum in the Grassland Biome.' Temperature: MAT 19.1°C (Bashee, southwest) to ~22°C (Mozambique border); i.e. a narrow, warm band. Evaporation is the lowest of any biome — MAPE 1 549–1 904 mm, and Chapter 3 notes 'The mean annual potential evaporation is the lowest for the IOCB'. Humidity high, 'may reach saturation point'; relative humidity at 14:00 at Richards Bay 59–72%. WIND/CYCLONES: 'rain-bearing southern and southwestern winds, eastern afternoon sea-breezes, and autumn anticyclonic föhns'; wind run ~160 km/day at Empangeni; 'Cyclones originating over the Indian Ocean occasionally hit the region from the northeast, causing major climatic and hydrological havoc, for example the 1984 cyclone called Domoina.' SOILS: on the Msikaba and Natal Sandstones, 'the soils developing over both Msikaba and Natal Sandstones are sandy, highly leached, acidic and mostly very shallow', with frequent rock outcrops; on the Maputaland/Zululand dune cordons, 'Dystric regosols (formed by well-drained and acidic sands) are formed on elevated slopes and crests of the dune cordons. Humic gleysols (wet, acidic sands with abnormal accumulation of organic matter) are found in depressions'; the coastal dune cordons themselves are 'calcareous young Quaternary sands'. FARM DIVERGENCE: on climate alone this is the best rain-fed envelope in South Africa — 819–1 272 mm, zero frost, lowest rainfall variability, lowest evaporation, no true dry season. The constraint is entirely edaphic and mechanical. The sandy leached acidic soils have almost no nutrient- or water-holding capacity despite the high rainfall, so a farm palette needs organic-matter building and liming even though rainfall looks generous — high rainfall on leached sand means nutrients wash straight through. Depressions with humic gleysols are waterlogged and acidic (drainage problem, not a fertility problem). Immediately behind the beach the sands turn calcareous — a pH inversion within a few hundred metres. Add salt-laden onshore wind and periodic cyclone damage, and windbreaks plus perennial cover matter more here than irrigation. The wild vegetation's answer is closed forest with tight internal nutrient cycling; a farm palette that clears that canopy inherits bare leached sand and must replace the cycling deliberately.

FOREST (Afrotemperate, Subtropical and Azonal Forests). Rainfall thresholds: Strelitzia 19 Ch.12 — 'Forest persists in areas with mean annual rainfall >525 mm with strong winter rainfall and >725 mm with strong summer rainfall (Rutherford & Westfall 1986, Geldenhuys 1991).'
