Note carefully: the thresholds attach to STRONG winter / STRONG summer rainfall regimes, i.e. the summer-rainfall threshold is higher because summer rain is lost to evaporation. The authors add that 'a summer aridity index may be a better predictor of forest distribution than rainfall per se'. Unit MAPs from the climate diagrams: FOz 1 Southern Afrotemperate Forest 863 mm (APCV 22%, MAT 16.7°C, MAPE 1 647 mm); FOz 3 Southern Mistbelt Forest 988 mm (APCV 20%, MAT 15.7°C, MAPE 1 674 mm); FOz 5 Scarp Forest 1 030 mm (APCV 19%); FOa 1 Lowveld Riverine Forest 532 mm (APCV 30%, MAPE 2 115 mm). Note the forest climate diagrams in Strelitzia 19 report MAP, APCV, MAT and MAPE but NOT MFD — the frost criterion comes from SANBI's PlantZAfrica account: forests are 'restricted to frost-free areas'. WATER, NOT JUST RAIN: 'Forest is limited to regions with high water availability... the water availability to forest vegetation is a function of amount of precipitation (rainfall and mist), evapo-transpiration, availability of groundwater and, in addition, soil structure and seasonality of precipitation.' Mist precipitation 'supplements the rainfall considerably' along the Great Escarpment. Riverine and kloof forests break the rainfall envelope entirely by using groundwater, flood water and 'deep gorges with low solar irradiation, hence lower evaporation'. Geldenhuys (1991) recorded southern Cape forests across 500 mm (Great Brak River) to 1 200 mm (Jonkersberg, Diepwalle, Storms River). Temperature: max ~30°C mean-hottest-month and MAT 22°C on the KZN north coast, decreasing southwest to a mean max of 25°C in the Knysna afrotemperate forests. FIRE: forests 'rarely burn, mainly due to the high humidity' (PlantZAfrica), though fires occur under extreme berg-wind conditions; internal disturbance is gap dynamics at 0.005–0.5 ha scale. Patch size is tiny — 'few of which cover areas greater than 1 km²'; the biome is <0.25% of southern Africa's surface, the smallest on the subcontinent, and despite that has the third-longest boundary with other biomes (a measure of its fragmentation). SOILS — the key management fact: 'The high rainfall in areas supporting forests has major effects on forest soils. It causes waterlogged conditions in clayey soils and leaches the soluble nutrients deeper into the soil. The result is that the trees develop very shallow root systems... roots are confined to the top 30 cm of the soil. A dense mat of fine, feeder roots concentrates in the upper 10 cm of the soil... The main function of the feeder roots is to absorb nutrients from decomposing litter in the upper part of the soil profile. Disturbance of the root and litter layers will have significant negative effects on forest nutrition... The trees are also particularly sensitive to poor soil aeration caused by standing water resulting from disturbance of the natural drainage patterns and from soil compaction.' FARM DIVERGENCE: forest sites read as the most fertile land on a farm and are not — the fertility is in a 10 cm litter-and-feeder-root mat, not in the soil profile, which is leached and often waterlogged below. Clearing or cultivating destroys the entire nutrient capital in one pass. For an agroforestry or forest-margin palette the operational rules are: do not till, do not compact (vehicle traffic and livestock trampling are direct threats via aeration), do not alter drainage, and build shade-tolerant understorey production on top of the existing litter layer rather than into the soil. The 525/725 mm thresholds are useful in the other direction too — they tell you where a forest-style multistorey system is climatically plausible at all, and the kloof/riverine exception tells you that a sheltered gorge or a groundwater-fed site can carry a forest palette several hundred millimetres below the nominal threshold.

CROSS-CUTTING FARM-PALETTE NOTES. (1) The wild-vegetation climate envelope is a SURVIVAL envelope for stress-adapted perennials with deep roots, dormancy strategies and decade-scale time horizons; a food-crop palette needs a PRODUCTION envelope, which is consistently narrower. Nama-Karoo is the cleanest illustration: the biome supports vegetation across 70–500 mm, but the chapter's own arithmetic (March rain peak, first heavy frost late April/early May) leaves almost no frost-free wet window for a frost-sensitive annual. (2) Where the wild flora is nutrient-limited (Fynbos, moist Grassland, IOCB sands, Forest), fertility must be imported or built and the constraint is chemical; where it is water-limited (Succulent Karoo, Nama-Karoo, Desert, dry Grassland, western Savanna), soils are usually base-rich and shallow and the constraint is water plus rooting depth. These need opposite interventions, and Grassland contains both — the ~600 mm sourveld/sweetveld line is the switch. (3) Evaporation, not rainfall, is what separates several of these biomes: MAPE runs ~1 550–1 900 mm in the IOCB against ~2 400–2 600 mm in the Succulent Karoo and Nama-Karoo. Two sites with identical MAP in different biomes are not equivalent farms. MASMS (the % of days when evaporative demand exceeds double the soil moisture supply) sits at 80–84% in the karoos versus 63–68% in the IOCB. (4) Fire status is a design input, not just an ecological fact. Fynbos and Grassland REQUIRE fire (fynbos 5–50 yr, usually 15–25 yr; renosterveld 2–10 yr; grassland frequent), so a farm on those biomes has to plan firebreaks and accept periodic burns on retained vegetation. Albany Thicket, Forest, Succulent Karoo, Nama-Karoo and Desert are effectively fire-free, so importing fire management there is actively destructive. Savanna sits in between and uses fire as a bush-encroachment or browse-height tool. (5) The single hardest constraint to design around is frost-day count, because it varies more within biomes than between them: Savanna spans 0 to >120 days, Grassland 11–158, Albany Thicket 0–64, Fynbos 0.3–93, Succulent Karoo ~0–60, Nama-Karoo 5–52, while IOCB is 0–1 and Forest is by definition frost-free. Any farm-scale palette should be driven by the site's own frost-day figure and bioregion, with the biome used only as a first filter. (6) The authors themselves warn against over-reading the climate envelope: Agenbach et al.'s reciprocal transplants across the Fynbos/Succulent Karoo boundary found 'at least some Fynbos species were environmentally (including soils) limited, whereas at least some Karoo species may be limited in their distribution by fire and biotic interactions and not by their environment', concluding that 'climate is not the sole determinant of vegetation distribution'.

ground.summary: Researched SA growing ranges for 16 exotic food-tree crops using ARC's Climate-Smart Agriculture subtropical module, SANBI horticultural zones, Hortgro (climate + 2021 tree census), CGA Key Industry Statistics 2025, SAAGA and SAMGA 2024 tree censuses, SAPPA, and SA Olive. Three gates decide SA reach in this order: (1) winter minimum temperature, (2) winter chill accumulation, (3) irrigation water. Only two crops clear all three across multiple biomes at smallholder scale — CITRUS (soft citrus/lemon in particular) and GUAVA — with LOW-CHILL PEACH a genuine third. The narrowest are LITCHI, BANANA, APRICOT and APPLE/PEAR, each effectively confined to 3-5 districts. Crucially, the popular assumption that "subtropical = broad" is wrong: mango tolerates 45°C and <300 mm rain yet is pinned to frost-free savanna below ~600 m, while macadamia at 65,516 ha is 90%+ in three provinces. Conversely olive and fig are temperature-hardy (-7°C and -5 to -10°C) but fail across the whole subtropical north for the opposite reason — winters too warm and summers too humid.
points: THE THREE GATES, IN ORDER. ARC's Climate-Smart module frames SA reach as frost first, then heat/chill, then water. SANBI's five horticultural zones give the frost baseline: Zone 1 coastal summer-rainfall (min 5-10°C, dry frost-free winters); Zone 2 coastal winter-rainfall (0-10°C, frost-free, occasional very light frost); Zone 3 winter-rainfall Karoo (-5 to 5°C, light frost); Zone 4 summer-rainfall Karoo/Highveld (below -5°C, SEVERE frost); Zone 5 Bushveld (-5 to 0°C, frost). ARC states plainly that Zone 4 (Grassland/Highveld biome) rules out every subtropical on this list. That single fact removes the entire interior plateau from citrus, avocado, mango, macadamia, banana, litchi and papaya.

CITRUS — THE BROADEST-REACH CROP ON THE LIST, BY A LARGE MARGIN. Frost: production confined to areas where temperature seldom drops below -2°C and almost never below -3°C; unprotected, the mean minimum of the coldest month must not fall below 2-3°C (ARC). No chill requirement, but navels need a coldest-month MEAN of 12-13°C (below 13°C to go dormant) and reliable crops fail once that mean exceeds 14°C. Water: rainfall is 'frequently unevenly distributed and in most situations insufficient' — irrigation is effectively compulsory everywhere in SA. Reach (CGA Key Industry Statistics 2025, 101,624 ha): Limpopo 40,353; Eastern Cape 25,154; Western Cape 19,204; Mpumalanga 7,571; KwaZulu-Natal 2,369; Northern Cape 1,866. That spans Savanna, Albany Thicket, Fynbos/winter-rainfall, Indian Ocean Coastal Belt and irrigated Nama-Karoo along the Orange River — more biomes than any other crop here.

BUT 'CITRUS' IS NOT ONE CROP — THE CGA TYPE SPLIT IS THE SHARPEST DATA IN THIS WHOLE RESEARCH. Soft citrus/mandarin (naartjie), 27,479 ha, is the most evenly spread of all: Western Cape 10,202 / Limpopo 7,600 / Eastern Cape 6,666 / Mpumalanga 1,935 / Northern Cape 285 / KZN 103 — cool Mediterranean AND hot savanna. Lemon, 17,970 ha, similarly broad: EC 7,525 / LP 5,727 / WC 2,371 / MP 869 / KZN 714 / NC 240; ARC notes lemon 'is well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions' than other citrus. Navel, 15,118 ha, is cool-biased (EC 6,238 / LP 3,926 / WC 3,694) — ARC says 'much of South Africa's subtropical area is unsuited' to navels. Valencia, 31,970 ha, is warm-biased (Limpopo alone 18,095). GRAPEFRUIT IS THE NARROWEST CITRUS: 9,087 ha listed as Limpopo 5,005 / Mpumalanga 1,570 / KZN 886 / Northern Cape 571 / Eswatini 367 / Zimbabwe 241 / Eastern Cape 240 — the Western Cape does not appear in CGA's regional table at all. ARC's explanation fits: grapefruit has a short fruit-development period and 'thrives in hot, humid climates with short, mild winters'. Independent horticultural sources rank citrus cold-hardiness mandarin > sweet orange > grapefruit > lemon/lime, so for a smallholder the frost-margin recommendation is naartjie first, then orange, then lemon — even though lemon has the widest climatic (not frost) range.

AVOCADO — HISTORICALLY NARROW, NOW MEASURABLY WIDENING. Frost: absolute survival floor -4°C; light frost tolerated EXCEPT during flowering and fruit set in August-September, which is precisely when SA frost still occurs — that timing, not the -4°C figure, is the real constraint. By race: Mexican mature trees to -4°C, Guatemalan to -2°C, West Indian minimum 1.5°C; Fuerte (Mexican x Guatemalan) has the most cold resistance of SA-planted cultivars, though it is more susceptible to bad weather at flowering than others. Daily mean must exceed 18.5°C during flowering; optimum 20-24°C; humidity above 50% at 14:00. Water: ARC wants >1,000 mm/yr evenly distributed with only June-July dry, which is why the Mpumalanga/Limpopo/KZN mist belts are the classic sites. No chill requirement. Reach (SAAGA 2024 census, 19,240 ha censused, ~20,240 ha industry estimate): Limpopo 10,743 (56%, of which Letaba 8,965); Mpumalanga 3,925; KZN 3,429; Western Cape 972 (unofficially ~1,200); Eastern Cape 171; North West 15. The widening is real and documented: SAAGA's own overview puts current plantings across 22°S to 33°S with annual rainfall from '±400 mm to >1,000 mm', and notes new plantings at higher elevations — clonal rootstocks and soil preparation have moved avocado into Western Cape sites previously considered unsuitable. Fails: anywhere with August-September frost, and >1,000 mm summer rainfall raises Phytophthora cinnamomi root-rot pressure.

MANGO — THE MOST CLIMATE-TOLERANT TREE ON THE LIST AND ONE OF THE MOST GEOGRAPHICALLY PINNED. ARC: mango 'can be grown effectively in a variety of circumstances, including extremely hot and humid, cold and dry, and extremely hot and arid'; survives below 300 mm annual rainfall and temperatures to 45°C (vegetative growth ceases above 46°C); optimum average maximum 27-36°C. So heat and drought are NOT the limits. The limits are three others: (1) winter average minimum should preferably exceed 5°C and cold at full bloom aborts fruit at golf-ball size; (2) ALTITUDE — mangoes grow to 1,200 m but 'production above 600 m altitude is widely regarded to be financially unviable in South Africa'; (3) HUMIDITY/RAIN — relative humidity should be 55% or LESS from October to harvest, and ARC gives monthly rainfall ceilings for disease-free fruit (Sept 50 mm, Oct 85, Nov 110, Dec 140, Jan 140, Feb 140). A wet summer is worse for mango than a dry one. Reach (SAMGA 2024 census, 5,775 ha): Limpopo 4,280 (74%) — Hoedspruit 2,513, Letaba 1,539, Venda 138, Soutpansberg 94; Mpumalanga 1,362 (Onderberg 1,275); Western Cape 101 (dry-warm Clanwilliam); KZN 16; North West 15; Gauteng 1. Verdict: physiologically broad, practically a low-altitude frost-free Savanna crop.

MACADAMIA — LARGE INDUSTRY, NARROW FOOTPRINT, AND NOT FROST-HARDY. ARC: requires 16-25°C; 'although the trees may withstand temperatures as low as 3°C, they should not be considered frost resistant'; frost typically kills young trees while older ones survive, and frost damages blooms and cuts nut set; above 35°C photosynthesis declines. No chill requirement. Water is the under-appreciated gate: published SA figures put a mature orchard at roughly 500-600 mm/yr minimum, with Water Research Commission/Mayo Macs work in the Nelspruit area measuring 750-850 mm/yr, and irrigation regarded as necessary wherever annual rainfall is below ~1,000 mm — Limpopo's main macadamia belt rarely exceeds 1,000 mm and is unevenly distributed. SA plantings run 600-1,200 m altitude in Mpumalanga and Limpopo. Industry scale (SAMAC tree census, via secondary reporting): ~65,516 ha total, Mpumalanga ~29,083, KZN ~23,806, Limpopo ~15,068, with only limited Eastern/Western/Southern Cape plantings because 'the climate in these regions is not ideal'. Verdict: 90%+ of the crop sits in three provinces — Savanna, mist-belt Forest and Indian Ocean Coastal Belt. Not a broad-reach smallholder tree, and the water bill is the reason as much as the frost.

PECAN — NARROW IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION: IT NEEDS THE FROST, AND IT NEEDS ENORMOUS IRRIGATION. ARC: 'low temperatures, including frost, are necessary for effective budding and flower growth from June to August', then high summer heat October-April. The stated window is summer average monthly maximum above 28°C and winter below 23°C; summer average monthly minimum above 16°C and winter below 8°C; humidity below 55% for most of the growing season, because scab is the disease that punishes humid river valleys — 'only scab-tolerant varieties should be planted' near rivers and low-lying subtropical sites. Water: SAPPA's own guidance divides SA into three zones with annual requirements of 10,000 m3/ha (wet east — parts of KZN, Mbombela, Makhado), 12,000 m3/ha (central — Cullinan, Parys, Potchefstroom, Kroonstad, Bloemfontein) and 15,000 m3/ha (warm dry west — Vaalharts, Douglas, Prieska, Upington, Augrabies), i.e. 1,000-1,500 mm equivalent, with peak daily use of 460-800 litres per tree per day. That is why 80-90% of SA pecan production sits in the Northern Cape on the Vaalharts and Orange River irrigation schemes. Verdict: an irrigation-scheme crop, not a rain-fed smallholder crop.

BANANA — NO PART OF SOUTH AFRICA IS OPTIMAL. ARC is unusually blunt: 'climate significantly limits banana cultivation in South Africa's subtropical zones, since optimum circumstances do not exist elsewhere in the nation'. World banana belts sit within 20°N-20°S; SA's are at 24-31°S. In midwinter, night air temperatures in SA banana regions fall to 12-5°C 'and occasionally much lower', producing yellowing, November dump, choke throat and under-peel discoloration; optimum flower initiation is ~22°C and mean night temperatures below 10°C badly damage flower initiation. Summer peaks of 40-45°C are 'almost as bad as cold'. Only three to four summer months have night minima above 18°C. Water: 'in South Africa, nearly all bananas are irrigated'. Additional exposure: winds above 50 km/h cause blowdowns, 20-50 km/h causes leaf tearing, and hail destroys plantations almost every year. Reach: Onderberg/Komatipoort (~42% of the national crop), Kiepersol, Levubu, Letaba (all frost-free Lowveld pockets) plus the KZN north and south coasts. Verdict: narrow, capital-intensive, and marginal even where it is grown.

LITCHI — THE NARROWEST CROP ON THE ENTIRE LIST. ARC gives a genuinely tight envelope that must ALL be satisfied: summer average monthly maximum below 32°C but above 26°C; for three to four winter months the average monthly minimum above 6°C but BELOW 14°C (the cool winter is what induces flowering — a warm winter means no crop); relative humidity above 50% from October to fruit maturity; frost-free, since temperatures below 0°C damage flowers and new shoots; and high summer rainfall with continuous water from flowering through harvest (August-January), the critical window being flowering plus the following 7-8 weeks. That is a needle-threading combination — warm enough to be frost-free, cool enough in winter to flower, not too hot in summer, and humid. ARC names the only qualifying areas: the Mpumalanga Lowveld, the Soutpansberg area and the KwaZulu-Natal coastal belt. Industry data bears it out: roughly 1,300-1,700 ha nationally, ~59-70% in the Mpumalanga Onderberg/Nelspruit/Hazyview belt, ~25-31% Tzaneen/Limpopo, ~5% KZN. For a smallholder outside those three pockets, litchi is a decorative tree, not a crop.

GUAVA — THE QUIET BROAD-REACH WINNER, AND THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE UNDERRATED. ARC: 'guavas are fairly versatile and thrive in tropical and subtropical climates'; yield and quality actually RISE where there is a distinct winter; best where frost-free, but they 'can flourish in most regions where the winters are not too harsh', with young trees needing protection where frost is periodic and mature trees able to withstand the rare cold; grows to 1,515 m above sea level (higher than any other subtropical here); drought tolerance increases with tree age; the real soil constraint is waterlogging, not drought. The distribution proves the breadth: of ~1,200 ha nationally, the LARGEST production province is the Western Cape (~547 ha), ahead of Limpopo (~442 ha) and Mpumalanga (~140 ha). No other crop on this list has its biggest block in winter-rainfall Fynbos and its second-biggest in summer-rainfall Savanna. Caveat for anyone recommending it: guava wilt disease is the industry's dominant constraint in SA and cultivar/rootstock choice matters more than climate in the north.

OLIVE — TEMPERATURE-HARDY BUT CLIMATICALLY NARROW, AND IT FAILS IN THE SUBTROPICS FOR A REASON MOST PEOPLE GET BACKWARDS. Frost: whole trees can die at -7°C, with young trees, new shoots and inflorescences most vulnerable — so it is far hardier than any subtropical here. The binding constraint is the opposite: olive is an obligate thermoperiodic species requiring at least 10 weeks below 12.2-13.3°C to flower fully, with cultivar chill requirements from 600 to over 1,000 hours, AND maximum June-July day temperatures must stay below 21°C or no fruit is borne at all. A Lowveld or coastal KZN winter is simply too warm. Second constraint: high-humidity summer-rainfall regions bring pest and disease pressure. Water: SA Olive states drip or micro-sprinkler irrigation 'is a prerequisite for the regular production of high quality fruit' — roughly 800 mm equivalent — so this is not a plant-and-forget dryland tree despite the reputation. Reach: ~2,400-2,850 ha, with 93-95% in the Western Cape (Paarl, Wellington, Robertson, Montagu, Swartland, Klein Karoo), plus workable summer-rainfall pockets with cold dry winters — Hartswater/Vaalharts, Prieska, Upington in the Northern Cape, Alicedale in the Eastern Cape, Brits in North West, and the eastern Free State. Verdict: Fynbos + Karoo + cold-winter irrigated interior. Not the subtropical north.

FIG — MEDITERRANEAN-PINNED, SMALL, AND LIMITED BY HARVEST-SEASON RAIN RATHER THAN BY COLD. Frost: most cultivars withstand about -5°C and some to -10°C — comfortably the second-hardiest tree here after pomegranate. Chill: a modest winter chill requirement, well below the pome fruits. The real limit is that figs need warm DRY weather during summer harvest, because moisture cracks ripening fruit, and they originate in hot low-humidity areas with long sunny summers and short cool winters. That excludes the whole summer-rainfall east and the humid coast, not on temperature grounds but on fruit-integrity and disease grounds. Reach: only ~222 ha commercially (2019) — Klein Karoo (Kammanassie near Oudtshoorn, Prince Albert) is the core, plus Swartland (Porterville, Riebeek Valley, Malmesbury, Hermon), Paarl, Worcester and Napier in the Overberg. Verdict: Succulent Karoo and Fynbos. As a smallholder tree it is hardy and easy; as a crop it is a niche with a tiny national footprint.

POMEGRANATE — THE HARDIEST TREE ON THIS LIST AND THE LOWEST CHILL REQUIREMENT OF ANY CROP WITH ONE. Frost: mature trees tolerate roughly -10°C, moderate frosts of about -5°C are handled well, and trouble starts only with prolonged severe frost at -10°C or below; trees under three years old remain vulnerable because they still carry green growth. Chill: only about 200 hours to stimulate flowering — the lowest genuine chill requirement in this set, which is why it can sit in both a Western Cape winter and a Limpopo one. Heat: up to 38°C actively helps fruit development. Water: wants warm-to-hot climates with DRY summers and mild winters, so it is an irrigated crop in dry inland areas and is at risk from rain and wind at ripening. Reach: ~1,167 ha nationally with Western Cape 81%, Limpopo 10%, Northern Cape 7% — the northern regions harvest from late December while the Western Cape starts around end-February. Verdict: genuinely multi-biome (Fynbos, Karoo, Savanna) on the physiology, but a small industry, and the fruit's value depends on export-grade appearance that smallholder conditions rarely achieve.

DECIDUOUS GROUP — THE CHILL NUMBERS EXPLAIN WHY SOUTH AFRICA'S POME FRUIT IS SQUEEZED INTO FIVE DISTRICTS. SA sits at ~30-34°S, not the 40° latitude of world apple belts. Measured chill accumulation ranges from close to 2,000 Utah chill units in the Koue Bokkeveld in good seasons (average ~1,400) down to as little as 200-350 CU in poor seasons in Elgin-Grabouw-Vyeboom-Villiersdorp (average ~700). Against that, apples are 'widely accepted to need ca. 1,000-1,200 Utah model chill units to break dormancy', yet in SA 'apples are often produced successfully with 500 chill units' — achieved with rest-breaking agents and cytokinins in late winter, a distinctive single-central-leader training system developed specifically as a response to insufficient chill, and branch manipulation. In other words SA apple production is a managed workaround, not a natural fit. Hortgro/Schulze national mapping (Infruitec daily-positive model) shows 250 PCUs reached by May in the Cape Fold mountains, escarpment, Drakensberg and parts of the Karoo and Highveld, June across the rest of the deciduous areas; 500 PCUs in May-July; 700 PCUs only by June-August, and by mid-century some regions (Berg and Breede River valleys) may never reach 700 PCUs at all. Note the model caveat: Utah, daily-positive Utah/Infruitec and Dynamic models disagree, all were calibrated on peaches, and the Dynamic model is now regarded as the best performer — so treat any single chill figure as indicative.

DECIDUOUS REACH, MEASURED (Hortgro Tree Census 2021). APPLES, 24,956 ha: Ceres 7,625; Groenland/Elgin-Grabouw 7,262; Villiersdorp-Vyeboom 4,054; Langkloof East 2,933; Langkloof West 1,214 — that is 92% in five districts. Everything outside the Western Cape and Langkloof is a rounding error: Free State 527, Mpumalanga 205, Northern Provinces 186, Eastern Cape 15. PEARS, similar: Ceres 4,734; Groenland 1,672; Langkloof East 1,621; Wolseley/Tulbagh 1,429; Villiersdorp-Vyeboom 1,228; Klein Karoo 984. APRICOTS ARE THE NARROWEST CROP IN THE WHOLE STUDY: of 1,604,338 trees nationally, 1,134,388 (~71%) are in the Klein Karoo alone, with trivial amounts in Northern Provinces (22,321 trees), Orange River (7,245), Eastern Cape (2,902) and Free State (700). PLUMS, 10.6 million trees, are Western Cape-centred (Klein Karoo 3.63m, Wolseley/Tulbagh 1.26m, Franschhoek 1.00m, Wellington 874k, Paarl 694k, Ceres 738k) with small outposts at Orange River 34,658, Northern Provinces 28,621, Eastern Cape 10,858, Free State 1,750.

THE STANDOUT DECIDUOUS FINDING: LOW-CHILL PEACH IS THE ONLY TEMPERATE FRUIT WITH A GENUINELY NATIONAL FOOTPRINT. In Hortgro's 2021 dessert-peach table (1,277 ha total), LIMPOPO IS THE LARGEST SINGLE DISTRICT at 216 ha — ahead of Ceres (213 ha), Citrusdal (202 ha) and Klein Karoo (174 ha) — followed by Wolseley/Tulbagh 118, Berg River 91, FREE STATE 74, MPUMALANGA 49, Worcester 32, NORTH WEST 27, Langkloof East 17, Olifants River 13, EASTERN CAPE 12, Boland 10, Orange River 9, Langkloof West 7, EGVV 6, GAUTENG 5. (Canning/cling peaches, 4,201 ha, are the opposite — Klein Karoo 2,206 ha, i.e. concentrated.) This is the practical answer to the smallholder question: ARC Infruitec's low-chill breeding programme has released peach, nectarine and plum selections that perform in areas accumulating as few as 200-500 chill units, explicitly aimed at reducing climatic risk for emerging and small-scale producers, and ARC has since presented low-chill APPLES for warmer climates too. A low-chill peach reaches Savanna, Grassland margins, Karoo and Fynbos; a Granny Smith apple does not.

VERDICT — BROAD REACH (recommend widely, several biomes each): (1) SOFT CITRUS/NAARTJIE and LEMON — no chill requirement, frost floor -2 to -3°C, present in all six citrus provinces across Fynbos, Savanna, Thicket, Coastal Belt and irrigated Karoo; naartjie is the most cold-hardy citrus and lemon the most climatically adaptable. (2) GUAVA — frost-tolerant once mature, to 1,515 m, drought-tolerant with age, biggest single block in the Western Cape and second-biggest in Limpopo. (3) LOW-CHILL PEACH — 200-500 CU cultivars put it in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North West, Gauteng, Free State, Eastern Cape and the Cape simultaneously. (4) POMEGRANATE — ~200 chill hours, -10°C mature hardiness, 38°C tolerance; spans WC/Limpopo/NC, limited only by needing dry summers and by market quality standards. (5) MANGO with an asterisk — enormous physiological tolerance (45°C, <300 mm) but hard-capped by frost, by ~600 m altitude economics, and by needing DRY summer air.

VERDICT — NARROW (site-specific; do not recommend on general principles): LITCHI is the narrowest — needs frost-free AND winter minima above 6°C but below 14°C AND summer maxima below 32°C AND humidity above 50%, which qualifies only the Mpumalanga Lowveld, Soutpansberg and the KZN coast (~1,300-1,700 ha nationally). BANANA — ARC states optimum conditions exist nowhere in SA; five frost-free irrigated pockets only. APRICOT — 71% of national trees in the Klein Karoo alone. APPLE and PEAR — 92% of apples in five Western Cape/Langkloof districts, sustained only by rest-breaking chemistry and specialised training. AVOCADO — -4°C floor with the fatal exposure at August-September flowering, wants >1,000 mm evenly distributed; widening into the Western Cape via clonal rootstocks but still 74% in Limpopo+Mpumalanga. MACADAMIA — 65,516 ha but 90%+ in three provinces, not frost resistant, 750-850 mm/yr of water. PECAN — needs winter frost AND long hot summers AND low humidity AND 10,000-15,000 m3/ha/yr of irrigation; 80-90% on Northern Cape irrigation schemes. OLIVE and FIG — hardy to cold (-7°C, -5 to -10°C) but excluded from the entire subtropical north by too-warm winters (olive needs June-July maxima below 21°C) and humid summers.

BIOME SUMMARY FOR REPORT/APP USE. Savanna/Bushveld (frost-free, low altitude): citrus, mango, banana, litchi, macadamia, avocado, guava, low-chill peach, pecan (Limpopo). Indian Ocean Coastal Belt (KZN): banana, macadamia, avocado, citrus, litchi (small). Forest/mist belt: avocado, macadamia. Fynbos (winter rainfall): apple, pear, plum, apricot, peach, citrus (Citrusdal/Olifants), olive, fig, pomegranate, guava, avocado (new). Succulent/Nama-Karoo: fig, olive, pomegranate, apricot (Klein Karoo), plus pecan and citrus where the Orange and Vaalharts schemes supply water. Albany Thicket (Eastern Cape): citrus (Sundays/Gamtoos), some avocado. GRASSLAND/HIGHVELD: essentially nothing on this list — SANBI Zone 4 has severe frost below -5°C and ARC excludes all subtropicals; only small apple (527 ha Free State), peach (74 ha) and plum pockets, plus pecan at the margins.

PROVENANCE CAVEAT — read before quoting any number. Figures I extracted directly from primary PDFs/pages are: all ARC climate thresholds; SANBI zone table; Hortgro chill-accumulation and PCU mapping; every Hortgro 2021 hectare/tree figure (apple, pear, apricot, peach, plum by district); every CGA 2025 citrus hectare figure by province and by type; SAAGA 2024 avocado hectares by province and region; SAMGA 2024 mango hectares by province and region; SAPPA pecan water requirements; SA Olive and Olives SA climate thresholds. Figures that came from search-result summaries rather than a direct fetch — and should be verified before publication — are: SAMAC macadamia hectares (65,516 total; MP 29,083 / KZN 23,806 / LP 15,068) and macadamia water figures; litchi hectares and regional shares (SALGA census); guava hectares (WC 547 / LP 442 / MP 140); pomegranate hectares (1,167; WC 81% / LP 10% / NC 7%); fig hectares (222); olive hectares (~2,400-2,850) and the 600-1,000+ hour cultivar chill range; banana regional hectare shares; and the generic non-SA chill ranges for apple/pear/plum/apricot. Two authoritative sources were unreachable during this session — DALRRD's own production guidelines at nda.agric.za and daff.gov.za both refused connections, and the 18 MB Hortgro 2024 statistics PDF timed out repeatedly (I used the fully-downloadable 2021 edition instead), so deciduous hectares are 2021 vintage while citrus, avocado and mango are 2024-2025.

entries.why: Named for the Kei River and native to exactly this valley-bushveld country, it is the one plant that is simultaneously a stock-proof hedge, a heavy vitamin-C fruit crop, bulk livestock fodder and bee forage — SANBI: 'usually 3-5 m in height, but sometimes reaches 8 m', 'drought- and frost-resistant' (recently renamed from D. caffra under Madrid Code Art. 61.6).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-afra

entries.why: The most climate-proof indigenous fruit tree on a thicket farm — SANBI records '2-8 m' with a dense closed crown and says it 'can tolerate both cold and heat as well as prolonged periods of drought', and the tart juicy fruit makes preserve, jelly and vinegar.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/pappea-capensis

entries.why: For the coastal Albany Thicket units (Albany Coastal Belt, Buffels Thicket) it is the fruiting hedge of choice — SANBI: 'can grow into a small tree up to 4 m high', wind-resistant, 'plant 1 m apart to form a dense, impenetrable hedge', fruit rich in vitamin C; frost-tender so keep it off cold inland valley floors.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carissa-macrocarpa

entries.why: A genuine four-function shrub for the thicket understorey — SANBI records it 'up to 3 m', 'both frost- and drought-hardy', with dried edible fruit, leaves 'browsed by cattle, goats and game' and flowers that 'feed honeybees' plus butterfly larval host duty.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-occidentalis

entries.why: The best large indigenous fruit tree here but only for the wetter coastal thicket units (655-677 mm) or a place with groundwater — SANBI: 'grows up to 15 m tall', naturally a riverine-forest tree, 'popular tree in frost-free areas', fruit used for jam and jelly (renamed from H. caffrum under Madrid Code Art. 61.6).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/harpephyllum-caffrum

entries.why: The drought-reserve species: SANBI records it 'reaching an approximate size of 7 m in height and very often with an equal width', 'very suitable for small drier gardens, especially in the Karoo and semidesert areas', with fruit eaten by people and birds and leaves browsed — plant it as the evergreen backbone of a dry-side windbreak, not as a dessert fruit.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/euclea-undulata

entries.why: Albany Thicket contains South Africa's second-largest citrus region (Sundays River Valley around Kirkwood/Addo and the Gamtoos), the Eastern Cape carries 6,666 ha of soft citrus, and mandarin is the most cold-hardy citrus type — but ARC is explicit that rainfall is 'insufficient in most situations', so this is an irrigated crop, never rain-fed.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf

entries.why: The Eastern Cape's biggest single citrus type at 7,525 ha, and ARC notes lemon 'is well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions' than other citrus — the safest citrus for a marginal thicket site, still needing frost protection below about -2°C and year-round irrigation.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf

entries.why: Figs are ruled out of summer-rainfall South Africa because harvest rain cracks the fruit — but Albany Thicket's driest months are December to February, exactly when figs ripen, and the tree already tolerates about -5°C, so this biome is one of the few summer-side places where fig genuinely works unirrigated.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/

entries.why: The lowest chill requirement of any temperate fruit (about 200 hours), mature hardiness to roughly -10°C and active benefit from 38°C heat — it spans the whole biome from near-frost-free coast to 19-25 frost-day inland valleys, and it wants the dry ripening window this biome has.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/

entries.why: ARC Infruitec has released peach and nectarine selections that fruit on as few as 200-500 chill units specifically for emerging and small-scale growers, which puts a real deciduous fruit into inland Albany Thicket (mean 7-25 frost days) where apples and pears cannot go — buy a named low-chill cultivar, not a Ceres variety.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.nembaStatus: Category 1b — BUT 'spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed', and 'the fruit of the sweet prickly pear is not listed if used for human consumption' (2020 Lists, List 1 item 238). Plant only named spineless cultivars; spiny plants and spiny volunteers are Category 1b and must be controlled.
entries.why: The Eastern Cape's proven drought crop that is both fruit and emergency stock fodder at 250-400 mm, and the one NEMBA carve-out worth using — but the app must hard-enforce the cultivar rule, because the spiny form of the same species is Category 1b.
entries.source: https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: Alicedale in the Eastern Cape is a named South African olive district and sits in this biome; olive needs at least 10 weeks below about 13°C and June-July maxima under 21°C, which the inland thicket valleys deliver and the frost-free coastal strip does not — and SA Olive is clear that drip or micro irrigation 'is a prerequisite'.
entries.source: https://www.saolive.co.za/olive-growing/

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but WHITE mulberry (Morus alba) IS Category 3 nationally, so buy black mulberry specifically
entries.why: The classic chicken-and-pig forage tree plus a heavy human fruit crop, and the legal distinction is the whole point: white mulberry may not be planted, propagated, moved or given away in South Africa, while black mulberry is entirely unlisted.
entries.source: https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: The single most useful indigenous tree in the biome and the natural emergent above thicket canopy — SANBI records 'a maximum of about 12 m where there is good water', 'frost and drought hardy', nitrogen-fixing so 'grasses and other plants thriving in its shade', 'a particularly good fodder tree', and a long flowering season that makes it a top bee tree.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo

entries.why: Endemic to precisely this country — SANBI gives '9-12 x 7-11 m' and a range 'from the Humansdorp district to Port Shepstone and inland to about 57 km into the Albany district' — and it is planted from truncheons at least 40 mm thick in late winter, so the fence post literally roots and becomes the living fence while feeding sunbirds 7-10 drops of nectar per flower (renamed from E. caffra).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/erythrina-afra

entries.why: The fastest way to real shade on a thicket homestead — SANBI expects 'a height of up to 12 m' in cultivation with a 'dense, semi-circular' canopy, growth of '1 to 2 m per year' when young, and it 'can withstand frost' and is 'fairly drought resistant', so it works on both the cold inland and mild coastal ends of the biome.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/celtis-africana

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA — but a Protected Tree under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998: you may plant one, you may never cut, damage, move or fell one without a permit
entries.why: The evergreen coastal-thicket anchor with a 'large, dense, rounded crown' at '10-15 m' and edible purple-black berries; plant it as the second rank of a coastal shelterbelt because SANBI warns 'direct sea wind can result in considerable burn damage from salt-laden wind' — and flag its protected status before anyone plans a hedge trim.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/sideroxylon-inerme

entries.why: The riverbank and donga-head tree: SANBI records '4-6 m in three years', often multi-stemmed and 'surprisingly drought and frost resistant', growing 'alongside rivers or away from rivers where sufficient groundwater is available' — use it to hold the Sundays, Great Fish and Gamtoos banks rather than as a dryland shade tree.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/combretum-erythrophyllum

entries.why: SANBI gives '9 x 12 m' with 'a dense spreading crown', calls it 'frost-, drought- and wind-resistant' and 'virtually indestructable', 'an excellent fodder tree', a honeybee plant and a small edible fruit — the one indigenous tree that covers shelterbelt, shade, browse and bee forage on a single planting.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana

entries.why: The fastest legal shelterbelt and the best bee tree available here — SANBI: 'evergreen, frost hardy and drought resistant', growth 'up to 800 mm per year', 'the large amounts of pollen and nectar it produces makes it popular with bee farmers', and it makes 'a very good clipped hedge' and 'a pioneer tree for your forest garden'.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/buddleja-saligna

entries.why: SANBI gives 'a height of 7 m and a width of 7 m', 'drought resistant' and 'frost resistant', useful for 'natural soil stabilisation and increasing infiltration of rainwater', and critically 'does not have an aggressive root system and can be used near paving' — the safe evergreen shade tree next to buildings, tanks and water lines on inland thicket sites.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea

entries.why: SANBI records '3-10(-20) m high; with a spreading canopy', 'withstanding heat and cold equally well', edible berries, leaves and fruit 'sought after by birds of many species, wild animals and domestic stock', thorny branches historically used to build predator-proof kraals, and flowers that 'produce abundant nectar and often yield a good honey' — accept that it is slow at 0.3 m a year.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ziziphus-mucronata

entries.why: SANBI puts it at 'max. height 5 m', drought-resistant and water-wise, occurring 'along the banks of dry streams and small rivers in the Little Karoo, the drier areas of Eastern Cape' — i.e. the dry thicket units themselves — with seeds 'edible either green or mature', browsed leaves and flowers producing 'copious amounts of nectar'.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/schotia-afra-var-afra

entries.why: The defining plant of this biome and the highest-leverage thing a thicket farmer can plant — SANBI gives '2-5 m in height', 'moderate degree of frost, especially when mature', browsed by game and stock, edible sour leaves, hedge, and 'soil binder for preventing soil erosion' — planted from truncheons on contour riplines at 350-500 mm rainfall across the Baviaanskloof and Camdeboo, but you MUST exclude goats for the first years because herbivory is the documented cause of restoration failure.
entries.source: https://sti-portal.fao.org/innovations/spekboom-portulacaria-afra-planting-within-riplines-thicket-biome-restoration

entries.why: One of only two woody legumes the DFFE national agroforestry guideline actually names for South African improved fallows and hedgerows (cut at 90 cm), it fixes 40-97 kg N/ha/yr in Africa and 'continues growing with rainfall as low as 250 to 375 mm' — the legal replacement for the Leucaena and Tithonia that imported permaculture lists will push at you.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf

entries.why: SANBI describes 'a large shrub of about 3 m high, or a small, weather-beaten, evergreen tree, up to 7 m tall', 'frost hardy and drought resistant' and able to thrive in exposed sites, with sharp spines making it a real stock barrier and its flowers a magnet for insects and insectivorous birds — the toughest indigenous living fence for the cold, dry inland units.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/gymnosporia-buxifolia

entries.why: The coastal counterpart to karee: SANBI gives '3-5 m', 'semi frost-hardy' with excellent salt and wind tolerance, dense multi-stemmed habit, and a documented sand-stabilising role on coastal and inland dunes — this is the front rank of a shelterbelt on the Albany Coastal Belt where wild olive and karee will scorch.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-crenata

entries.why: SANBI gives 'up to 2-3 m high and spread more than 2.5 m', 'remarkably tolerant of periods of drought', distributed along the Eastern Cape coast, pollinated by sunbirds and visited by honeybees and butterflies, and it 'withstands clipping and can be trained into a neat hedge' — the nectar hedge that carries pollinators through the shoulder seasons.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tecomaria-capensis

entries.why: The best-fitting exotic fodder legume for a 350-500 mm non-seasonal-rainfall site — evergreen dry-season browse at 17-22% crude protein, thrives on 350-1,600 mm, roots to 10 m or more, and is used in South Africa — but it is less documented locally than pigeon pea and is a broom relative, so watch for self-seeding and remove volunteers.
entries.source: http://www.tropicalforages.info/key/forages/Media/Html/entities/chamaecytisus_prolifer_var._palmensis.htm

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (note: Sesbania punicea, red sesbania, IS Category 1b — do not confuse them)
entries.why: The other species DFFE names for South African improved fallows, with maize established directly into its prunings — grow it on the irrigated or greywater side of the homestead purely as a mulch factory, because Mahlathini's KZN/Eastern Cape work found mulching uptake stalled at 32% simply for lack of mulch material.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf

entries.why: SANBI puts it at 2-3 m, drought resistant, flowering May to August — exactly the winter nectar gap when nothing else is out — and it is the backbone of a 200-year-old Eastern Cape bitter-aloe tapping industry, so this is the rare species that is simultaneously ecosystem service, medicine cabinet and cash crop on rocky ground you cannot farm.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-ferox

entries.why: SANBI gives '0.5 to 1 m in height', 'quite drought-tolerant', a natural range that runs 'in the western Karoo to Eastern Cape', sunbird pollination, and as a legume it 'fixes nitrogen in the soil' — the shrub-layer nitrogen source plus South Africa's best-known indigenous medicinal, on ground too dry for comfrey.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lessertia-frutescens

entries.why: Named on SANBI's own bee-forage lists and recorded as 'bushy evergreen shrubs up to 1 metre' on 'clay and granite slopes throughout the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Namaqualand', with a taproot to 6 m and lateral roots out to 2 m — an aromatic insectary and light browse plant that holds soil on the driest edges of the plan.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eriocephalus-africanus

entries.why: SANBI records 'tall stems up to 2 m high, but sometimes as low as 0.6 m', tough clumps that slowly thicken, and a use list running from coughs and colds to fever and intestinal worms — the standard home-medicine shrub of the region, best sited on the damper side of the homestead where SANBI notes it grows on 'damp slopes, along streamsides and forest margins'.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/artemisia-afra

entries.why: SANBI describes 'a fast growing semi-succulent, spreading shrub to 2 m tall' with 'fleshy, egg-shaped, edible and sweet' fruits, 'very popular among frugivorous birds', flowers 'particularly attractive' to bees, and a pioneer role that is why it was exported to Australia to stabilise soil — use it to cover bare, eroding thicket quickly while slower species establish (formerly Chrysanthemoides monilifera).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/osteospermum-moniliferum

entries.why: SANBI gives '100 to 200 mm tall, with long, thick, trailing stems that root at the nodes', occurring 'in the Western and Eastern Cape provinces', fruit 'sweet and juicy when ripe' for jam, and a sandbinder role that 'stabilizes the soil and prevents erosion' — the coastal-thicket edible mat, but it is 'damaged by temperatures lower than 1°C' so keep it off cold inland valley floors.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carpobrotus-deliciosus

entries.why: The workhorse of the herb layer: ECHO's South African trials recorded over 100 kg N/ha accumulated in above-ground biomass, the dry seed is a staple, and the leaves are eaten as imifino — plant it in both the spring and autumn rainfall peaks this biome uniquely offers.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.why: The one edible living mulch that will actually hold ground under young fruit trees through a thicket summer, giving a storable staple root plus a leafy green plus pig and poultry fodder from the same square metre — note it is unrelated to the listed ornamental Ipomoea species (I. alba, carnea, indica, purpurea are all Category 1b).
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: Vetiver SA gives the actual spec — slips 10-15 cm apart in a single row across the slope, planted in the rainy season, hedgerow visible within 3 months, trimmed to 20-30 cm — and hedges on contour above a gully head stop head advance, which is the standing problem on overgrazed thicket footslopes; the trimmings are the mulch by-product, not the point.
entries.source: https://www.vetiver.co.za/vetiver-grass-faq/

entries.why: Top of ARC-VOPI's researched indigenous-crop set, nutrient-dense in vitamin A and iron, tolerant of harsh conditions and grain-bearing as well as leafy — and in practice it is a managed volunteer in disturbed ground rather than a sown crop, so the design job is to leave it room, harvest at 4-6 weeks and 15-30 cm.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.why: SANBI notes it 'reaches its peak in the succulent-rich, dry valleys of Eastern Cape' — this biome — as 'a fast growing, branched, succulent perennial' forming spreading clumps, drought resistant, and its leaf jelly is the standard first-aid remedy for burns, insect bites and cracked skin; the most useful hard-wearing edging groundcover on the list.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/bulbine-frutescens

entries.why: SANBI gives 'a height of 0.5 m' with tuberous roots that spread to form clumps, tolerating 'prolonged drought', with 'both the leaves and flowers used in salads', a long medicinal record, and a smell that 'repels fleas, ticks and mosquitoes' and discourages moles — the bed-edge plant that earns its place three ways.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tulbaghia-violacea

entries.why: SANBI records 'a possible spread of 10-15 m' or a loose 1.5 m shrub, tolerating 'moderate frost and drought' once established, occurring in Eastern Cape bush and coastal dunes from 0-600 m, with grape-like tart berries used for jam — and it is 'often the pioneer species on dunes' and 'especially effective in stabilizing open sandy areas', so it doubles as a fruiting bank cover.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-digitata

entries.why: The best-eating indigenous 'grape' — SANBI calls the fruit 'edible and pleasant tasting but acidic' with flesh 'similar to that of the cultivated grape', good for jam, jelly, wine or vinegar — but it is a forest and riverine-fringe liane, so restrict it to shaded kloofs, the wetter coastal thicket units or a north-shaded pergola rather than open dry veld.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-tomentosa

excluded: Guava (Psidium guajava) — NEMBA Category 3 in the Eastern Cape for anything that is not a commercial plantation (Category 2, permit required, for plantations). Growing, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are all prohibited under s71A, so it cannot legally go into an Eastern Cape food forest even though it is one of the broadest-reach subtropicals in the country. The 'fruit not listed if used for human consumption' carve-out exempts the fruit, never the tree.

Purple granadilla (Passiflora edulis) — Category 2 in the Eastern Cape outside the proclaimed urban edge, so a permit (with a paid risk-assessment practitioner) is required, and reg 4(4) means an unpermitted vine is treated as Category 1b. Explicitly NOT listed inside urban areas of the Eastern Cape, so a town garden in Gqeberha or Makhanda is lawful while a Sundays River Valley smallholding is not — a genuinely place-dependent answer the app must compute, not hardcode.

White mulberry (Morus alba) — Category 3 nationally. A staple of chicken-forage and silvopasture designs, but new plantings, propagation, movement and gifting are all prohibited. Black mulberry (Morus nigra) is entirely unlisted and is in the palette instead.

Leucaena leucocephala — Category 2 nationwide with no area qualifier (Category 1a in the Western Cape). The single most likely trap in any imported tropical-permaculture species list. Pigeon pea and tagasaste replace it here.

Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — Category 1b. The global permaculture chop-and-drop default is flatly illegal to plant in South Africa. Sesbania sesban, pigeon pea and spekboom prunings are the legal biomass sources.

Old man saltbush (Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia) — Category 2, permit required. The standard dryland fodder shrub of Karoo advice; spineless cactus pear and spekboom do the same job legally in this biome.

Spiny prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica, spiny forms) and all other Opuntia species — Category 1b or 1a. Only named spineless cactus-pear cultivars and selections sit outside the listing; spiny volunteers on the property must be controlled, not tolerated.

Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia), honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos), Paraserianthes lophantha, Sesbania punicea — all Category 1b nitrogen-fixers that appear in international permaculture literature. No permit route exists.
Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) — Category 1b. Elderflower/elderberry hedgerows are illegal to plant in South Africa.

Eucalyptus for windbreaks, woodlots or bee forage — the six listed eucalypts (E. camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis) are Category 1b BY NAME in the Albany Thicket biome, with a Category 2 permit route only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenues, and no exemption at all in riparian areas, protected areas or listed ecosystems. Wild olive, karee, dune crow-berry and false olive do the shelterbelt job with no permit.

Avocado (Persea americana) — ARC wants over 1,000 mm evenly distributed and the fatal exposure is August–September frost at flowering; Albany Thicket vegetation units run 259–677 mm MAP. The Eastern Cape has only 171 ha nationally, almost all of it in wetter Kat River and coastal sites outside this biome. Possible on an irrigated, frost-free coastal thicket site with clonal rootstocks; not a general recommendation.

Macadamia — 'should not be considered frost resistant', needs roughly 750–850 mm/yr of water, and industry data puts 90%+ of the national 65,516 ha in Mpumalanga, KZN and Limpopo, with Eastern/Western Cape plantings limited because the climate is not ideal.

Litchi, banana and mango — all pinned to frost-free low-altitude Lowveld and coastal-KZN pockets. Litchi additionally needs summer maxima below 32°C, which fails outright against Albany Thicket summers that exceed 40°C on occasion. ARC states optimum banana conditions do not exist anywhere in South Africa.

Apple and pear — 92% of South Africa's apples sit in five Western Cape/Langkloof districts on 500–1,400 chill units, sustained by rest-breaking chemicals and specialised training. Albany Thicket's 2–25 mean frost days and 17°C MAT do not deliver the chill. Low-chill peach and pomegranate are the honest substitutes and are in the palette.

Pecan — needs winter frost AND long hot summers AND humidity below 55% AND 10,000–15,000 m³/ha/yr of irrigation (SAPPA); 80–90% of national production is on Northern Cape irrigation schemes. It is a scheme crop, not a thicket smallholding crop.

Marula (Sclerocarya birrea) and green monkey orange (Strychnos spinosa) — top-ranked South African indigenous fruits in the KZN domestication studies, but both are frost-sensitive hot-savanna and coastal-KZN species outside their climatic range here.

Fire-managed species and burn-cycle design generally — Albany Thicket 'does not support a regular or widespread fire regime' because succulence has largely excluded fire (Mucina & Rutherford Ch.10). Importing fire as a management tool, or fire-adapted fynbos/grassland species that need it, is actively destructive here.

Comfrey (Symphytum) as the standard mulch/dynamic-accumulator plant — not NEMBA-listed and therefore legal, but it wants moisture and shade this biome does not supply at 259–677 mm with 72–81% mean annual soil moisture stress; spekboom prunings and Sesbania are the local answer.
palettes.notes:
CLIMATE ENVELOPE USED (Mucina & Rutherford, Strelitzia 19, Ch.10). MAP 200–950 mm across the biome, with the individual vegetation units running 259–677 mm: dry inland units Gamka Thicket 267, Sundays Noorsveld 267, Groot Thicket 299, Camdeboo Escarpment 352, Southern Cape Valley 399, Great Fish Noorsveld 420; mid units Great Fish Thicket 449, Eastern Cape Escarpment 520; wet coastal units Buffels Thicket 655, Albany Coastal Belt 677. MAT ~17°C. MAPE 1,695–2,396 mm; MASMS 72–81%. Frost 0–64 days inland, fewer than 10 near the coast, unit means 2–25 days.

THE THREE THINGS THAT MAKE THIS BIOME DIFFERENT, AND WHICH DRIVE THIS PALETTE.
1. NON-SEASONAL RAINFALL WITH SPRING AND AUTUMN MAXIMA, AND A DRY DECEMBER–FEBRUARY. Every Albany Thicket vegetation unit has non-seasonal rainfall. That gives two planting windows a year instead of one — the only semi-arid biome in South Africa where that is true — and it is why fig and pomegranate work here and fail across the summer-rainfall east: the fruit ripens into the driest months rather than into harvest rain.
2. IT IS A FIRE-FREE SYSTEM. High succulence has largely excluded fire. No firebreak planning, no burn cycles, no fire-adapted regeneration to fall back on if you damage the stand — which also means a cleared thicket does not come back the way a burnt grassland does.
3. BROWSE IS THE PRIMARY FAILURE MODE, NOT DROUGHT. Strelitzia 19 warns the biome has 'low annual production, thus giving a false impression of the amount of forage available' — stocking rates set by eyeballing standing biomass are exactly the mechanism that collapsed spekboom thicket over the last century, and the published spekboom restoration work names herbivory (Boer and Angora goats) as the leading constraint on planting success. Any design here must fence or exclude browse for the first two to three years on new plantings, and stock conservatively thereafter.

THREE SUB-ZONES THE APP SHOULD SPLIT ON. (a) COASTAL (Albany Coastal Belt, Buffels Thicket, ~655–677 mm, mean 2 frost days): Carissa macrocarpa, Searsia crenata, Sideroxylon inerme, Harpephyllum afrum, Carpobrotus, Rhoicissus, avocado marginally possible; olive and low-chill peach get less reliable because winters are too warm. (b) MID VALLEY (Southern Cape Valley, Great Fish Thicket, ~400–450 mm, 3–7 frost days): the full palette. (c) DRY INLAND (Gamka, Groot, Sundays Noorsveld, Great Fish Noorsveld, Camdeboo, ~259–420 mm, up to 19–25 mean frost days and 40°C+ summers): drop the frost-tender coastal set, lean on spekboom, spineless cactus pear, wild olive, Euclea, Schotia afra, Aloe ferox, Pappea, Lessertia and Eriocephalus, and treat any fruit tree as irrigated.

WATER IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, NOT FERTILITY. Thicket soils on Karoo Supergroup sediments, Enon conglomerate and dolerite are generally base-rich and lime-rich; with MAPE around 1,700–2,400 mm against MAP of 260–680 mm, the limitation is water and rooting depth. So the interventions that pay are swales, riplines, mulch, shade and windbreaks — not liming and heavy fertilising (the opposite of the Fynbos and coastal-belt prescription).

CITRUS IS REAL HERE BUT ONLY IRRIGATED. The Sundays River Valley (Kirkwood/Addo) and the Gamtoos sit inside this biome and carry a large share of the Eastern Cape's 25,154 ha of citrus. ARC is explicit that rainfall is 'frequently unevenly distributed and in most situations insufficient' — do not present citrus as a rain-fed option anywhere in this palette, and hold the frost floor at about -2°C.

SPECIES OVERLAP AND DELIBERATE DUPLICATION. Olea europaea appears twice on purpose: subsp. europaea (the oil/table olive, exotic, needs 10 weeks below 13°C and drip irrigation) and subsp. africana (the indigenous wild olive, a fodder/shade/windbreak tree needing none of that). They are agronomically different plants and should be shown as different entries.

NOMENCLATURE. Three names in this palette were formally corrected at the 2024 International Botanical Congress in Madrid under new Art. 61.6, which retroactively treats the epithet 'caffra' and its derivatives as orthographic variants to be corrected by dropping the 'c' and the second 'f': Dovyalis caffra → Dovyalis afra, Erythrina caffra → Erythrina afra, Harpephyllum caffrum → Harpephyllum afrum. SANBI's PlantZAfrica has adopted the first two; its Harpephyllum page still carries the old spelling. Nurseries and the trade will use the old names for years, so the app should store both and search on both — and note the NEMBA rule that where a scientific name changes, 'the common name of the species takes precedence and determines whether a particular species is listed or not'.

NEMBA HANDLING. Every entry carries an explicit nembaStatus. Two carve-outs are load-bearing and must be enforced at cultivar level, not species level: spineless cactus-pear cultivars and selections are outside the Category 1b listing of Opuntia ficus-indica, and black mulberry (Morus nigra) is unlisted while white mulberry (Morus alba) is Category 3. Three structural rules also apply on any Albany Thicket plan: any Category 3 plant in a riparian area is deemed Category 1b (reg 5(2)); several listings switch on the proclaimed urban edge, which decides the granadilla answer; and the 'fruit not listed if used for human consumption' clauses exempt the fruit only, never the tree, so they never make planting lawful. The lists are the 2020 gazette (GN 1003, GG 43726) with no amendment published as at DFFE's October 2025 briefing — store them as versioned data with a gazette stamp, not hardcoded.

ONE NON-NEMBA LEGAL FLAG. White milkwood (Sideroxylon inerme) is a Protected Tree under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998. Planting one is fine; cutting, pruning, moving or felling one — including an existing tree on the property — needs a permit. Worth surfacing before a farmer plans a hedge line through mature coastal thicket.

SECTION COVERAGE NOTE. 'Indigenous fruit' returns 6 rather than 10 on purpose. The genuinely productive, well-documented indigenous fruits of this biome are few; the KZN domestication front-runners (marula, monkey orange) are outside their climatic range here, and padding the list with marginal species would give farmers trees that fruit poorly. The strata are otherwise fully covered: 5 canopy, 12 sub-canopy, 15 shrub-layer, 9 herb/groundcover and 2 climbers, 45 entries in total.

entries.why: The one tree that does everything in the Karoo: SANBI records it as frost and drought hardy, growing up to 1 m/year, fixing nitrogen so 'grasses and other plants thrive in its shade', feeding stock with leaves/flowers/pods, and carrying a long nectar flow for bees — it is also the indicator of sweetveld, so it belongs on the good soils you are already farming.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo (SANBI PlantZAfrica: 'frost and drought hardy', up to 12 m, up to 1 m/yr, nitrogen fixation, 'particularly good fodder tree', bee forage)

entries.why: SANBI names it specifically as 'an excellent shade tree especially in hot regions such as the Karoo and Kalahari since it is evergreen and drought resistant' — evergreen shade matters where MAPE is ~2 500 mm against 200 mm of rain, and its non-aggressive roots let you plant it right at the house, kraal or water point.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea (SANBI: ~7 m height and spread, frost resistant, highly drought resistant, shade/windbreak/erosion, edible fruit, lime-rich substrates)

entries.botanicalName: Olea europaea subsp. africana (= O. e. subsp. cuspidata)
entries.why: SANBI gives its working range as −5°C to 40°C, which brackets the Nama-Karoo's own −5°C to 43°C almost exactly, and calls it an 'excellent fodder tree' used to stabilise erosion dongas — slow, but effectively permanent once its roots are down, and it makes fence posts on site.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana (SANBI: 9 x 12 m, tolerates −5°C to 40°C, extremely hardy, excellent fodder tree, stabilises erosion dongas, edible fruit)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA — but a PROTECTED TREE under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998: planting is free, cutting/damaging/removing an existing tree needs a DFFE licence
entries.why: For the dry western half (Bushmanland, Prieska, Kenhardt) this is the only real canopy tree — SANBI records it surviving on as little as 40 mm annual rainfall with a 60 m taproot, tolerating 'hot summer temperatures and severe frosts', and its pods are prized cattle fodder that drop in the dry season.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-erioloba (SANBI: 2 m shrub to 16 m tree, taproot to 60 m, rainfall as low as 40 mm, severe frosts, pods as cattle fodder, protected tree in South Africa)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (no Salix appears anywhere in the 2020 NEMBA plant list)
entries.why: Plant this ONLY on the watercourse, spruit or donga — it is the indigenous replacement for exotic weeping willow, hardy to frost and drought but preferring damp feet, and in a biome where 'the high erodibility of soils poses a major problem' it is the single best woody bank-binder you can strike from truncheons.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/salix-mucronata and https://treesa.org/salix-mucronata/ (indigenous riverine willow, up to ~10–15 m, hardy to frost and drought, prefers damp, riverbank stabilisation; recorded in the Ceres Karoo)

entries.why: Naturally a Gariep/Orange River tree, so it is already adapted to the exact corridor where most Nama-Karoo irrigated farming sits — SANBI notes it 'withstands the wind and summer drought', grows fast to a real canopy, and has non-aggressive roots, making it the best quick shade tree near buildings, dams and furrows.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-pendulina (SANBI: 4–9 m, fast growing, withstands wind and summer drought, hardy to about −1 to −7°C, native along the Orange/Gariep River through the Northern Cape)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — and the gazette explicitly warns the four listed alien Tamarix (aphylla, chinensis, gallica, ramosissima, all Cat 1b) are 'not to be confused with indigenous Tamarix usneoides'
entries.why: The answer to brak (saline/sodic) patches, calcrete pans and borehole overflow that kill everything else — SANBI records it as 'highly tolerant of ... heat, cold, drought, floods, and high concentrations of dissolved solids', a halophyte with a 30 m taproot, and it is SA's standard species for arid mine and dune rehabilitation.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tamarix-usneoides (SANBI: 0.6–6 m, narrowly columnar, halophyte tolerant of heat/cold/drought/floods/dissolved solids, taproot to 30 m, windbreak/dune/riverbank stabilisation, leaves eaten by stock, Northern Cape karoo river systems)

entries.why: The toughest indigenous fruit-bearer in the biome — evergreen, dense and twiggy, 'extremely hardy, drought-tolerant, and frost-resistant', explicitly recommended for 'small drier gardens, especially in the Karoo and semidesert areas', producing edible black berries plus a genuine evergreen windbreak and bird refuge in a landscape that has almost no other cover.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/euclea-undulata and https://www.africanlegacy.org.za/indigenous-plant/euclea-undulata-common-guarri (evergreen dense shrub to small tree ~7 m with often equal width, edible black berries, extremely hardy/drought-tolerant/frost-resistant, suited to Karoo and semi-desert)

entries.why: SANBI's own bee-forage infosheet names it as one of the two indigenous trees that 'stand out' for South African beekeepers, and it is a fast-growing, drought- and frost-resistant summer-rainfall tree whose leaves and fruit are valuable fodder — the hooked-and-straight thorns make it a genuine stock barrier when you plant it as a boundary line.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ziziphus-mucronata + https://www.feedipedia.org/node/81 (3–10 m, spreading crown, fast growing, drought and frost resistant, leaves and fruit valuable fodder); bee value from SANBI indigenous honey-bee forage infosheet

entries.why: The best-tasting reliably-available indigenous fruit here — SANBI describes the mature deep-red berries as having 'a pleasant sweetish taste' — and it doubles as a hedge/screen, dry-region shelter plant, bee plant and bird magnet, with the roots still used as a toothbrush.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/diospyros-lycioides (SANBI: up to 5 m, tolerates light frost in bushveld and Karoo regions, drought tolerant, edible deep-red berries with pleasant sweetish taste, hedge/screening, bees and birds)

entries.why: SANBI records it as 'restricted to the arid areas of the Karoo' — i.e. it is a true endemic of this biome, not a borrowed savanna species — is both frost- and drought-tolerant, gives edible fruit eaten raw or cooked, and is 'a valuable fodder plant' heavily browsed by game and livestock.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-robusta (SANBI: multi-stemmed shrub or small tree up to 3 m, restricted to arid Karoo and arid Eastern Cape, frost- and drought-tolerant, edible fruit, valuable fodder heavily browsed)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA — but a PROTECTED TREE under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998; plant freely, do not remove an existing one without a licence
entries.why: For the Bushmanland/Kalahari-edge west this is the classic stock shade tree and famine food — edible fruit, roots roasted as a coffee substitute, top-quality evergreen browse — with a root system recorded to 68 m, the deepest known of any plant, so it survives where nothing else holds leaf.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/boscia-albitrunca and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boscia_albitrunca (up to 10 m but usually much smaller, drought-resilient Kalahari/bushveld species, edible fruit and coffee-substitute, root system to ~68 m, culturally protected)

entries.why: A legume with genuinely edible seeds — eaten green, or roasted and ground as a meal — that naturally grows along dry stream banks in the Karoo, so it is the right species for the ephemeral drainage line you are already water-harvesting on, and its red nectar-rich flowers are a heavy sunbird and bee draw.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/schotia-afra-var-afra and https://suntrees.co.za/schotia-afra-karoo-boer-bean-karoo-huilboerboon/ (3–5 m, non-invasive roots, frost hardy when established but protect when young, high drought tolerance, edible seeds green or roasted, occurs along dry stream banks in the Little Karoo and drier Eastern Cape)

entries.why: Its tangled arching branch structure is exactly what a treeless, cover-poor landscape lacks — it is the best small-bird nesting and predator-refuge plant on this list, flowers July to November (bridging the pre-rain hungry gap for bees) and carries edible fruit, while being hardy, deciduous and drought resistant.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ehretia-rigida and https://suntrees.co.za/ehretia-rigida-puzzle-bush-deurmekaarbos/ (hardy, deciduous, drought-resistant shrub/small tree to ~5 m, tangled arching branches, edible fruit, flowers July–November attracting bees, heavily used by birds)

entries.why: The one indigenous plant here that is simultaneously a sweet-sour edible fruit and a genuine impenetrable stock-and-people barrier — 4–5 cm pronged spines on a dense evergreen frame — but it only survives to about −3°C once established, so keep it to the warmer eastern Karoo and to frost-sheltered north-facing slopes, never a valley bottom.
entries.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carissa_haematocarpa and https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/528768-Carissa-haematocarpa (evergreen densely branched spiny shrub/small tree to 2 m, spines 4–5 cm, edible sweet–sour purple-black fruit, survives −3°C when well established, young plants need protection below 0°C)

entries.why: The best climate fit of any exotic fruit for this biome: mature trees take about −10°C, it needs only ~200 chill hours (the lowest genuine chill requirement of any fruit crop), heat up to 38°C actively helps fruit development, and it wants dry summers — which is precisely a 200–400 mm Nama-Karoo year with a cold winter.
entries.source: Research brief on SA exotic-crop ranges (Hortgro/industry synthesis): mature trees tolerate ~−10°C, moderate frosts ~−5°C handled well, ~200 chill hours, up to 38°C aids fruit development; SA plantings ~1 167 ha, Western Cape 81% / Limpopo 10% / Northern Cape 7%

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only Opuntia ficus-indica matches 'ficus' in the 2020 list — no Ficus species is listed)
entries.why: Hardy to about −5°C and some cultivars to −10°C, it originates in hot low-humidity country with long sunny summers and short cool winters, thrives on the alkaline lime-rich soils that dominate 80% of this biome, and gives dense summer shade plus leaf fodder — the one caution is that a heavy March storm at ripening splits fruit, so pick early-season cultivars.
entries.source: Research brief on SA exotic-crop ranges: most fig cultivars withstand about −5°C, some to −10°C; modest chill requirement; needs warm dry weather during summer harvest as moisture cracks ripening fruit; SA core is the Klein Karoo (Prince Albert, Oudtshoorn)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only Prunus serotina, black cherry, is listed — Cat 1b)
entries.why: The Karoo's traditional dried-fruit tree, and the biome's 27–52 frost days actually supply the winter chill it needs; the real risk is not winter but SPRING — apricot blooms earliest of all the stone fruit, so a late-August frost can take the whole crop, which means north-slope, above-the-valley-floor siting and never a cold-air pocket.
entries.source: Research brief on SA deciduous ranges (Hortgro Tree Census 2021): of 1 604 338 national apricot trees, ~71% are in the Klein Karoo, i.e. the crop is Karoo-adapted; SA chill accumulation and rest-breaking context from Hortgro chill mapping

entries.why: Olive fails across most of subtropical South Africa because winters are too warm — it needs at least 10 weeks below ~13°C and June–July maxima under 21°C — and the cold dry Nama-Karoo winter delivers exactly that; the proven summer-rainfall pockets are Prieska, Upington and Hartswater, all on or near this biome, and it doubles as a permanent evergreen windbreak.
entries.source: Research brief on SA olive ranges (SA Olive / Olives SA): whole trees can die at −7°C; requires ≥10 weeks below 12.2–13.3°C to flower and June–July maxima below 21°C; workable summer-rainfall pockets named as Hartswater/Vaalharts, Prieska, Upington, Alicedale; drip or micro irrigation a prerequisite

entries.why: The classic Cape and Karoo werf hedge — it is one of the hardiest of all pome fruits, tolerates the wet feet at the edge of a flood-irrigation furrow that would kill an apricot, suckers into a dense stock-turning boundary, and gives a fruit that keeps and processes without refrigeration, which matters where power and cold chain are unreliable.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/ and Hortgro deciduous statistics context; quince is a traditional South African hedge-and-preserve crop, very frost hardy, low chill relative to apple/pear

entries.nembaStatus: Morus nigra is NOT listed. WARNING: Morus alba (white/common mulberry) IS Category 3 — existing trees may stand, but planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving one away is prohibited under s71A. SA nursery stock is frequently mislabelled or hybridised, so demand a verified M. nigra and keep the receipt.
entries.why: The classic Karoo homestead tree — deep summer shade, heavy fruit, and leaves that are prime chicken and stock fodder — and it is the LEGAL mulberry: the white mulberry every permaculture list recommends is Category 3 here and may not be planted at all.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, List 1 item 215 (Morus alba, Cat 3) — Morus nigra does not appear anywhere in the 383-taxa list (verified by parsing the gazette PDF locally)

entries.why: ARC Infruitec's low-chill breeding programme released peach, nectarine and plum selections performing on as few as 200–500 chill units, explicitly aimed at reducing climatic risk for emerging and small-scale producers — that makes peach the only temperate fruit with a genuinely national footprint, and it fruits early enough to beat the worst summer heat.
entries.source: Research brief on SA deciduous ranges (Hortgro Key Deciduous Fruit Statistics 2021 + ARC Infruitec low-chill programme): dessert peach 1 277 ha with Limpopo the LARGEST single district at 216 ha, ahead of Ceres (213 ha); ARC low-chill releases perform at 200–500 chill units

entries.why: The IDC identified Prieska — in this biome, on the Orange River — as one of the 'best-suited areas in the world' for pistachio, on hot dry summers, cold winters and good soils, and most of South Africa's pistachios still come from there; it is also one of very few nut crops that tolerates alkaline, saline and calcareous soils. Needs irrigation plus male pollinators (~1:8).
entries.source: https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-04-07-from-the-karoo-to-the-world-south-africas-r118bn-pistachio-dream/ and https://www.engineeringnews.co.za/article/new-nut-plant-gets-cracking-in-n-cape-1999-03-05 (Green Valley Nuts, 35 km from Prieska on the Orange River; IDC named Prieska among the world's best-suited pistachio areas for its hot dry summers, cold winters, Orange River water and soils)

entries.why: Only for the Orange River and Vaalharts irrigation corridor, where 80–90% of SA's pecans already grow: it actively NEEDS the Karoo's winter frost for budbreak, then the long hot low-humidity summer, and the low humidity keeps scab out — but SAPPA specifies 15 000 m³/ha/yr in the warm dry west (Prieska, Douglas, Upington), so do not plant it on a rainfed farm.
entries.source: https://www.sappa.za.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/sappa-water-requirement-per-production-area.pdf (SAPPA: 15 000 m³/ha/yr for the warm dry west — Vaalharts, Douglas, Prieska, Upington, Augrabies; peak 460–800 L/tree/day) + ARC Climate-Smart module (winter frost June–August needed for budding; humidity below 55%)

entries.why: MARGINAL — include only on a walled town erf, a north wall, or the frost-moderated Orange River corridor. Citrus needs the mean minimum of the coldest month above 2–3°C and dies below about −3°C, which the open Nama-Karoo plateau breaks most winters; but Northern Cape carries 1 866 ha along the river, and Graaff-Reinet's streets have been lined with orange and lemon trees for two centuries. Naartjie is the most cold-hardy citrus, so start there, not with lemon or grapefruit.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf (Northern Cape 1 866 ha; soft citrus 27 479 ha nationally and the most evenly spread type) + ARC Climate-Smart subtropical module (production confined to areas where temperature seldom drops below −2°C and almost never below −3°C; irrigation effectively compulsory); Graaff-Reinet street citrus per https://londontraveller.org/2016/03/19/flowers-trees-in-graaff-reinet/

entries.why: South Africa's best-documented stock-proof living fence — SANBI says it can be 'used to form an impenetrable hedge around a garden to keep unwanted animals and people out' — while also giving apricot-flavoured fruit, bulk leaf fodder and bee forage; in this biome plant it as the werf/kraal boundary in the eastern Karoo where it gets some run-off, not on the open western plains.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra (SANBI: impenetrable hedge to keep out unwanted animals and people, leaves used as bulk fodder, edible fruit, bee forage; ranked among priority indigenous fruit for KZN domestication)

entries.why: It flowers May to August — dead winter — in a fire-free biome where almost nothing else is in bloom, so it is the keystone winter nectar source for bees, sunbirds and mousebirds, and the bitter sap (Cape aloes) is a real cash crop that can be tapped by hand without machinery. Best in the eastern Nama-Karoo toward the Camdeboo and Sneeuberg.
