entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-ferox (SANBI: 2–3 m, flowers May–August, attracts sunbirds, weavers, glossy starlings and mousebirds, bitter yellow juice = Cape aloes, distribution spans Western/Eastern/Northern Cape into karoo edges, adapts from frost-free coast to winter-frost zones)

entries.why: A true central-to-eastern Karoo endemic that SANBI records as frost tolerant through cold Karoo winters, heavily browsed by game and stock, and feeding honeybees — critically, it flushes bloom opportunistically after each rain event rather than on a calendar, which is exactly the behaviour you want in a biome with 35–38% rainfall variability.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhigozum-obovatum (SANBI: 1.0–4.5 m, frost tolerant in cold Karoo winters, highly drought resistant, heavily browsed by game and stock, feeds honeybees, native to central to eastern Karoo, several flushes of bloom with sporadic rainfall)

entries.why: Planted at landscape scale on riplines across the Baviaanskloof and Camdeboo in the 350–500 mm zone, browsed by goats, cattle and kudu, and providing cattle fodder from about year three — but it is FROST-SENSITIVE, damaged around −2 to −3°C, so restrict it to the warm eastern Nama-Karoo and to mid-slopes; published SA restoration work maps cold-air pooling precisely because valley-bottom plantings fail.
entries.source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7183751/ (site selection for subtropical thicket restoration: mapping cold-air pooling in the South African sub-escarpment lowlands) + Baviaanskloof/Camdeboo ripline restoration practice; frost damage around −2 to −4°C per horticultural sources

entries.nembaStatus: CATEGORY 2 — a permit is required to possess, grow, propagate, move, sell or give it away. Without a permit it is legally treated as Category 1b (reg 4(4)). Apply to DFFE Biosecurity (AISpermits@environment.gov.za) BEFORE planting.
entries.why: The Karoo's standing drought reserve: evergreen, frost resistant, productive down to 150–200 mm once established, tolerant of the alkaline and saline soils that dominate this biome, and planted at up to 10 000/ha as a fodder bank that carries small stock through the years when the March rains fail. Included because it is genuinely standard Karoo practice — but it is the one entry on this list that is illegal without paperwork.
entries.source: NEMBA Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, List 1 item 47 (Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia — Category 2, verified by parsing the gazette locally) + https://www.feedipedia.org/node/184 and https://www.biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/amaranthaceae/atriplex_nummularia.htm (1.5–3 m tall, 2.5–3 m diameter, evergreen, frost resistant, drought tolerant, grows at 150–200 mm when established, up to 10 000 plants/ha)

entries.botanicalName: Opuntia ficus-indica (named spineless cultivars ONLY, e.g. the Burbank selections)
entries.nembaStatus: The species Opuntia ficus-indica is Category 1b, BUT the gazette states 'Spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed' and 'the fruit of the sweet prickly pear is not listed if used for human consumption'. Plant only certified spineless cultivar material — spiny plants and seedlings are Cat 1b and may not be planted at all. Research shows spinelessness can revert, so inspect and rogue.
entries.why: A living feed bank: cladodes are ~90% water, so in a drought a Karoo farmer feeds the plant instead of trucking water. Grootfontein Agricultural Development Institute imported 22 spineless Burbank cultivars in 1974 specifically as a drought-tolerant crop for the arid Karoo, and SA is now the only country still cultivating the Burbank lines. Fruit and cladodes are both human food.
entries.source: NEMBA Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, List 1 item 238 (verified locally: 'a. 1b; b. Spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed; c. The fruit ... not listed if used for human consumption') + https://agriorbit.com/growing-spineless-cactus-pear-as-livestock-feed-source/ and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140196318318810 (spinelessness stability / invasiveness)

entries.why: The single most important veld-restoration species in this biome and the reason erosion is fixable here: its stoloniferous habit means branches that touch the ground root and form new plants, anchoring and binding sandy soil, it is a key sheep fodder shrub, and it performs where annual rainfall is as low as ~200 mm. Commercial Karoo restoration seed is available (Renu-Karoo, Prince Albert).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/pentzia-incana and https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Pentzia-incana.pdf and https://www.feedipedia.org/node/118 (aromatic densely-branched shrublet 300–600 mm, stoloniferous habit prevents erosion and roots where branches touch ground, important sheep fodder in arid areas, occurs 900–1 700 m where rainfall can be as low as ~204 mm, sold for Karoo veld restoration)

entries.why: On SANBI's Kirstenbosch honey-bee forage list and a staple Karoo browse — SANBI notes these aromatic shrubs are readily browsed by livestock and, with the other Karoo bossies, give Karoo lamb its distinctive taste, so this shrub is literally the product differentiator for anyone marketing Karoo meat, as well as an aromatic pest-confuser between vegetable beds.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eriocephalus (SANBI genus account: readily browsed by livestock, contributes the distinctive taste to Karoo lamb) + SANBI Kirstenbosch list of plants that provide food for honey bees, https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.why: A legume, so it fixes nitrogen into these shallow base-rich soils, it is drought tolerant and naturally occurs 'in the western Karoo to Eastern Cape', its red flowers are a sunbird and bee magnet, and it is one of South Africa's most traded medicinal plants — real income from a metre-square plant. SANBI places it in light-to-no-frost zones, so give it shelter on the colder high plateau.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lessertia-frutescens (SANBI: shrublet 0.5–1 m, quite drought-tolerant, light to no frost, legume that fixes atmospheric nitrogen, sunbird-pollinated, occurs in the dry parts of southern Africa including the western Karoo to Eastern Cape)

entries.why: The engine of every irrigated Karoo farm: a deep-taprooted perennial legume that fixes nitrogen, cuts 6–8 times a season under flood or pivot irrigation, is the highest-value bee forage in the district, and supplies the mulch and hay you cannot otherwise generate in a biome where farmers report they simply have no mulching material. Frost-hardy, so the crown survives the −5°C nights.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/ (lucerne as SA's principal irrigated fodder legume; Karoo/Orange River flood-irrigation practice) — verified not listed against NEMBA Lists 2020 List 1 (no Medicago entry in the 383-taxa list)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed in South Africa (note: it is regarded as an invader in arid Australia and the Americas — plant it here as the indigenous species it is, but do not export the recommendation)
entries.why: Indigenous, tufted, rhizomatous and able to survive on as little as 300 mm a year — SANBI and SA pasture literature single it out as the drought-resistant summer grazing and hay grass for the drier parts of the country, and its growth form makes it ideal for soil cover and erosion control, which is the primary degradation risk in this biome. 'Molopo' is the standard SA cultivar.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/cenchrus-ciliaris + https://sagrainmag.co.za/2019/03/05/integrated-crop-and-pasture-based-livestock-production-systems-part-6-blue-buffalo-grass-cenchrus-ciliaris/ (indigenous tufted perennial with underground rootstocks, 'Molopo' cultivar to 1 500 mm, survives on as little as 300 mm rainfall/yr, ideal for soil cover and erosion control)

entries.why: The indigenous answer to a summer with no reliable irrigation: about 90% water, it stores drinkable moisture on the plant for months into the dry season — the San could not live permanently in the Kalahari without it — grows in low-fertility sandy soil, feeds stock, and its creeping habit is valuable as an intercrop providing soil cover to reduce erosion and water loss. Sow with the first real summer rain; frost kills the vine, which is fine because the fruit keeps.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/citrullus-lanatus + https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/tsamma-melon/ (fruit ~90% water, San/Nama dry-season water and survival food, drought resistant and hardy in low-fertility sandy soils, valuable intercrop providing soil cover to reduce erosion and water loss, seedcake used as livestock feed; occurs in the Kalahari area of the Northern Cape)

entries.why: The only nitrogen-fixing cover crop that fits the Nama-Karoo's brutally short window — rain peaks in March, first heavy frost arrives late April to early May — because it matures in 60–90 days, and it is triple-purpose: leaves eaten as a traditional green, dry grain stored, haulms fed to stock. ECHO trials in South Africa recorded over 100 kg N/ha in above-ground biomass from cowpea.
entries.source: DFFE national Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline, https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf + ARC-VOPI indigenous crops programme, https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (cowpea leaves eaten as a traditional vegetable); ECHO southern Africa N-accumulation trials

entries.why: ARC-VOPI's indigenous-crops programme names Amaranthus first among the traditional leafy vegetables it researches and promotes, precisely because it tolerates harsh conditions and is nutrient-dense (vitamin A, iron); as a C4 plant it thrives in 40°C heat when exotic spinach bolts, and it largely volunteers in disturbed ground, so the practice is managed encouragement rather than annual sowing. Harvest at 4–6 weeks / 15–30 cm.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (ARC-VOPI indigenous crops: Amaranthus spp. named as a core traditional leafy vegetable, tolerant of harsh conditions, nutrient-dense) + https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: Both the fruit and the young leaves are eaten (ARC lists Cucurbita leaves among the traditional greens), the thick-skinned landrace types store for months on a stoep without refrigeration — which matters where the nearest town is 80 km away — and the sprawling vine is the cheapest living mulch you can lay over bare, hot, evaporating soil between young fruit trees.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (ARC-VOPI: Cucurbita spp. traditional pumpkin, leaves eaten) + https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: South Africa's most used indigenous medicinal herb and one of the very few that is genuinely frost- and drought-hardy on the high Karoo plateau; it is on SANBI's Kirstenbosch bee-forage list, and its strong aromatic foliage makes it the standard confuser plant to interplant along vegetable-bed edges in a landscape with no natural pest-predator hedgerow.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/artemisia-afra (SANBI PlantZAfrica) + SANBI Kirstenbosch list of plants that provide food for honey bees, https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.why: SANBI describes it as the go-to plant 'where a drought-resistant, tough groundcover is required', it occurs naturally through the Northern, Western and Eastern Cape, its flowers feed bees almost year-round, and the leaf jelly is the household first-aid plant for burns, cracked skin and insect bites — which is not a garnish on a farm four hours from a clinic.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/bulbine-frutescens (SANBI: spreading clumps, horticultural zones 1–4 including light frost and winter frost, drought resistant/waterwise, used where a tough drought-resistant groundcover is required, leaf jelly for burns/rashes/blisters/insect bites, flowers attract bees, occurs Northern/Western/Eastern Cape)

entries.why: The only serious climber for this biome, and it is doing double duty: the Orange River corridor through the Nama-Karoo is South Africa's raisin and table-grape heartland, so the crop is proven here, and a vine trained over a north-facing pergola gives deciduous shade — dense cover through a 43°C January, bare branches letting winter sun into the house — which no evergreen can do.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/ and CGA/SATI regional context: the Orange River (Upington, Keimoes, Kanoneiland, Kakamas, Prieska, Douglas) is SA's principal raisin and early table-grape region, within/adjoining the Nama-Karoo; verified not listed against NEMBA Lists 2020 List 1 (no Vitis entry among the 383 taxa)

excluded: Prosopis glandulosa var. torreyana and P. velutina (mesquite / suidwesdoring) — NEVER PLANT. Category 1b in Eastern Cape, Free State, North-West and Western Cape; Category 3 in Northern Cape. This is the species that was actively promoted to Karoo farmers as a drought fodder and shade tree and became the biome's worst invader, drinking down water tables. Only 'the utilisation of the pods for fodder' from existing stands is unlisted in NC/EC/FS/NW/WC — harvesting pods is legal, planting is not.

Leucaena leucocephala — Category 2 nationwide (permit required; unpermitted = treated as Cat 1b). The single most likely trap in any tropical-permaculture species list. It would be frost-killed here in any case.
Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — Category 1b. The global permaculture chop-and-drop default; illegal to plant, propagate, move, sell or give away anywhere in South Africa.

Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) and Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust) — both Category 1b. Both are marketed internationally as the ideal dryland nitrogen-fixing fodder/timber trees. No permit route exists.

Morus alba (white mulberry) — Category 3. Existing trees may stand and the fruit may be eaten, but planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving away another one is prohibited under s71A. Use Morus nigra instead (included above) and verify the nursery label.

Eucalyptus camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis — LEGALLY PERMITTED here (the 2020 gazette states they are 'not listed within the Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes'), but excluded on hydrology, not law. At MAP 100–400 mm against MAPE ~2 400–2 600 mm, a bluegum windbreak is a net water extractor that will draw down shallow groundwater and boreholes; and the exemption falls away — reverting to Category 1b — the moment the tree is in a riparian area, a Protected Area or a Listed Ecosystem, which is exactly the drainage line a Karoo farmer would plant it on.

Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea) and Sesbania sesban — the two woody legumes DFFE's national Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline names for South African improved fallows and alley cropping. Both are warm-climate species; with 27–52 frost days and −5°C minima on this plateau they are killed or repeatedly set back to nothing. Use Vachellia karroo, Lessertia frutescens, lucerne and cowpea instead.
Moringa oleifera — frost-tender; killed outright by a normal Nama-Karoo winter despite being heavily promoted to SA smallholders.

Avocado, macadamia, mango, banana, litchi, papaya — all fail the frost gate. Avocado's survival floor is −4°C with the fatal exposure during August–September flowering; macadamia is explicitly 'not frost resistant'; mango wants winter average minima above 5°C; ARC states outright that optimum banana conditions exist nowhere in South Africa.

Apple and pear — chill is actually available here (27–52 frost days), but excluded on water and heat: they need consistent moisture through a 43°C summer and suffer severe sunburn, and 92% of SA apples sit in five Western Cape/Langkloof districts sustained by rest-breaking chemistry. Low-chill peach and apricot are the correct temperate fruit for this biome.

Chrysopogon zizanioides (vetiver) — the global erosion-control default and legal in SA, but it needs establishment irrigation and a longer warm growing season than the March-rain/May-frost window allows. Cenchrus ciliaris, stoloniferous Pentzia incana and stone bunds do the same work here without a water bill.

Agave americana and spiny Opuntia ficus-indica — both are genuinely used as live fences in the Karoo and Eastern Cape, but spiny prickly pear is Category 1b (only spineless cultivars are unlisted) and Agave escapes readily. Use Carissa haematocarpa, Ziziphus mucronata, Dovyalis caffra and Vachellia karroo brushwood instead.
Salix babylonica (weeping willow) — not NEMBA-listed, but DFFE's October 2025 briefing flags it as a Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer amplifier host. Use indigenous Salix mucronata for watercourses.

Sclerocarya birrea (marula), Strychnos spinosa (monkey orange), Vangueria infausta (wild medlar) — the top-ranked South African indigenous fruit species nationally, but all are frost-free savanna and coastal-belt trees that will not survive here.
Erythrina lysistemon (coral tree) — SA's traditional truncheon-planted living fence, but frost-tender and needing more water than this biome supplies.

Azolla spp., Nasturtium officinale (watercress), Pennisetum purpureum (Napier grass), Sambucus nigra (elderberry) — all NEMBA-listed (1b, 2, 2, 1b respectively) and standard fixtures of international permaculture designs. All excluded on legal grounds regardless of climate.
palettes.notes:
CLIMATE ENVELOPE USED (Mucina & Rutherford 2006, Strelitzia 19, Ch.7 + SANBI PlantZAfrica): MAP 70–500 mm, unit values 103–384 mm; rainfall peaks in MARCH in every vegetation type; APCV 35–38%; MFD 5–52 days; mean July minimum near zero in the Upper Karoo; extremes −5°C to 43°C; MAPE 2 360–2 615 mm and MASMS 82–84%; altitude 600–2 000 m, mostly 1 000–1 400 m; over 80% of the area on lime-rich, weakly developed, base-rich soil over rock, most soils shallower than 300 mm; effectively FIRE-FREE.

THE ONE CONSTRAINT THAT DRIVES THIS WHOLE PALETTE. Strelitzia 19 states it directly: rainfall peaks in March, and the average first date of heavy frost in the Western Upper Karoo is the first half of May (late April in the extreme south) — so the wet window and the frost-free window barely overlap, and 'the shortness of the growing season is further exacerbated in some years when rains arrive even later than usual or frost occurs earlier than average or, most seriously, when both occur in the same year'. Practically this means: (a) frost-sensitive annuals must be very short-season and planted the day the first real rain falls (cowpea, tsamma, pumpkin, amaranth); (b) the reliable production system is deep-rooted frost-hardy perennials plus irrigated winter/shoulder-season crops; (c) anything you plant that needs a five-month frost-free season will fail here in roughly one year in three.

WATER IS THE LIMIT, NOT FERTILITY — THE OPPOSITE PRESCRIPTION TO FYNBOS OR THE COASTAL BELT. These soils are base-rich and often high in potassium; the Bushmanland duribanks are 'high in most plant nutrients'. Do not spend money on general fertiliser here. Spend it on water harvesting (swales, riplines, stone bunds), mulch, windbreaks and shade — an evaporation-to-rainfall ratio of roughly 15:1 means those are structural, not decorative. The corollary is that the soils are ALKALINE and lime-rich, so expect phosphorus, zinc and iron lock-up on calcrete, and do not plant acid-loving species (blueberry, most proteas) at all.

TWO SUB-REGIONS AND A THIRD FARM ENTIRELY. (1) Western Bushmanland / Upper Karoo west of about Carnarvon–Prieska: under 200 mm, hotter, lower frost in the Blouputs/river country — this is Vachellia erioloba, Boscia albitrunca, Tamarix usneoides, spineless cactus pear, old man saltbush country, and rain-fed cropping is not realistic. (2) Eastern Upper Karoo / Camdeboo / Sneeuberg around Graaff-Reinet, Middelburg and Colesberg: 300–400 mm, colder (MFD to 52 days), grading into Albany Thicket — this is where Portulacaria afra, Dovyalis caffra, Carissa haematocarpa, Aloe ferox, Rhigozum obovatum and the deciduous fruit belong. (3) The ORANGE RIVER / VAALHARTS irrigation corridor is a different farm in the same biome: frost-moderated, unlimited scheme water, and it carries grapes, pecans, pistachios, citrus and lucerne at commercial scale. If the site is on the river, unlock the high-water entries; if it is on the open plateau, they are traps.

FIRE-FREE — DO NOT IMPORT FIRE MANAGEMENT. Unlike Fynbos and Grassland, 'the amount and nature of the fuel load is insufficient to carry fires and fires are rare within the biome'. There is no burn cycle to plan around, no fire-adapted regeneration to fall back on, and no firebreak requirement on retained veld. The corresponding risk is the opposite one: soil erodibility under overgrazing is the primary degradation mechanism, so ground cover and stocking discipline outrank every soil amendment on this list. That is why Pentzia incana, Cenchrus ciliaris and tsamma groundcover rank as highly as they do — they are the erosion answer.

FROST DAYS VARY MORE WITHIN THIS BIOME THAN THE BIOME LABEL SUGGESTS (5 to 52 days), and Strelitzia 19's MFD is a SCREEN-temperature statistic — real ground frost in a valley bottom will exceed it. Every 'light' and 'moderate' frost rating above (spekboom, Karoo num-num, soft citrus, bluebush) should be read as: north-facing mid-slope yes, cold-air-pooling valley floor no. Published South African thicket-restoration work maps cold-air pooling for exactly this reason.

WHY SOME SECTIONS ARE SHORT. The Medium trees section has only two entries and Small trees & large shrubs only four, because the Nama-Karoo genuinely has a thin woody sub-canopy — the natural vegetation is a drought-deciduous DWARF SHRUBLAND, so most of the biological action is in the shrub and groundcover layers, which is where this palette is deliberately deepest (13 of 43 entries). Padding the tree layers would be dishonest and would produce designs that fail. Conversely, the Climbers section has one entry because grape is the only climber with a real track record here.

THE ONE PERMIT ENTRY. Atriplex nummularia (old man saltbush) is Category 2 — the app must warn, not just label. Category 2 means a permit is required for possession, growing, moving, selling or giving away, and regulation 4(4) converts an unpermitted Category 2 plant into a Category 1b obligation to control it. It is included only because it is genuinely standard Karoo drought-reserve practice; every other entry is either unlisted or (spineless cactus pear) covered by an explicit cultivar carve-out in the gazette.

NEMBA VERIFICATION METHOD. Every species above was checked by grep against a locally parsed copy of the 383-taxa List 1 of the Alien and Invasive Species Lists, 2020 (GN 1003, GG 43726, in force 1 March 2021 per GN 115, GG 44182) — not from memory. Absences confirmed by alphabetical position: no Vitis, Medicago, Cenchrus, Punica, Cydonia, Pistacia, Carya, Citrus, Citrullus, Amaranthus, Cucurbita, Vigna, Salix, Searsia (only Rhus glabra, Cat 3), Vachellia, Ziziphus, Euclea, Diospyros, Grewia, Boscia, Schotia, Ehretia, Carissa, Dovyalis, Aloe, Portulacaria, Rhigozum, Pentzia, Eriocephalus, Lessertia, Artemisia, Bulbine or Tamarix usneoides entry exists. Note the gazette's own naming rule: where a scientific name changes or is misspelt, 'the common name of the species takes precedence' — so an app must match on both. Also note the list is versioned data, not a constant: DFFE's Risk Analysis Review Committee has ~140 taxa under review since March 2023, with 54 of 123 completed analyses recommending substantive listing changes. Stamp any stored status with 'GN 1003 of 2020' and re-check against https://www.dffe.gov.za/legislation/gazetted_notices.

entries.why: The one savanna fruit tree with a real commercial chain behind it (Marula Natural Products), it grows up to 1.5 m a year, is drought-resistant and feeds people, stock and bees from the same canopy.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/sclerocarya-birrea (frost-sensitive, drought resistant, 1.5 m/yr); size 9-12 m, occasionally 18 m, rounded spreading crown per https://www.feedipedia.org/node/27381

entries.why: Ranked first for domestication and commercialisation potential in the KZN indigenous-fruit prioritisation study, and its hard-shelled fruit stores for months without processing — rare in an indigenous fruit.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/strychnos-spinosa (sensitive to severe frost, prefers warmer climate, moderate water); 1-9 m tall, spread to 8 m per https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/speciesprofile.php?Spid=1562

entries.why: The most frost-tolerant of the top indigenous fruits, so it reaches the higher, colder bushveld where marula and monkey orange fail; fruit eats fresh, dries for storage or ferments.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vangueria-infausta — "varies in height from 3-7 m", hardy, withstands moderate cold, drought resistant

entries.why: The single most efficient plant on this list — a stock-proof thorn hedge, a fruit crop, livestock bulk feed and bee forage from one planting, and both frost- and drought-resistant.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra — "usually 3-5 m in height, but sometimes reaches 8 m", drought- and frost-resistant, impenetrable hedge, leaves used as fodder

entries.why: Sweet high-vitamin-C fruit ripening April to September fills the late-dry-season hunger gap when nothing else is bearing, under a dense evergreen shade canopy as wide as it is tall.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/mimusops-zeyheri — "up to 15 m under ideal conditions", crown "as wide as the tree is high", will not survive extreme frost, protect young trees 3 years

entries.why: Both frost- and drought-resistant and native to quartzite ridges, so it is the fruit tree for the rocky, shallow-soil ground on a bushveld farm that nothing else will crop.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/englerophytum-magalismontanum — "varies in height from 3-15 m", "hardy, frost and drought resistant", characteristic of rocky outcrops and quartzite ridges, fruit 40 mg vit C/100 g

entries.why: Very sweet, heavily-borne fruit on a drought-resistant shade tree — but strictly for the frost-free Lowveld and Mopane half of the biome, not the highveld margin.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/berchemia-discolor — "up to 20 m tall", "frost sensitive, therefore suitable for the frost free areas", drought resistant, fruit "edible, very sweet in taste"

entries.why: The most cold-hardy citrus and the most evenly spread crop in SA (27,479 ha nationally, 7,600 ha in Limpopo alone) — no chill requirement, so it works from Lowveld to bushveld margin wherever irrigation exists.
entries.source: CGA Key Industry Statistics 2025 (soft citrus by province) https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf; frost floor -2 to -3 degC and irrigation compulsory per ARC CSA module 6 https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: ARC rates lemon as suited to a broader range of climates than any other citrus; 5,727 ha in Limpopo, it bears almost year-round and sells locally without a packhouse.
entries.source: ARC CSA module 6: lemon "well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions" https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf; hectares from CGA 2025 https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf

entries.why: 74% of SA's mangoes are in Limpopo savanna: it survives 45 degC and under 300 mm, but only frost-free and below about 600 m, and it wants a DRY summer (humidity 55% or less) — a wet summer hurts it more than a dry one.
entries.source: SAMGA Mango Tree Census 2024 (LP 4,280 ha of 5,775 ha) https://mango.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Mango-Tree-Census-2024.pdf; 600 m altitude limit, 45 degC tolerance and monthly rainfall ceilings per ARC CSA module 6

entries.why: The only temperate fruit that genuinely reaches savanna: ARC Infruitec low-chill selections need only 200-500 chill units, and Limpopo is the single largest dessert-peach district in SA at 216 ha — the answer for frosty high-altitude bushveld where citrus and mango fail.
entries.source: Hortgro Key Deciduous Fruit Statistics 2021, dessert peach by district (Limpopo 216 ha, largest) https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.why: Actively promoted to Limpopo smallholders as a leaf crop, livestock feed supplement and medicinal; it coppices hard, so it doubles as a cut-and-carry protein and mulch source in the frost-free half.
entries.source: Not on the NEMBA 2020 plant list (verified against parsed GN 1003, GG 43726). SA promotion and uses per North West Dept of Agriculture production guide and https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/

entries.why: Bears within 10-14 months from seed with almost no footprint, so it is the fastest return on a new frost-free savanna plot while the slow indigenous trees establish.
entries.source: Not on the NEMBA 2020 plant list (verified against parsed GN 1003, GG 43726). Subtropical siting per ARC CSA module 6 https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: About 200 chill hours, mature trees to roughly -10 degC and fruit development helped by 38 degC — the widest temperature window of any fruit here, so it bridges the frosty and hot ends of the biome; 10% of SA's plantings are already in Limpopo.
entries.source: Pomegranate Association of SA / industry hectares (1,167 ha; WC 81%, LP 10%, NC 7%) and 200-hour chill, -10 degC mature hardiness; corroborated in https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/

entries.nembaStatus: Category 2 for plantations in Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West; Category 3 ELSEWHERE in those same provinces; not listed in Gauteng, Free State, Northern Cape and Western Cape. Fruit not listed if used for human consumption.
entries.why: Climatically the most forgiving exotic here (fruits to 1,515 m, drought-tolerant with age, takes light frost when mature) — but legally it is the biggest trap in the biome: in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North West and KZN a non-plantation guava is Category 3, so planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving one away is prohibited. Only recommend it in Gauteng, Free State, Northern Cape savanna, or under a Category 2 plantation permit.
entries.source: Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, List 1 item 292 (parsed text verified locally) https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf; climate/altitude per ARC CSA module 6

entries.why: Africa's defining agroforestry canopy: it drops its leaves in summer so crops grow in full light beneath it, then leafs up and drops protein-rich pods through the dry season when grazing has failed — a nitrogen-fixing canopy you can farm under.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/faidherbia-albida — "can grow up to 30 m tall", erect to roundish crown, "can survive occasional frost (up to 5 days per year)", "loses its leaves in summer, thus providing fodder during the winter", KZN/Limpopo/Mpumalanga

entries.why: A flat crown 16 m wide gives filtered shade over a wide area from a narrow trunk footprint, it fixes nitrogen and feeds bees, and it takes -2 degC to 40 degC — the widest-climate large tree in the biome. Limit pod feeding: they contain hydrocyanic acid.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-sieberiana-var-woodii — "12 m high, 16 m wide", "perfectly flattened crown", "tolerates temperatures ranging from about -2 degC to 40 degC", drought resistant, feeds honeybees, pods eaten by cattle and game but contain HCN

entries.why: The best single large shade tree for a homestead or kraal in hot dry bushveld — dappled shade rather than dense shade, so grass and understorey keep growing underneath it.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/senegalia-galpinii — "25-30 m" tall, "dappled shade on hot summer days", frost-tolerant but severe frost kills young branches, drought resistant, bees and wasps visit flowers

entries.why: The indigenous bank-stabiliser for the seasonal drainage lines that carry a savanna farm's runoff — reaches 4-6 m in three years, occurs in all nine provinces, and is surprisingly both drought- and frost-resistant once past two years.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/combretum-erythrophyllum — 4-6 m in three years, "surprisingly drought and frost resistant", seedlings frost-resistant after two years, occurs alongside rivers or where groundwater is available

entries.why: Fastest indigenous shade at 1-2 m a year, frost-hardy enough for the highveld margin, and deciduous — so it cools buildings and stock pens in summer and lets the winter sun through.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/celtis-africana — "up to 25 m" in forest, "up to 12 m" in gardens, dense semi-circular crown, "can withstand frost", "fairly drought resistant", 1-2 m per year, leaves browsed by cattle and goats

entries.why: The highest-value multi-function tree in South African practice — fixes nitrogen so grass thrives in its shade, feeds stock and game leaves flowers and pods, has one of the longest bee-forage seasons SANBI records, makes brushwood and live fencing, and grows a metre a year on almost nothing.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo — up to 12 m where water is adequate, rounded crown, frost hardy, drought resistant, nitrogen fixation "enables other plants to thrive in its shade", 1 m/yr; bee value per SANBI honey-bee forage infosheet https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/infosheet-indigenous-plants-honey-bee-forage-19-11-2014.pdf

entries.why: The default SA windbreak tree: evergreen, dense, frost- and drought-resistant, and with a non-aggressive root system so it can be planted along fence lines, dam walls and next to buildings without lifting them.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea — "usually grows to a height of 7 m and a width of 7 m", frost resistant, drought resistant, "suitable for use as a screen or barrier against wind", reduces erosion, leaves are valuable livestock fodder (taints dairy milk)

entries.why: Withstands intense heat, cold and drought equally, yields abundant nectar for a good honey crop, and its thorn branches are the traditional kraal-building material — the classic predator-proof livestock enclosure that costs nothing but labour.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ziziphus-mucronata — "3-10(-20) m high; with a spreading canopy", withstands "intense heat, cold and drought", flowers "produce abundant nectar and often yield a good honey", thorny branches used for kraals and hedges

entries.botanicalName: Olea europaea subsp. africana subsp. cuspidata
entries.why: Frost-, drought- AND wind-resistant from -5 to 40 degC with a 12 m dense evergreen spread, so it is the windbreak for the frostiest, driest savanna margin; its hard heavy wood also makes genuinely durable fence posts where termites destroy soft exotic poles.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana — "9 x 12 m" dense spreading crown, tolerates roughly -5 degC to 40 degC, "frost-, drought- and wind-resistant", "excellent fodder tree", feeds honeybees, "used to stabilize erosion dongas", wood used for "durable fence posts"

entries.why: Plant a dried branch section (truncheon) in a line and it roots in place — the fence post literally becomes the fence. Traditionally used exactly this way around kraals and waterholes, and its winter nectar carries sunbirds through the dry season.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/erythrina-lysistemon — "usually grows up to 10 m in height, occasionally reaching 12 m", spreading stocky crown, cold-sensitive (protect young plants), "planted as living fences around kraals, homesteads and waterholes", propagates from truncheons, abundant nectar for birds and insects

entries.why: A high-yield nectar and pollen tree — the best mid-summer bee crop in the bushveld — with young leaves and pods taken by livestock. Note: despite being a legume, nitrogen fixation is not documented for it, so do not count it as an N source.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/peltophorum-africanum — "about 15 m" with a spreading untidy canopy, frost tender for the first three years, drought resistant, "flowers provide a high yield of nectar and pollen", young leaves and pods eaten by livestock; nodulation NOT stated

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only Sesbania punicea, red sesbania, is listed — Category 1b)
entries.why: One of only two woody legumes DFFE's national agroforestry guideline actually names for South African improved fallows; it hits 4-5 m in six months, and maize is established directly into its prunings as a nitrogen-rich mulch.
entries.source: DFFE Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline ("Establishing maize into the mulch from Sesbania prunings") https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf; 7-8 m mature, 4-5 m in 6 months, tolerates light frost but killed by heavy frost per https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/speciesprofile.php?Spid=1522

entries.why: Planted a metre apart it forms a genuinely impenetrable evergreen thorn hedge, and unlike most security hedging every fruit — seed included — is edible.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carissa-bispinosa — "up to 5 m" but more often a dense bush, fast-growing evergreen, "rather frost-tender", moderately drought-resistant, plants a metre apart form "an impenetrable hedge", berries edible including the seed

entries.why: SANBI names it among the indigenous forage that "stands out" for SA beekeepers because it flowers May to September — it feeds the hive and the sunbirds straight through the savanna dry season when nothing else is in flower.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-marlothii — "usually 2-4 m tall (occasionally up to 6 m)", flowers "between May and September", tolerates frost, survives months without water, nectar-rich, feeds honeybees and sunbirds; bee ranking per SANBI honey-bee forage infosheet https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/infosheet-indigenous-plants-honey-bee-forage-19-11-2014.pdf

entries.why: Frost-hardy and drought-resistant understorey that produces edible fruit, feeds honeybees and is browsed by cattle, goats and game — a three-function filler for the gaps between bigger trees.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-occidentalis — "up to 3 m in height", scrambling deciduous shrub or small tree, frost-hardy, drought-resistant, fruits collected and dried, "leaves are browsed by cattle, goats and game", feeds honeybees

entries.why: Grows 600-700 mm a year into a dense tangled shrub that is the best beneficial-insect and bird refuge on this list, prunes into a hedge, and feeds kudu and impala. Fruit is technically edible but not worth harvesting — this one earns its place on habitat, not food.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ehretia-rigida — "up to 9 m in height" with untidy rounded crown, growth 600-700 mm/yr, hardy and drought resistant, light frost (Zone 5 Bushveld), "very attractive to birds and insects", can be used as a hedge, fruit "edible but not tasty"

entries.why: DFFE's guideline names it as one of only two woody legumes actually used in SA improved fallows, cut at 90 cm for hedgerow alley cropping — and it is already grown as a live fence in home gardens in Mpumalanga, Limpopo and KZN. Nitrogen, mulch, protein fodder and a storable pulse from one drought-tolerant shrub.
entries.source: DFFE Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline (pigeon pea improved fallow in KwaZulu-Natal, hedgerows cut at 90 cm) https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf; live-fence use in MP/LP/KZN and frost susceptibility at all growth stages per SA Journal of Plant and Soil 34(3) https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/02571862.2016.1266044

entries.why: A dry-bushveld and Kalahari native that is both frost-hardy and drought-resistant, giving vitamin-C-rich fruit for eating or brewing plus browse for kudu, giraffe and stock on deep sands where almost nothing else fruits.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-flava — "2-4 m tall" shrub or small tree, "quite hardy and can withstand frost", drought resistant, grows in dry bushveld on sandy soils, sweet vitamin-C fruit, leaves and fruit eaten by livestock and game

entries.why: Handles severe frost and extreme drought, so it is the shelterbelt understorey for the coldest, driest savanna sites; its camphor-scented foliage is a traditional insect repellent, useful where termite and pest pressure is high.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tarchonanthus-camphoratus — grows 2-9 m, semi-deciduous small tree, suitable for areas with severe frost, highly drought resistant, "excellent tree for creating tall hedges or windbreaks", binds sand, insect repellent properties

entries.why: A practitioner staple on the Kirstenbosch bee-forage list that tolerates moderate to severe frost and flowers late into autumn — the cheapest way to hold sunbirds, honeybees and beneficial insects on a savanna plot between tree flowerings.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/leonotis-leonurus — 2-3 m tall and 1.5 m wide, "can tolerate moderate to severe frost", drought and frost hardy, nectar attracts sunbirds and honeybees; listed in the Kirstenbosch honey-bee plant list https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.why: Planted on riplines at landscape scale in SA restoration work and browsed by goats, cattle and game — the highest fodder-per-drop-of-water plant available. Restrict it to the frost-free warm half of the biome: it takes only light frost and only once mature.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/portulacaria-afra — "2-5 m in height, although usually around 1.5-2 m in a garden situation", "can tolerate a moderate degree of frost, especially when mature", highly drought-resistant, heavily browsed by game and domestic stock, "indicated as a soil binder for preventing soil erosion", can be clipped as a hedge

entries.why: The single most useful herbaceous plant for savanna: ARC lists it among the traditional crops whose leaves are eaten, it fixes over 100 kg N/ha in above-ground biomass in SA trials, it smothers weeds as a living mulch, and the dry grain stores.
entries.source: ARC-VOPI Indigenous Crops programme (cowpea leaves eaten as a traditional vegetable) https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx; >100 kg N/ha in SA cover-crop trials per ECHO Community southern Africa data

entries.why: Savanna rain arrives as short intense convective storms on shallow soils — vetiver contour hedges are the practitioner default for stopping that runoff, forming a visible hedgerow within 3 months, and the trimmings become mulch and bedding. Use only the sterile SA cultivar.
entries.source: https://www.vetiver.co.za/vetiver-grass-faq/ — sterile non-invasive cultivar used in SA, slips 10-15 cm apart in a single row across the slope, establishment 3-6 weeks, hedgerow within 3 months, trim to 20-30 cm at 3-4 months, mature plants tolerate light frost and regrow after black frost. Not on the NEMBA 2020 plant list (verified)

entries.why: Top of ARC-VOPI's researched indigenous-vegetable set: nutrient-dense in vitamin A and iron, tolerant of harsh conditions, and largely self-seeding — in practice it is managed encouragement of a volunteer rather than a sown crop.
entries.source: ARC-VOPI Indigenous Crops programme https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx; also listed in https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: ARC includes it in the traditional-crop set because the leaves are eaten as a green long before the fruit matures — and its sprawl is the cheapest living mulch under young fruit trees through the hot wet months.
entries.source: ARC-VOPI Indigenous Crops programme (Cucurbita spp., traditional pumpkin, leaves eaten) https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only ornamental Ipomoea species — alba, carnea, indica, purpurea — are listed 1b)
entries.why: A dense edible mat that suppresses weeds, holds soil against summer storm runoff, and yields both storable tubers and edible leaves — the only groundcover here that is a staple carbohydrate in its own right.
entries.source: Not on the NEMBA 2020 plant list — verified against parsed GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 items 175-178, which list only I. alba, I. carnea subsp. fistulosa, I. indica and I. purpurea

entries.why: An ARC-researched traditional green that thrives in exactly the hot disturbed ground a savanna plot generates; harvest at 4-6 weeks and 15-30 cm, roughly half adult height, for the best leaf.
entries.source: ARC-VOPI Indigenous Crops programme (Cleome gynandra, spider plant) https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.why: Cited in southern African conservation-agriculture work as delivering large biomass for groundcover plus residual nitrogen; run it up maize stalks or a fence and it produces an edible pulse, dry-season fodder and a nitrogen-rich mulch from the same planting.
entries.source: Southern African conservation-agriculture cover-crop literature (5-50 t/ha biomass, 50-350 kg/ha residual N for the cowpea/lablab/velvet bean/sunn hemp group); not on the NEMBA 2020 plant list (verified against parsed GN 1003 GG 43726)

entries.why: A genuinely eaten indigenous climber — a Tsonga and Venda staple green in Limpopo, cultivated in smallholder home gardens alongside staple crops, and it climbs existing fences and maize rather than needing its own space.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/momordica-balsamica (indigenous, occurs in savanna, grassland and woodland); Limpopo Tsonga/Venda food use, 1-3 m stems and home-garden cultivation per J. Applied Pharmaceutical Science review https://www.japsonline.com/admin/php/uploads/4569_pdf.pdf

entries.why: Drought-resistant indigenous creeper with edible grape-like berries and a tuberous rootstock that survives fire and drought — useful scrambling through thorn hedges where it adds a fruit layer without adding footprint.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-tridentata — deciduous scrambling shrubby creeper to 3 m tall and about 1.5 m spread, drought-resistant, horticultural zones 1-5 including light to moderate frost, "clusters of red to black, edible, grape-like berries" 15-20 mm

excluded: Leucaena leucocephala (leucaena) — NEMBA Category 2 nationwide: a permit is required to possess, grow, move or sell it, and without one reg 4(4) treats it as Category 1b. It is the single most likely trap in any tropical-permaculture species list and it is exactly the tree an international savanna guide would recommend first.

Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — NEMBA Category 1b. The most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture literature is flatly illegal to plant here, and it is already invading Lowveld Mpumalanga and Limpopo, i.e. inside this biome.

Morus alba (white mulberry) — NEMBA Category 3. A staple of chicken-forage and silvopasture designs, but Category 3 prohibits growing, propagating, moving, selling and giving away; only trees that already stand may remain, and any Category 3 plant in a riparian area is deemed Category 1b.
Melia azedarach (syringa) — NEMBA Category 1b (Category 3 in urban areas). A ubiquitous bushveld shade tree that farmers already have, but it may not be planted or propagated.

Passiflora edulis (purple granadilla) — NEMBA Category 2 in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North-West, Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape (not listed only inside the proclaimed urban edge in those provinces). A permit is required across effectively the whole savanna, so it cannot be a default climber recommendation.

Eucalyptus camaldulensis, E. cladocalyx, E. conferruminata, E. diversicolor, E. grandis, E. tereticornis — Category 1b IN THE SAVANNA BIOME specifically, with Category 2 only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenue lining, plus narrow exemptions for cultivated land 50 m from untransformed land and within 50 m of the main farmhouse. Do not default to a gum windbreak here.
Pennisetum purpureum (elephant / Napier grass) — NEMBA Category 2, permit required. The obvious cut-and-carry fodder and biomass grass for this rainfall, and it is not freely plantable.

Prosopis glandulosa var. torreyana and P. velutina (mesquite) — Category 1b in North-West (and EC, FS, WC), Category 3 in Northern Cape; only the utilisation of pods for fodder is unlisted. Rules it out for the western Kalahari savanna where it would otherwise be tempting.
Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) and Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust) — both Category 1b. The two standard temperate permaculture nitrogen-fixers, both prohibited.

Azadirachta indica (neem) — NOT NEMBA-listed (verified against the 2020 list), and genuinely useful against termite and insect pressure, but it is a documented invader of riparian zones in tropical Africa and northern South Africa. Left out deliberately: unlisted is not the same as safe, and the indigenous alternatives here do the same jobs.

Opuntia ficus-indica (sweet prickly pear) — Category 1b, with spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections expressly not listed. Legal as a registered spineless cultivar and standard dryland fodder practice in drier biomes, but at 500-700 mm of summer rain the legume and grass fodder options here are better, and the spiny/seedy forms a farmer is likeliest to obtain are prohibited.

Dichrostachys cinerea (sickle bush) — indigenous, nitrogen-fixing, good pods and a natural thorn barrier, and still excluded: it is one of the primary bush-encroachment species degrading South African savanna rangeland. Never plant it deliberately.

Avocado (Persea americana) — ARC wants >1,000 mm evenly distributed and the survival floor is -4 degC, with the fatal exposure at August-September flowering, which is precisely when savanna frost still occurs. At 500-700 mm with a hard winter dry season it is an irrigation-and-microclimate gamble, not a palette species.

Litchi (Litchi chinensis) — the narrowest fruit envelope in South Africa: frost-free AND winter minima above 6 degC but below 14 degC AND summer maxima below 32 degC AND humidity above 50%. Only the Mpumalanga Lowveld, Soutpansberg and KZN coast qualify. Site-specific, not biome-wide.

Banana (Musa spp.) — ARC states outright that optimum conditions do not exist anywhere in South Africa; SA plantings sit in a handful of frost-free irrigated Lowveld and coastal pockets and are hit by hail and blowdowns most years.

Macadamia (Macadamia integrifolia) — SA's biggest nut industry and 15,068 ha of it is in Limpopo, but measured orchard water use is 750-850 mm/yr with irrigation regarded as necessary below ~1,000 mm rainfall. At 500-700 mm it is a fully irrigated capital crop, and it is explicitly not frost resistant. Excluded as a smallholder recommendation, not as a commercial one.

Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) — needs winter frost AND long hot summers AND low humidity AND 10,000-15,000 m3/ha/yr of irrigation (peak 460-800 litres per tree per day). That is why 80-90% of SA production sits on Northern Cape irrigation schemes. An irrigation-scheme crop, not a rain-fed savanna tree.

Apple and pear (Malus domestica, Pyrus communis) — 92% of SA apples sit in five Western Cape and Langkloof districts, sustained by rest-breaking chemistry. Savanna chill accumulation cannot carry them; low-chill peach is the temperate fruit that actually reaches this biome.

Fig (Ficus carica) — hardy to about -5 degC and low-chill, but it needs warm DRY weather through summer harvest because moisture cracks ripening fruit. A savanna harvest window falls in the December-February rain peak. Excluded on fruit integrity and disease, not on temperature.

Adansonia digitata (baobab) — indigenous, and its leaves and fruit are genuinely eaten, but it takes decades to bear, is confined to hot low-altitude Limpopo, and is effectively unplantable at farm-planning timescales.

Parinari curatellifolia (mobola plum) — a real indigenous fruit on Agribook's working list, but very slow-growing and confined to specific deep sandy sites; it does not justify a slot in a curated 45-species palette.
Sambucus nigra (elder) — Category 1b. Elderflower and elderberry hedgerows are a permaculture staple and are illegal to plant in South Africa.
palettes.notes:
SPLIT THIS BIOME BY FROST DAYS BEFORE USING THE PALETTE. Strelitzia 19 is explicit that only the lower-lying Mopane, Lowveld and Sub-Escarpment Savanna bioregions can be regarded as frost-free, while the Ghaap Plateau exceeds 120 frost days a year and the highveld margin of Central Bushveld drops below 0 degC in mean July minimum. A single "Savanna" list is therefore misleading: marula, brown ivory, mango, papaya, moringa and spekboom belong to the frost-free half, while low-chill peach, wild olive, camphor bush, karee, sweet thorn, buffalo thorn, crossberry, brandybush and Transvaal milkplum carry the cold half. The app should drive the palette off the site's own frost-day figure and bioregion, using the biome only as a first filter.

THE BIGGEST LEGAL GOTCHA HERE IS GUAVA, NOT THE USUAL SUSPECTS. Everyone knows to warn about leucaena and Tithonia. Almost nobody realises that Psidium guajava is Category 3 outside a permitted plantation in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North-West and KwaZulu-Natal — which is most of the South African savanna — meaning planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving one away is prohibited with no permit route. It is unlisted in Gauteng, Free State and Northern Cape. The exotic-fruit research correctly rates guava as one of the climatically broadest crops in SA; the law removes it from most of this biome. This must be geo-gated by province, not shown as a flat national status.

CATEGORY IS A FUNCTION OF PLACE, NOT JUST SPECIES. Guava, granadilla, mesquite and the six listed eucalypts all change category by province, biome or land-use in this biome alone, and reg 5(2) converts ANY Category 3 plant in a riparian area into Category 1b. A species-only lookup will be wrong a large fraction of the time on savanna farms, which typically contain a seasonal drainage line.

SOIL SPLITS THE BIOME AS HARD AS FROST DOES. Huntley's moist/dystrophic broad-leaved savanna (deep leached sands, genuinely nutrient-poor, the Nylsvley situation) needs imported phosphorus and nitrogen for annual crops, so the nitrogen-fixers and chop-and-drop species in this palette are doing real work, not decorative work. Arid/eutrophic fine-leaved savanna on basalt and dolerite is naturally fertile but often on cracking swelling clays that root-prune perennials seasonally — fine for annual grains and greens, hard on fruit trees. Site the orchard by soil, not by aspect.

TERMITE PRESSURE CHANGES THREE PRACTICAL DECISIONS. First, fence posts and structural poles: wild olive, buffalo thorn and monkey thorn heartwood are documented durable timbers, whereas soft exotic poles are consumed — plan for indigenous or treated posts. Second, mulch: coarse woody mulch in a termite-active savanna is consumed fast and can draw termites onto young trees, so favour living mulch (cowpea, lablab, sweet potato, pumpkin sprawl) over thick dry mulch collars, and keep mulch off the stem. Third, nursery stock: young transplants are the most-attacked stage, so plant larger, well-hardened stock and protect collars for the first two seasons. Camphor bush's insect-repellent foliage is a traditional adjunct, not a control.

WATER IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON EVERY EXOTIC FRUIT HERE. Savanna rainfall is sharply unimodal — most of the area receives under 5 mm in each of June, July and August — so all eight exotic fruit entries assume irrigation or serious water harvesting through the dry season, and citrus in particular is described by ARC as requiring irrigation in essentially all South African situations. The indigenous entries do not carry that assumption.

FIRE IS A DESIGN INPUT. Savanna burns near-annually and its wild vegetation is adapted to it (under 10% of plants killed, resprouting from stem bases). A farm here must plan firebreaks around the orchard and homestead, and fire remains a legitimate bush-encroachment and browse-height tool on retained veld — unlike Albany Thicket, Forest or the karoos where importing fire is destructive.

WHAT THIS PALETTE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM. Peltophorum africanum is a legume but nodulation is not documented for it, so it is listed for nectar, fodder and shade only — do not count it as a nitrogen source. Ehretia rigida fruit is edible but poor, so it earns its slot on habitat and hedging. Vachellia sieberiana pods contain hydrocyanic acid, so pod feeding must be limited. Vachellia karroo is itself a bush encroacher on overgrazed rangeland — plant it deliberately in rows and hedges, and manage it, rather than letting it thicken. Sesbania sesban and pigeon pea are both frost-killed, so on the cold half of the biome they are summer annuals in practice rather than standing shrubs.

palettes.biome: Indian Ocean Coastal Belt (IOCB) — KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape coast; MAP 819–1272 mm summer-dominant with no true dry season; mean frost days 0–1; MAT 19–22°C; lowest rainfall variability (APCV 18–21%) and lowest potential evaporation (MAPE 1549–1904 mm) of any South African biome; humid, cyclone-exposed, salt-laden onshore wind; sandy, leached, acidic soils turning calcareous within a few hundred metres of the beach

entries.why: The one species that does everything the seaward edge of an IOCB farm needs at once — it grows natively on the dunes 'from Humansdorp in the Eastern Cape northwards through KwaZulu-Natal', is wind- and salt-resistant, planted 1 m apart makes a genuinely impenetrable stock- and people-proof hedge, and still gives vitamin-C-rich fruit off the same plants.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carissa-macrocarpa (SANBI PlantZAfrica: 'can grow into a small tree up to 4 m high'; 'wind resistant and can grow in coastal areas'; 'plant 1 m apart to form a dense, impenetrable hedge')

entries.why: Ranked among the priority indigenous fruits for KZN domestication and the classic South African stock barrier, it stacks four functions on one line of planting — fruit for jam, an impenetrable boundary hedge, browse for livestock and bee forage — and at 600 mm of growth a year it closes a boundary fast.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra (SANBI: 'usually 3-5 m in height, but sometimes reaches 8 m'; growth 'approximately 600 mm per year'; 'used to form an impenetrable hedge'; 'the leaves are used as fodder'). Note: SANBI now gives the accepted name as Dovyalis afra following the 2024 IBC vote replacing 'caffra' epithets.

entries.why: The IOCB's waterlogged depressions and humic-gleysol hollows are a liability for almost every other fruit tree, and this is the species that turns them into production — a water-loving streambank tree that fruits, stabilises the bank and is one of the biome's heaviest nectar producers for bees.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/syzygium-cordatum (SANBI: 'grows to a height of 8-15 m'; 'a water-loving tree… best planted in full sun near a stream or river bank or any damp area'; flowers 'produce abundant nectar')

entries.why: An evergreen coastal-forest canopy tree that carries a real fruit crop for jams and jellies while doing the structural work of the upper storey — shade, litter and a bird-feeding station — which is exactly the nutrient-cycling role you must deliberately replace when you clear IOCB dune forest.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/harpephyllum-caffrum (SANBI: 'grows up to 15 m tall'; 'usually found in riverine forests'; fruit 'commonly used for making jams and jellies'). Accepted name now Harpephyllum afrum (2024 IBC emendation); H. caffrum is the widely-used synonym.

entries.why: Ranked first for domestication and commercialisation potential in the KZN indigenous-fruit prioritisation study, it grows natively in coastal bush and sand forest, the hard-shelled fruit stores and sun-dries without a cold chain, and its thorns make it useful on a boundary line.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/strychnos-spinosa (SANBI: habitat 'bushveld, riverine fringes, sand forest and coastal bush'; 'grows relatively fast from seed'; fruit 'edible and often sun dried as a food preserve') and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8703348/ (size 'typically 4-5 m tall, but up to 10 m')

entries.why: This is the tree for the first line of defence against salt-laden onshore wind — it grows naturally in dune forest 'from the high tide mark' and 'flourishes even within reach of the salty sea sprays', dropping to a shrub in full exposure, and it still gives sweet edible fruit where nothing else survives.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/mimusops-caffra (SANBI: 'up to 15 m high'; 'in an exposed habitat it forms a shrub'; 'dune forest from the high tide mark in KwaZulu-Natal and the former Transkei'; fruits 'edible and pleasantly sweet'). Accepted name now Mimusops afra; M. caffra is the familiar synonym.

entries.why: Its South African range starts 'just north of Durban', so it is a genuinely IOCB-north species rather than a generic recommendation, and the combination of a delicious fruit, tolerance of both drought and heavy rain, and a slow narrow habit makes it the best fit for a tight understorey slot in a Zululand or Maputaland food forest.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/garcinia-livingstonei (SANBI: 'a small tree reaching 18 m in East Africa, pyramidal when young but later spreading'; 'these trees grow slowly'; 'from just north of Durban as far as Somalia'; 'quite hardy to both drought and heavy rain'; 'notably sensitive to cold')

entries.why: Plant it where the water table sits high and roots would drown anything else — it tolerates waterlogging, holds a streambank or wetland margin, and yields date-like fruit, palm heart, sap for palm wine and leaf fibre for weaving from a single multi-stem clump.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/phoenix-reclinata (SANBI: 'up to 12 m but is most often between 3 and 6 m'; 'sometimes forming a dense, bushy clump'; 'almost always associated with water'; 'tolerant of waterlogged conditions in cultivation'; fruits 'edible and apparently taste quite similar to the commercial date')

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA, but PROTECTED under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998 — a licence from DFFE is required to cut, damage or remove it once planted
entries.why: Only worth planting in the Maputaland and Zululand wooded-grassland end of the IOCB, where it belongs and where it is the highest-yielding indigenous fruit tree with a real commercial chain, growing up to 1.5 m a year — but flag the protected-tree status on the plan, because siting one badly commits the farm permanently.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/sclerocarya-birrea (SANBI: 'a growth rate of up to 1.5 m per year'; distribution 'KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga'; 'very sensitive to frost') and https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/saprotectedtrees2011.pdf (National Forests Act protected tree list)

entries.why: The KZN north and south coasts are one of only about five frost-free pockets in the country where bananas are commercially viable, and on a smallholding the clump is a two-for-one — the highest calorie return per square metre available here, plus a standing supply of pseudostem and leaf for the mulch that these leached sands constantly demand.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf (ARC Climate-Smart Agriculture module 6: SA banana regions are Onderberg/Komatipoort, Kiepersol, Levubu, Letaba and the KZN north and south coasts; 'nearly all bananas are irrigated'; winds above 50 km/h cause blowdowns)

entries.why: KwaZulu-Natal carries roughly 23 800 ha of macadamia — the biome's dominant cash crop and the one exotic here with an established buyer network — and the IOCB's ~1000 mm of evenly distributed rain plus the lowest evaporation in the country is the closest South Africa gets to its water demand without irrigation.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf (ARC: requires 16–25°C, 'should not be considered frost resistant'); SAMAC tree census ~65 516 ha national, KZN ~23 806 ha; Water Research Commission/Mayo Macs measured 750–850 mm/yr in the Nelspruit area

entries.why: KZN carries 3 429 ha and the biome's >1000 mm evenly distributed rainfall matches ARC's stated requirement almost exactly — but plant it on a raised bed on the free-draining dune sand, never in a depression, because the same rainfall that makes it viable also makes Phytophthora cinnamomi root rot the main way it fails here.
entries.source: https://avocado.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/SAAGA-Industry-Census-Report-2024.pdf (KZN 3 429 ha of 19 240 ha censused) and https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf (ARC: >1 000 mm/yr evenly distributed; absolute floor −4°C; Mexican race hardiest)

entries.why: The fastest fruit on the list to first harvest and the ideal gap-filler in a young IOCB food forest — it needs the frost-free, humid, year-round-moist conditions this biome uniquely supplies, occupies almost no ground area, and is short-lived enough that it can be planted knowing the canopy trees will replace it.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/ (Agribook: papaya is a frost-free subtropical grown in the SA coastal and Lowveld belt) and https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: Citrus has the broadest reach of any fruit crop in South Africa, but on this humid coast the type matters more than the genus — KZN's 714 ha of lemon against 103 ha of soft citrus reflects that lemon 'is well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions', while navels need a cold-month mean below 13–14°C the IOCB never delivers.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf (CGA 2025: KZN lemon 714 ha, soft citrus 103 ha, of 2 369 ha total KZN citrus) and https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf (ARC on lemon adaptability and navel coldest-month means)

entries.why: Litchi is the narrowest-range fruit crop in South Africa and the KZN coastal belt is one of only three areas in the country that satisfies its whole envelope at once — frost-free, winter minima above 6°C but below 14°C to trigger flowering, summer maxima under 32°C, and humidity above 50%.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf (ARC names the Mpumalanga Lowveld, the Soutpansberg and the KwaZulu-Natal coastal belt as the only qualifying areas; full climatic envelope as stated)

entries.why: The best shade-tolerant cash crop for the layer under macadamia or banana — the KZN south coast supports South Africa's longest-standing coffee farm and its largest, and the region's acidic soils, high humidity and coastal winds are exactly what arabica wants, which lets a smallholder monetise the understorey rather than leaving it idle.
entries.source: https://www.kzn-southcoast.com/beaver-creek-coffee-farm/ (Beaver Creek near Port Edward, 60 000 trees, SA's oldest and Africa's most southern coffee farm) and https://iol.co.za/mercury/2025-09-24-bid-to-transform-kzns-south-coast-into-a-coffee-production-hub/ (Mpenjati Coffee Farm, 55 ha, SA's largest; regional production compact)

entries.why: The single most valuable canopy tree for an IOCB design — a nodulating legume that puts nitrogen into these nutrient-poor leached sands, drops fine feathery litter for mulch, and whose flat crown and small leaflets cast dappled rather than dense shade, so a crop layer can genuinely work beneath it.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/albizia-adianthifolia-var-adianthifolia (SANBI: 'can reach a height of over 40 m'; 'a conspicuous flat crown'; occurs Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, Mpumalanga in 'moist and tropical areas such as forests'; 'naturally the tree occurs in frost-free areas'; planted 'to conserve soil and control erosion'). Height/width given are a farm allowance at 25–30 years, not the forest maximum.

entries.why: A fast-growing evergreen with a dense spreading crown — the tree to plant for deep shade over the homestead, the kraal and the water point rather than over crops, and its heavy leaf drop is the most reliable free mulch source on a coastal farm where soil organic matter has to be built deliberately.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/trichilia-emetica (SANBI: 'up to 25 m high… it has a dense, spreading crown'; 'a fast grower and can be planted throughout the year'; 'able to tolerate moderate winter drought and slight frost'; oil extracted from the seeds)

entries.why: The highest-value wildlife tree you can plant here — heavy crops of edible figs turn it into a bird and bat feeding station that pulls pollinators and pest predators onto the farm — but keep it 15 m from any building, pipe or paving, because the root system is aggressive.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ficus-sur (SANBI: 'reaching up to 35 m high, with… a massive, spreading crown'; 'fast-growing'; 'restricted to frost-free areas with moderate rainfall'; 'inadvisable to plant… near buildings, paving, sewer lines or walls as they may damage them with their aggressive root system'; figs 'readily eaten by local people'). Height/width given are a managed farm allowance.

entries.why: The only fast large tree on this list that is deciduous, which is precisely why it earns a place — it shades the growing season and then drops its leaves so winter sun reaches whatever is planted beneath, and the leaves are browsed by cattle and goats, so the leaf fall is fodder rather than waste.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/celtis-africana (SANBI: garden height 'up to 12 m', forest 'up to 25 m'; young trees put on '1 to 2 m per year'; occurs 'from the coast up to 2 100 m' including coastal dunes; 'can withstand frost'; 'leaves are browsed by cattle and goats')

entries.why: The backbone of an IOCB shelterbelt — fast, evergreen, dense, salt- and wind-hardy, native to the dune forests it will be protecting, tolerant of hard pruning so you can hold it at the porosity you want, and an excellent honey tree into the bargain.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/brachylaena-discolor (SANBI: 'in the garden this tree grows to a height of 4-10 m'; 'fast growing evergreen'; 'tolerates pruning and coastal conditions'; 'often used to stabilise dunes'; 'makes excellent hedge or windbreak'; 'an excellent bee tree'). Aim for 40–60% porosity in a shelterbelt, the design target used by the SA macadamia industry.

entries.why: The only tree here where the fence post is the fence — a whole dried branch pushed into the ground roots and grows, so a boundary can be established in one afternoon at zero nursery cost, and it happens to be a nodulating legume that pours winter nectar into the sunbird and insect guild when almost nothing else is flowering.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/erythrina-lysistemon (SANBI: 'usually grows up to 10 m in height, occasionally reaching 12 m'; 'a fast-growing, undemanding tree'; survives 'a winter minimum of −7 to −1 °C'; occurs in 'coastal dune bush'; truncheons 'planted into a pot filled with sand or even directly into the soil'; trees 'were planted as living fences around kraals, homesteads and waterholes')

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but Sesbania punicea (red sesbania) is Category 1b; do not let a nursery substitute it
entries.why: South Africa's own agroforestry guideline names this and pigeon pea as the two woody legumes actually used as improved fallows here, and it is the rare N-fixer that thrives in the waterlogged hollows of an IOCB farm, initiating floating adventitious roots and aerenchyma when flooded, then coppicing for high-nitrogen chop-and-drop mulch.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf (DFFE Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline: Sesbania prunings as mulch for maize; improved fallows in South Africa) and https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb2/speciesprofile.php?Spid=1522 (World Agroforestry: grows to 7–8 m; 'outstanding ability to withstand waterlogging'; 'coppices readily and provides mulch of high nutrient content')

entries.why: A fast informal hedge that pays for itself in ecosystem services — nectar-rich flowers borne on the old wood feed sunbirds and bees, the berries feed fruit-eating birds, and it can flower in its second year, so a beneficial-insect and bird corridor is functioning within two seasons rather than ten.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/halleria-lucida (SANBI: '2-5 m' in exposed situations, 'up to 12 m' where well watered and protected; 'fast growing'; 'young plants may flower for the first time in their second year'; 'hardy to frost (zone 9: minimum −7 °C)'; 'suitable for use as an informal hedge'; berries 'edible, but never tasty')

entries.why: Specifically for the black-mud estuarine margins and permanently wet hollows that the IOCB's humic gleysols create — it grows rapidly in conditions that would kill every fruit tree on this list, holds the bank, and its young leaves are edible, so a boggy corner becomes a functioning part of the design instead of dead ground.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/barringtonia-racemosa (SANBI: 'usually 4-8 m tall, but occasionally reaches 15 m'; 'grows rapidly from the seed or cuttings'; habitat 'black mud on the banks of the estuaries', prefers 'very humid, moist conditions'; 'cannot tolerate even mild frost'; 'young leaves are edible'; conservation status 'not threatened in any way')

entries.why: The most documented support species in South African smallholder practice and the honest replacement for the Tithonia and Leucaena that global permaculture lists push and NEMBA prohibits — a protein grain, high-nitrogen chop-and-drop cut at 90 cm, cattle fodder and a hedgerow, all from one shrub that tolerates the acid sands of this coast.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf (DFFE: 'pigeon pea being grown as an improved fallow in KwaZulu-Natal'; hedgerows cut at 90 cm) and https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/02571862.2016.1266044 (SA Journal of Plant and Soil: six KZN smallholder landraces trialled at Makhathini and Newlands; 'up to 4 m high')

entries.why: South Africa's most consistently recommended multi-function indigenous tree, and it has its own dune-forest form along the KZN coast north of the Tugela — it fixes nitrogen so well that 'grasses and other plants thrive in its shade', gives leaves, flowers and pods as fodder, produces heavy nectar flows for bees, and its thorny brush makes kraal fencing.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo (SANBI: 'a maximum of about 12 m where there is good water'; growth 'up to 1 m per year'; a dune-forest form occurs 'along the coast of KwaZulu-Natal northwards of the Tugela river'; 'frost and drought hardy'; 'a particularly good fodder tree'; 'the flowers produce lots of nectar and pollen for bee-farming')

entries.why: At 800 mm of growth a year it is the fastest evergreen screen available in coastal bush, it clips into a formal hedge, its root system is not aggressive so it can go tight against buildings and beds, and beekeepers rate it for the sheer volume of pollen and nectar it produces.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/buddleja-saligna (SANBI: 'up to 10 m tall in warm moist areas but usually 4 to 5 metres in Highveld areas'; 'grows up to 800 mm per year'; occurs 'in coastal bush'; 'evergreen, frost hardy and drought resistant'; 'the large amounts of pollen and nectar it produces makes it popular with bee farmers'; 'does not have an aggressive root system')

entries.why: A tough evergreen from the coastal scrub and dune forest of exactly this biome — it makes an attractive dense hedge on the salt-exposed second line behind the milkwoods, carries edible fruit, and provides the shrub-layer bird cover that a cleared IOCB site loses first.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-natalensis (SANBI: 'up to 5 m tall' as 'a scrambling, evergreen shrub or a small tree'; occurs in 'coastal scrub and dune forests of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape'; fruits edible and 'eaten, and dispersed, by birds'; functions as 'an attractive garden hedge')

entries.why: The shrub layer under a closing canopy is where most IOCB designs go empty, and this is the species that fills it — it grows equally well in sun or deep shade, comes from dune bush and forest margin, and its berries are the single most reliable bird magnet in the understorey.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/psychotria-capensis (SANBI: '3-8 m tall, with a slender stem, horizontal branches'; habitat 'evergreen forests, forest margins, shrub and dune bush'; 'growing equally well in sun or shade'; berries 'irresistible' to bulbuls, starlings, robins and barbets)

entries.why: Planted around kraals across South Africa as a living stock fence, it is also the plant that fills the biome's nectar gap — it flowers in May to July when almost nothing else does, holding sunbirds and bees on the farm through winter — and it grows from sea level upward, propagates free from cuttings and is a first-aid medicine plant.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-arborescens (SANBI: 'develops into a multiheaded shrub 2-3 m high'; 'fast-growing'; grows 'at sea level right up to the tops of mountains'; flowers 'during the cold winter months (May-July)'; 'planted around kraals… as a living fence'; 'can tolerate moderate frost')

entries.why: One of the very few plants that is simultaneously human food, browse for cattle and goats, honeybee forage and bird habitat, and it grows natively in coastal dune bush and in the shade of other trees, so it can be tucked under a canopy rather than competing for open ground.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-occidentalis (SANBI: 'up to 3 m in height', a 'scrambling deciduous shrub or small tree'; occurs in 'coastal dune bush'; 'frost- and drought-hardy'; fruits 'collected and dried for later use'; 'leaves are browsed by cattle, goats and game'; 'feeds honeybees')

entries.why: The workhorse pollinator hedge of the KZN and Eastern Cape coast — fast, evergreen here, native to exactly this coastal scrub, clips formal or bushes out informal, and it is sunbird-pollinated with honeybees and butterflies working the same flowers, which is a lot of beneficial-insect traffic for a plant that costs nothing to strike from cuttings.
