entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tecomaria-capensis (SANBI: 'may grow up to 2-3 m high and spread more than 2.5 m'; 'fast growing'; occurs in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape coasts; 'commonly planted as a hedge, both formal (clipped) and informal'; 'pollinated by nectar-feeding birds, especially sunbirds'). Tecomaria capensis is the widely-used synonym.

entries.why: A fast-growing narrow shrub that pumps copious nectar and pulls in at least six sunbird species plus bees and butterflies, flowering in autumn and winter in many areas — plant it in the gaps along paths and bed ends where a wider shrub would not fit, and harvest the leaves for the traditional cough and fever remedies.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/leonotis-leonurus (SANBI: '2-3 m tall and 1.5 m wide'; 'fast-growing'; occurs 'at altitudes ranging from 5-1980 m'; 'can tolerate moderate to severe frost'; 'flowers profuse copious nectar which attracts birds, bees and butterflies'; six named sunbird species)

entries.why: The default living mulch of this coast — a dense running mat that keeps 1000 mm of summer rain from splashing bare leached sand, suppresses weeds under young fruit trees, and yields both a storage tuber and leaves eaten as imifino, so the ground cover and the crop are the same plant.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/ (Agribook, SA indigenous and traditional food crops) and https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (ARC-VOPI indigenous crops programme)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA 2020 — but it is under active invasion-risk assessment in South Africa, so keep it in managed beds and out of natural wetlands
entries.why: The staple carbohydrate of this exact strip of coast — taro is 'mainly produced in the subtropical coastal belt, stretching from Bizana in the Eastern Cape to the KwaZulu-Natal north coast' — and it turns the biome's waterlogged humic-gleysol depressions into the most productive ground on the farm, while being far less blight-prone than potato in these humid conditions.
entries.source: https://researchspace.ukzn.ac.za/items/c7065b4f-68db-4269-87e8-fd25c8a44d32 (UKZN: small-scale taro production in KwaZulu-Natal, wetland and dryland propagule performance) and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0254629924007622 (SAJB: taro global invasion history and prognosis for South Africa)

entries.why: The N-fixing cover crop with the strongest South African trial record — ECHO trials here measured over 100 kg N/ha in above-ground biomass — and unusually it is a triple crop, giving dry beans, leaves eaten as morogo, and livestock fodder, so the fertility-building rotation feeds the household in the same season.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (ARC-VOPI names Vigna unguiculata among its traditional leafy vegetable crops) and https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf

entries.why: South Africa's two pineapple districts — Bathurst on the Eastern Cape coast and Hluhluwe in Zululand — sit inside this biome, and planted on the contour the dense tufts act as a living terrace that holds sandy slopes, which is the single most useful thing a cash crop can also do here.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/ (Agribook: SA pineapple production concentrated in the Eastern Cape coastal Bathurst/Peddie area and Hluhluwe in northern KwaZulu-Natal)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (the commercial South African material is the sterile, non-seeding Sunshine/Monto type)
entries.why: The IOCB has the country's highest rainfall on its most erodible substrate, and vetiver is the practitioner default for holding it — slips at 10–15 cm in a single contour row form a visible hedgerow within three months, stop gully heads advancing, and the twice-yearly trim comes off as mulch and bedding.
entries.source: https://www.vetiver.co.za/vetiver-grass-faq/ (Vetiver SA: slips 10–15 cm apart in a single row across the slope, planted in the rainy season, establishment 3–6 weeks, hedgerow within 3 months, trim to 20–30 cm at 3–4 months)

entries.why: The flagship of ARC-VOPI's indigenous-crops programme and the most-eaten traditional leafy green on this coast — it volunteers in disturbed ground so the practice is managed encouragement rather than sowing, it delivers vitamin A and iron on soils too poor for exotic spinach, and it can be cut at 4–6 weeks and 15–30 cm.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx (ARC-VOPI indigenous crops: Amaranthus spp. named first among the traditional leafy vegetables it researches and promotes)

entries.why: The indigenous answer to bare soil in shade — a perennial scrambler native to the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal that covers ground under trees where sweet potato and cowpea will not run, flowers almost continuously for pollinators, and its leaves are foraged as a leafy vegetable.
entries.source: https://www.africanlegacy.org.za/indigenous-plant/asystasia-gangetica-subsp-micrantha-creeping-foxglove (indigenous perennial groundcover/scrambler, 30–60 cm) and http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3885-4 (SANBI Red List: indigenous, Eastern Cape to KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo)

entries.why: Native to eastern and southern Africa and already intercropped with maize by KZN smallholders at Bergville, it is the climber that fixes nitrogen up a trellis, over a fence or through a young orchard while producing an edible bean, palatable hay, weed suppression and erosion control from the same planting.
entries.source: https://sagrainmag.co.za/2019/03/04/integrated-crop-and-pasture-based-livestock-production-systems-part-20-lablab-lablab-purpureus-l-dolichos-lablab-l/ (SA Grain: cover crop, green manure, erosion control, weed suppression; grazed by cattle, sheep, goats and pigs; KZN Bergville maize intercrop; native to eastern and southern Africa)

entries.why: The highest-nitrogen, highest-biomass green manure with real KZN trial data behind it — it fixed the most nitrogen of the legumes compared and produced the highest biomass at both Ukulinga and Bergville — which matters enormously here, where 1000 mm of rain on leached sand washes nutrients straight through and organic matter has to be manufactured on site.
entries.source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-32-9783-8_23 (review of Mucuna pruriens in eastern and southern African smallholder systems: fixes 34–108 kg N, mean 7.9 t/ha dry biomass, weed density reduced up to 92%; highest biomass at Ukulinga and Bergville, KwaZulu-Natal)

entries.why: Fills the January-to-March hole when true spinach and Swiss chard bolt and rot in IOCB heat and humidity — a frost-tender perennial vine that produces succulent leaves continuously through the hottest, wettest months, trained up a fence or the shady side of a shade house where it occupies no bed space.
entries.source: https://herbgarden.co.za/mountainherb/herbinfo.php?id=397 (South African supplier listing) and https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Basella+alba (evergreen perennial climber, fast rate, frost tender, leaves and stems used as a vegetable). Exotic and unlisted; it self-seeds readily, so cut before seed set if you are near a river or wetland.

excluded: Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — NEMBA Category 1b. The single most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture writing, and it is already invading coastal KZN. Growing, propagating, moving, selling or giving it away are all prohibited under s71A and there is no permit route. Use Cajanus cajan or Sesbania sesban instead.

Leucaena leucocephala (leucaena) — NEMBA Category 2 nationwide, no area qualifier. Every activity including mere possession requires a permit; without one, regulation 4(4) converts it into a Category 1b obligation to control it. The classic tropical-permaculture N-fixer, and the most likely legal trap in any species list for this biome.

Psidium guajava (guava) — in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape it is Category 2 for plantations and Category 3 everywhere else in those provinces. Category 3 prohibits planting, propagating, moving, selling and giving away; only what already stands may stay. Guava is ubiquitous on this coast and a design tool must not generate a plan that instructs a farmer to plant one. (The fruit itself is exempt if used for human consumption — that exempts the fruit, not the tree.)

Passiflora edulis (purple granadilla) — Category 2 in KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and North-West; not listed only inside proclaimed urban edges in those provinces. On rural coastal farmland it needs a permit, so it cannot be the default trellis crop here despite being the obvious one.
Morus alba (white mulberry) — Category 3. A staple of chicken-forage and silvopasture designs; existing trees may stay but you may never plant, propagate, move or give away another one.
Syzygium jambos (rose apple) — Category 3; Syzygium cumini (jambolan) is Category 1b. Both are frequently suggested for humid subtropical coasts.
Solanum betaceum (tree tomato / tamarillo) — Category 3 in Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Mpumalanga. Often proposed as a fast subtropical understorey fruit.

Eucalyptus spp. (E. camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis) — Category 1b in the Indian Ocean Coastal Belt, dropping to Category 2 only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenue lines, and hard-blocked at 1b inside riparian areas, protected areas and listed ecosystems. The default farm windbreak in South Africa, and it is a permit matter here. Brachylaena discolor does the job legally.

Casuarina equisetifolia (horsetail tree) — Category 2, and Casuarina cunninghamiana is Category 1b within 100 m of riparian areas or untransformed land. The classic coastal dune windbreak, permit-only. Mimusops afra and Brachylaena discolor replace it.
Sesbania punicea (red sesbania) — Category 1b, and listed here specifically because it is the species most likely to be sold or collected in error when a farmer goes looking for Sesbania sesban.

Azolla filiculoides / A. cristata / A. pinnata and Canna indica — all Category 1b. Named because duck-and-fish-feed ponds and greywater reed beds are standard on IOCB smallholdings and these are the two species most often specified for them.

Mangifera indica (mango) — excluded on climate, not law. ARC requires relative humidity of 55% or less from October to harvest and sets monthly rainfall ceilings (Nov 110 mm, Dec–Feb 140 mm) for disease-free fruit; the IOCB exceeds both, and the national tree census records just 16 ha in KwaZulu-Natal against 4 280 ha in Limpopo. Anthracnose, not cold, is what kills it here.

Olive, fig, apple, pear, apricot and plum — excluded on winter warmth and chill. Olive needs June–July maxima below 21°C and 600–1 000+ chill hours; figs need a dry summer harvest and crack in summer rain; pome and stone fruit need 500–1 200 chill units. IOCB winters (MAT 19–22°C, MFD 0–1) supply none of it. Low-chill peach, which reaches most of the country, is still marginal on this humid coast because of brown rot pressure.

Pecan — excluded on climate. It requires winter frost for budbreak, summer humidity below 55% (scab is the disease that punishes humid valleys) and 10 000–15 000 m³/ha/yr of irrigation; 80–90% of SA production is on Northern Cape irrigation schemes.

Portulacaria afra (spekboom) — excluded on climate. It is the Albany Thicket restoration species, used on riplines in 350–500 mm rainfall zones; at 1000 mm of summer rain on humid coastal sand it rots. It appears on almost every 'South African permaculture' list regardless of site and should not carry over to this biome.

Moringa oleifera — not NEMBA-listed and legal, but left out deliberately. Its established South African home is drier Limpopo; on waterlogging-prone IOCB sands with no dry season it is prone to root rot. Plant it only on a raised, sharply drained bed and treat it as an experiment, not a design element.

Sideroxylon inerme (white milkwood) — indigenous and superb on the coast, but excluded from an active farm plan for two reasons: it is a National Forests Act Protected Tree, so once planted it cannot lawfully be felled, moved or damaged without a DFFE licence; and SANBI notes that 'direct sea wind can result in considerable burn damage from salt-laden wind', so it is not actually the front-line species people assume. Retain and protect existing ones; use Mimusops afra for the seaward edge.

Solanum mauritianum (bugweed) and Chromolaena odorata (triffid weed) — both Category 1b and both dominant invaders of disturbed coastal KZN land. Listed because they colonise cleared ground so fast that farmers sometimes read them as a useful nurse or pioneer crop.
palettes.notes:
FORTY-FOUR ENTRIES ACROSS EIGHT SECTIONS. On climate alone the IOCB is the best rain-fed farming envelope in South Africa — 819–1272 mm, no true dry season, 0–1 frost days, the lowest rainfall variability (APCV 18–21%) and the lowest potential evaporation (MAPE 1549–1904 mm) of any biome. That means frostTolerance is almost never the binding filter here, which is why this palette looks nothing like a Karoo or Highveld one and why it can carry banana, litchi, papaya and marula. Treat the 'light' and 'moderate' frost ratings as relevant only on the inland and southern edge (Pondoland-Ugu Sandstone Coastal Sourveld records MFD 1) and in valley-bottom cold-air drainage, where real ground frost exceeds the screen-temperature figure Mucina & Rutherford report.

WHAT ACTUALLY LIMITS THIS BIOME IS SOIL AND WIND, NOT CLIMATE. Strelitzia 19 describes the substrate as 'sandy, highly leached, acidic and mostly very shallow' over Msikaba and Natal Sandstones, with dystric regosols on the dune crests and waterlogged, acidic humic gleysols in the depressions — so high rainfall on leached sand washes nutrients straight through. Every design here needs deliberate organic-matter building, liming of the acid sands, and heavy mulch, which is why this palette is unusually loaded with biomass producers (banana, Sesbania, Cajanus, Mucuna, Trichilia, sweet potato). Note the pH inversion within a few hundred metres of the beach: the dune cordon sands are calcareous young Quaternary material while the ground behind is strongly acidic. Test both, do not assume one figure for the farm. The wet depressions are a drainage problem, not a fertility problem — hence Syzygium cordatum, Phoenix reclinata, Barringtonia racemosa, Sesbania sesban and amadumbe are all placed specifically for them rather than being generic picks.

WIND AND SALT ARE A THREE-ZONE PROBLEM, AND THE PALETTE IS BUILT FOR IT. Zone 1, the salt-blasted seaward front: Mimusops afra and Carissa macrocarpa, both of which will drop to shrub form in full exposure and still function. Zone 2, the second line: Brachylaena discolor, Searsia natalensis, Dovyalis afra. Zone 3, sheltered production behind them: everything else. Design shelterbelts to roughly 40–60% porosity (the target the SA macadamia industry uses) rather than as solid walls. Cyclones periodically hit this coast from the north-east — Domoina is the reference case — so windbreaks and permanent perennial cover matter more here than irrigation ever will, and bananas in particular blow down above 50 km/h.

HUMIDITY IS THE HIDDEN CROP FILTER. Because there is no dry season (winter still carries 28–37% of annual rain and 14 rain days in June and July), fungal and bacterial disease pressure, not drought, decides what succeeds. This is why mango is excluded despite tolerating 45°C and under 300 mm of rain elsewhere, why fig and pecan are out, and why within citrus the answer is lemon rather than navel or soft citrus — KZN carries 714 ha of lemon against 103 ha of soft citrus, and ARC notes lemon 'is well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions'. Getting citrus right for this biome means naming the type, not the genus.

NEMBA HANDLING FOR THE APP. Every included species is unlisted under the Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020 (GN 1003, GG 43726, in force 1 March 2021, unamended as at DFFE's October 2025 briefing) — I checked each against the parsed 383-taxon List 1 rather than from memory. No Category 1a, 1b, 2 or 3 species is recommended for planting. Three structural rules the app must encode or it will give wrong answers here: (1) category is a function of place — Eucalyptus is 1b in the IOCB but 2 for plantations and wind-rows, and guava is 2 for plantations but 3 otherwise within KZN and the Eastern Cape; (2) regulation 5(2) makes any Category 3 plant in a riparian area a Category 1b plant automatically, which matters on a coast this well-watered; (3) Notice 1 states that where a scientific name changes or is misspelt, the common name takes precedence in determining whether a species is listed — so synonym matching on binomials alone is legally insufficient.

TAXONOMY WARNING FOR NAME MATCHING. The July 2024 International Botanical Congress voted to emend all 'caffra/caffrum/caffer' epithets to 'afra/afrum/afer'. Three species in this palette are affected: Dovyalis afra (was D. caffra), Mimusops afra (was M. caffra) and Harpephyllum afrum (was H. caffrum). Nurseries, older field guides and even some SANBI page URLs still use the old names, and the NEMBA gazette predates the change entirely. Store both forms and match on either, or the app will fail to find plants that are physically on sale under the old label.

TWO PROTECTED-TREE FLAGS. Sclerocarya birrea subsp. caffra (marula) is included and is a National Forests Act protected tree — planting is encouraged, but siting is permanent because removal later needs a DFFE licence. Sideroxylon inerme (white milkwood) is excluded for the same reason plus salt-wind burn; existing specimens should be retained and protected rather than cleared.

WHERE THIS LIST IS THINNEST. The climber section has only three entries and two of them are exotic, because the obvious IOCB climber — granadilla — is NEMBA Category 2 in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, and South Africa has no indigenous edible passionfruit to substitute. I would rather return three honest climbers than pad the section. Similarly, Permaculture South Africa's own food-forest guidance names zero species and defers entirely to bioregion, so most of the practice evidence behind this palette comes from DFFE's Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline, ARC-VOPI, SANBI and industry censuses rather than from permaculture organisations. Where a species is included on genuinely thinner evidence I have said so in its 'why' — Basella alba is the weakest entry here and is flagged as a self-seeder to cut before seed set near watercourses, and Colocasia esculenta is unlisted but under active invasion-risk assessment in South Africa and should be kept in managed beds, not natural wetlands.

entries.why: The Klein Karoo (Kammanassie, Prince Albert, Oudtshoorn) is SA's fig core precisely because figs need hot, dry, low-humidity air while the fruit ripens — the summer condition that cracks and rots figs almost everywhere else in the country — and at roughly -5 to -10°C hardiness it clears normal Succulent Karoo frost.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/ (SA fig industry ~222 ha, Klein Karoo/Kammanassie + Swartland core); ARC/Hortgro deciduous climate guidance

entries.nembaStatus: Category 1b — BUT 'spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed' and 'the fruit is not listed if used for human consumption' (GN 1003 of 2020, List 1 item 238). Plant only certified spineless cultivars; spiny/reverted plants are Category 1b and must be controlled.
entries.why: The only entry on this list that yields both human food and bulk stock fodder on rainfall alone at 150 mm — Grootfontein imported 22 spineless Burbank cultivars in 1974 specifically as a drought crop for the arid Karoo, and ~3 000 ha are now grown purely for fodder.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Plant%20Breeding/Cactus-Pear-Genebank.aspx (ARC spineless genebank, 42 accessions); GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 item 238

entries.why: Lowest genuine chill requirement of any crop on this list (~200 hours), mature trees take about -10°C, fruit development is actively helped by 38°C, and it demands the dry summer this biome cannot avoid giving it — the single most forgiving exotic fruit for a Succulent Karoo site.
entries.source: SA pomegranate industry ~1 167 ha, Western Cape 81% / Limpopo 10% / Northern Cape 7%; https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/

entries.why: The Klein Karoo — a Succulent Karoo rainshadow-valley unit — holds about 71% of every apricot tree in South Africa (1 134 388 of 1 604 338), which makes this the biome's signature deciduous crop rather than a hopeful suggestion.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf (Tree Census 2021, apricot by district)

entries.why: Olive fails across the whole subtropical north because its winters are too warm — it needs at least 10 weeks below ~12–13°C and June/July maxima under 21°C to flower, which is exactly what a Succulent Karoo winter supplies alongside the hot dry summer it wants; Robertson, Montagu and the Klein Karoo are established districts and the tree doubles as a permanent windbreak.
entries.source: https://www.saolive.co.za/olive-growing/ and https://olivessa.co.za/climatic-regions/ (93–95% of SA olives in Western Cape incl. Robertson, Montagu, Klein Karoo)

entries.why: The Klein Karoo is the single largest plum district in South Africa at 3.63 million trees, so plum is proven at scale in this biome's rainshadow valleys rather than merely climatically plausible.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf (Tree Census 2021, plum by district)

entries.why: ARC Infruitec's low-chill releases perform on as few as 200–500 chill units, which removes the chill gamble entirely in the warmer Karoo valleys, and the Klein Karoo already carries 2 206 ha of cling peach plus 174 ha of dessert peach.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf; ARC Infruitec low-chill stone-fruit programme

entries.why: The traditional Cape 'kweperheining' — frost-hardy, alkaline-tolerant, responds to hard pruning and forms a dense stock-proof boundary that also fruits, so one planting buys a windbreak, a hedge and a preserve crop.
entries.source: https://plantinfo.co.za/plant/cydonia-oblonga/ ; PFAF (Cydonia oblonga to 7.5 m x 7 m, hedge use)

entries.why: Chill requirement of 300–600 hours fits the Karoo winter and the Klein Karoo is named among SA's suited districts, but it flowers in late winter — so site it on a slope with cold-air drainage and never in a valley-bottom inversion pocket, where this biome's 15–30 frost days will take the crop.
entries.source: https://southafrica.co.za/almonds.html (Western Cape almond production; Klein Karoo, Breede River, Olifants River Valley named)

entries.why: An evergreen Mediterranean tree that tolerates drought, sea wind and any soil except heavy clay and acid — its pods are high-calorie stock fodder and a human staple, but it needs about 500–550 mm equivalent to actually set pods, so budget irrigation if you want yield rather than just shade.
entries.source: https://www.feedipedia.org/node/320 ; https://southafrica.co.za/carob-underutilised-food-tree.html (Western Cape carob cultivars, fodder use)

entries.why: Citrus has the broadest reach of any SA fruit crop but this is its frost edge, not its heartland — soft citrus and lemon survive mild -1 to -2°C winters in sheltered Robertson, Montagu and Oudtshoorn gardens, so plant only in a warm frost-free pocket near a wall or under canopy, and never in the Roggeveld, Tanqua or a cold valley floor.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf (Klein Karoo is not a listed citrus district); ARC frost thresholds (-2 to -3°C floor, no chill requirement)

entries.why: The best genuinely indigenous fruit for this biome — restricted to the arid Karoo, fruit up to 20 mm eaten raw or cooked with a pleasant acid taste, scented flowers that pull in birds and insects, and it is already commercially propagated by Karoo restoration nurseries.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-robusta (SANBI PlantZAfrica); Renu-Karoo Prince Albert sapling list

entries.why: A one-plant system: evergreen, drought-resistant, explicitly recommended by SANBI for small drier Karoo and semi-desert gardens, feeding honeybees, browsed by stock, edible (if unexciting) fruit, and it plants closely into an impenetrable stock hedge with durable heartwood for fence posts.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/euclea-undulata (SANBI: ~7 m tall, very often equal width)

entries.why: The edible groundcover layer this biome actually has — dense rooting mats that bind sand and embankments, tolerate drought, salt spray and poor soils, and give both a 35 mm edible fruit for konfyt and a first-aid leaf gel.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carpobrotus-edulis (SANBI: sand binder, dune and embankment stabiliser, edible fruit ~35 mm)

entries.why: A true Succulent Karoo native — the aromatic evergreen of the Namaqua Klipkoppe running south to the Little Karoo — carrying carbohydrate-rich edible fruits like every SA Searsia, and giving low evergreen shelter where nothing exotic will hold without irrigation.
entries.source: https://treesa.org/searsia-undulata/ ; distribution Namaqualand to Little Karoo; SANBI Searsia genus account

entries.why: Long-lived, evergreen and tolerant of cold, heat and prolonged drought, with a juicy tart fruit worth making into jelly, preserve or vinegar and a seed oil with real traditional value — the closest thing this biome has to a productive indigenous shade tree.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/pappea-capensis (SANBI); https://treesa.org/pappea-capensis/ (2–8 m)

entries.why: Very drought- and cold-hardy with fragrant flowers and 2 cm orange-red berries used for fermented drinks, plus the classic chewing-stick roots — and Karoo restoration nurseries already grow it as a sapling, which means seedstock is obtainable.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/diospyros-lycioides (SANBI); Renu-Karoo Prince Albert indigenous sapling list

entries.why: SANBI names it the excellent shade tree for hot regions such as the Karoo and Kalahari because it is evergreen and drought-resistant; it also takes frost to about -10°C and salinity, and its non-aggressive roots mean you can put it beside buildings, paving and beds without wrecking them.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea (SANBI); commonly 8 m x 5–6 m in cultivation

entries.why: The indigenous twin of the orchard olive and one of the toughest evergreens available here — drought- and frost-hardy on alkaline skeletal soil, named in SA farming press for windbreaks plus slope and riverbank stabilisation, and it doubles as the standard rootstock for cultivated olives.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana (SANBI; = subsp. cuspidata); https://farmersmag.co.za/2025/10/best-indigenous-trees-to-plant-for-windbreaks-and-soil-stability/

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (Vachellia karroo is indigenous; the Australian Acacia species on List 1 are a different genus)
entries.why: The one confirmed nodulating nitrogen fixer that reaches tree size here — recorded in Succulent Karoo vegetation near Springbok, spanning 200–1 500 mm rainfall and resistant to salinity, drought, fire and frost — but at 150 mm site it on a drainage line or run-on area, not on an open flat.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo (SANBI); PMC6558075 (alpha- and beta-rhizobia in V. karroo root nodules, South Africa); Kew POWO distribution

entries.nembaStatus: NOT LISTED within the Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes (GN 1003 of 2020, List 1 items 133–138 merged rule (b)) — but Category 1b inside riparian areas, Protected Areas, and Listed Ecosystems or ecosystems identified in a Bioregional/Biodiversity Management Plan, anywhere.
entries.why: The classic Klein Karoo farm wind-row and bee-forage tree, and one of the few places in the country where a eucalypt is legal without a permit — but it is a heavy water user in a 15:1 evaporation-to-rainfall biome, so use it as a single sparse shelterbelt on the windward boundary and keep it out of every watercourse and protected or listed ecosystem.
entries.source: GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 items 133–138 (parsed locally); https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — the NEMBA list explicitly flags the four alien Tamarix species (aphylla, chinensis, gallica, ramosissima, all 1b) as 'not to be confused with indigenous Tamarix usneoides'
entries.why: A halophyte with long taproots that reach deep brackish water tables — it is the answer to the brak flats, saline alluvium and dry watercourses that defeat everything else in this biome, working as an efficient windbreak, dune binder and riverbank fixer while its leaves feed stock.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tamarix-usneoides (SANBI: 0.6–6.09 m, semi-desert and karooid, brackish subterranean water, windbreak, dune binder, leaves provide fodder)

entries.why: Naturally occurs on the dry stream banks of the Little Karoo, is frost-hardy with high drought tolerance, produces seeds edible green or roasted and ground as a meal, gives nectar-heavy flowers for birds and bees, and its leaves are browsed by stock.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/schotia-afra-var-afra (SANBI); https://www.biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/fabaceae/schotia_afra.htm (max 5 m, edible seeds, browsed)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA invasive lists, but wild harvest of Aloe ferox is regulated and subject to SANBI Non-Detriment Finding assessments and provincial permits — cultivate your own, do not strip veld plants
entries.why: Flowers in midwinter and drips nectar for sunbirds and honeybees at the single leanest moment of the forage year, occurs naturally on the margins of the Karoo and the Little Karoo, and its bitter sap and gel feed a real commercial supply chain — a cash crop, a pollinator anchor and a spiny boundary plant in one.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-ferox (SANBI); https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Aloe-ferox_Oct-2024.pdf (NDF assessment)

entries.why: Native to the Little Karoo, planted from bare truncheons straight into riplines and brush packs (Karoo restoration practice names spekboom truncheons specifically for trapping litter and water on capped soils), browsed by goats, cattle and kudu, and the leaves are edible — but it takes only about -3°C, so keep it off valley-bottom frost pockets.
entries.source: https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/RenuKaroo-veld-rehabilitation-guide.pdf (truncheons of spekboom for Karoo soil-surface protection); https://www.africanlegacy.org.za/indigenous-plant/portulacaria-afra-spekboom

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (indigenous to South Africa; note it is a declared weed in Australia and New Zealand, which is irrelevant to its status here)
entries.why: Indigenous, evergreen, viciously spiny and drought-hardy — it makes the stock-proof and people-proof living boundary this biome needs, and carries edible red berries sporadically right through the year; the Karoo Lycium shrubs are collectively the kriebos of local usage.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lycium-ferocissimum (SANBI); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycium_ferocissimum (to 5 m, native Western and Eastern Cape through the interior)

entries.why: Fast-growing, evergreen, drought- and wind-resistant and frost-hardy, it responds well to pruning into a dense hedge — the practical inner windbreak behind the tree line — and in Namaqualand the boiled leaf extract is still used for colds and influenza.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dodonaea-viscosa-var-angustifolia (SANBI: to 5 m, screening and windbreaks, hedging, Namaqualand medicinal use); Renu-Karoo Karoo restoration seed list

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only the alien tumbleweeds Salsola kali and S. tragus are listed, both 1b)
entries.why: The lawful indigenous saltbush — a well-known Karoo fodder shrub of dry watercourses, floodplains and saline loamy soils where drought runs long — and the correct substitute for Category 2 old man saltbush, which Karoo restoration specialists advise against planting because it makes the soil surface brak and delays indigenous recovery.
entries.source: https://www.feedipedia.org/node/100 (ganna bush fodder, ~1.8 m); Renu-Karoo seed list (rivier ganna) and veld rehabilitation guide

entries.why: A long-lived drought-deciduous shrub of Karoo ridges and outcrops whose flowers, pods and young shoots are all palatable to stock and game, and which flowers after every major warm-season rain event — useful browse and a nectar pulse timed to rainfall rather than to season.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhigozum-obovatum (SANBI); https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Rhigozum-obovatum-Eng.pdf (1.0–2.0 m, to 4.5 m; browse value)

entries.why: A genuinely nodulating legume that occurs naturally through the western Karoo to Namibia, so it fixes nitrogen at 150 mm without irrigation — and it is simultaneously one of South Africa's most-used medicinal plants, giving the shrub layer both a soil function and a saleable product.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lessertia-frutescens (SANBI: shrublet 0.5–1 m, dry parts of southern Africa incl. western Karoo); Tandfonline 10.1080/09064710.2021.2003852 (rhizobial nodulation and N response)

entries.why: The top palatable climax forage bossie of Karoo rangeland — highly preferred by both stock and wild browsers, capable of rapid regrowth after grazing, and one of only three species whose seed is supplied specifically as suitable for sowing in Namaqualand and the Little Karoo.
entries.source: https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/RenuKaroo-veld-rehabilitation-guide.pdf (Worcester Veld Reserve seed for Namaqualand and Little Karoo); J. Grassland Soc. sthn Afr. 9(4) 1992 (flowering of O. sinuatum in arid Karoo rangeland)

entries.why: Silvery evergreen on clay and granite slopes right through the Western Cape, Eastern Cape and Namaqualand, it draws bees on warm days, is readily browsed, and is one of the aromatic Karoo shrubs that gives Karoo lamb its flavour — a forage, apiary and meat-quality plant at once.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eriocephalus-africanus (SANBI: bushy evergreen shrub to 1 m, bee-attracting, browsed, Karoo lamb flavour). Renu-Karoo supplies the closely related E. ericoides for Namaqualand and the Little Karoo.

entries.why: Its branches arch back to the ground and root where they touch, so a single plant anchors a spreading patch of soil — the reason the US Soil Conservation Service imported it — and it is a recorded Succulent Karoo species that stock will graze, making it the best bare-patch stabiliser you can also justify as forage.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/pentzia-incana (SANBI); https://www.feedipedia.org/node/118 (300–600 mm shrublet, stoloniferous, grazed; occurs in Succulent Karoo)

entries.why: A Mediterranean shrub that wants precisely what this biome enforces — winter rain, bone-dry summer, alkaline stony soil, full sun — so it needs no special treatment, holds a low bed-edge hedge, and flowers as bee forage over a long winter-spring window.
entries.source: Not on GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 (verified by search of the parsed 383-taxa list); Mediterranean climate/soil match per ARC and SANBI horticultural zone 3 guidance

entries.why: Ruschia is the largest mesemb genus of the Succulent Karoo and this one is eaten by small stock and springbok depending on conditions — a spiny, self-protecting soil-holder for the harshest stony ground, and seed is commercially available from Karoo restoration nurseries.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ruschia-spinosa (SANBI: waterwise, suitable for Karoo and Namib gardens, eaten by small stock and springbuck); Renu-Karoo seed availability list

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (unlike Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia, which is Category 2, and Atriplex inflata, which is 1b)
entries.why: An indigenous South African saltbush supplied by Karoo restoration nurseries for brak and degraded ground — it gives you the drought-fodder saltbush function without the Category 2 permit, and without the soil-salinisation and indigenous-suppression problem that Karoo specialists attribute to Australian old man saltbush.
entries.source: Renu-Karoo Seed Availability list, Prince Albert (Atriplex vestita, vaalbrak, shrubs for veld restoration); GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 items 46–47 for the listed Atriplex species

entries.why: The king of Karoo fodder crops under irrigation and the biome's existing anchor — the Oudtshoorn district alone produces about 90% of South Africa's lucerne seed — deep-rooted, alkaline-tolerant, nitrogen-fixing, and the cut-and-carry engine that makes livestock viable on a small Succulent Karoo holding.
entries.source: https://gadi.dalrrd.gov.za/articles/Agric/lucerne.php (Grootfontein: most important irrigated fodder crop in the Karoo); Oudtshoorn ≈90% of SA lucerne seed

entries.why: One of very few winter-rainfall grasses with real grazing value, which is exactly what this inverted-season biome needs — drought-tolerant, tolerant of low soil fertility, and named among the three species whose seed is supplied specifically for sowing in Namaqualand and the Little Karoo.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ehrharta-calycina (SANBI); https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/RenuKaroo-veld-rehabilitation-guide.pdf (rooisaadgras seed for Namaqualand and Little Karoo)

entries.why: An edible indigenous groundcover — young shoots boiled and served as a vegetable — that also binds soil and is palatable to stock and game, and which occurs naturally in Rainshadow Valley Karoo and Succulent Karoo, where it stays under 250 mm tall.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tetragonia-fruticosa (SANBI: rarely reaches 250 mm in Succulent Karoo and Karroid Broken Veld; young shoots eaten as a vegetable; important fodder)

entries.why: The right food legume for an inverted season — sown in autumn with the first rains, it grows through the cool wet months, fixes nitrogen, tolerates frost and alkaline soil, and is chopped down as mulch just as the killing summer dry begins.
entries.source: Not on GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 (verified against the parsed 383-taxa list); winter-rainfall Mediterranean legume rotation practice, ARC/DALRRD vegetable production guidelines

entries.why: A mat-forming Karoo mesemb sold by the kilogram specifically for veld restoration on damaged arid ground — it covers bare capped soil, breaks raindrop impact and traps litter and seed, which is the first step in every Karoo rehabilitation sequence.
entries.source: https://renu-karoo.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Renu-Karoo-Seed-Availability-2026.01.26-.pdf (Drosanthemum hispidum, douvygie); https://pza.sanbi.org/genus/drosanthemum

entries.why: A genuine indigenous winter vegetable of the Namaqualand and West Coast sands — flowering stalks harvested before the buds open and cooked like asparagus, a Khoisan food still eaten today — and its July-to-September season matches this biome's growing rhythm exactly.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/trachyandra-ciliata (SANBI: edible flower buds, flowering July–September, coastal sands southern Namibia to south-eastern Cape)

entries.why: The standard South African first-aid plant — leaf sap for burns, cuts and cracked skin — that survives on rainfall alone here, spreads into a clumping soil-holding cover under trees and along bed edges, and flowers over a long season for insects.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/bulbine-frutescens (SANBI); SANBI water-wise indigenous groundcover listings

entries.why: The obvious vertical crop for this biome — Robertson, Montagu and the Klein Karoo are established grape districts on exactly this alkaline, low-rainfall, hot-dry-summer ground — and trained over a pergola it delivers deciduous summer shade in the yard and lets the low winter sun back in.
entries.source: Not on GN 1003 GG 43726 List 1 (verified); Robertson Karoo and Klein Karoo viticulture; https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (SANBI Red List: Least Concern)
entries.why: The most important and best-known medicinal plant of the western Karoo and the only indigenous climber here worth a designer's attention — a twining perennial of sandy and granite-derived slopes whose inland form is genuinely xerophytic, so it climbs a fence or shrub without irrigation.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/cissampelos-capensis (SANBI: perennial climber to 1 m, western Karoo to Gqeberha, xerophytic inland forms); MDPI Molecules 16(4):3001 (alkaloid profile)

excluded: Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia (old man saltbush) — TWO independent reasons. (1) NEMBA Category 2 nationwide with no area qualifier: a permit is required to possess, grow, move or sell it, and without one reg 4(4) converts it into a Category 1b obligation to control. (2) Karoo restoration specialists working in this exact biome advise directly against it: 'Planting of Australian "oldman" saltbush into the veld is not recommended because it delays the return of indigenous plants and makes the soil surface brak.' Use indigenous Salsola aphylla and Atriplex vestita instead — both on this palette.

Prosopis glandulosa var. torreyana and P. velutina (mesquite) — Category 1b in the Western Cape and Category 3 in the Northern Cape, so planting, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are prohibited in every province this biome touches. It is also the single worst water thief in arid SA rangeland. (Utilisation of existing pods for fodder is not listed in NC, EC, FS, NW and WC — that exemption covers pods, never planting.)
Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — Category 1b, illegal to plant anywhere in SA, and in any case a moist-summer-rainfall chop-and-drop species that would need year-round irrigation here.

Leucaena leucocephala — Category 2 nationwide (permit required). It is also a tropical, frost-sensitive, summer-rainfall nitrogen fixer that would be killed by this biome's 15–30 frost days and bone-dry summer.

Sambucus nigra (elder), Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust), Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust), Morus alba (white mulberry), Grevillea robusta (silky oak), Casuarina cunninghamiana, Populus alba — all NEMBA-listed (1b or 3) and all prohibited to plant. Note Morus alba is Category 3: existing trees may stay, but you may not plant, propagate, move or give away another one. Morus nigra (black mulberry) is NOT listed and is a lawful substitute.

Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) and buchu (Agathosma betulina) — both are Fynbos species of acid, leached, sandy Cederberg/Sandveld soils with pH often below 4.5. They will not perform on the lime-rich, alkaline, calcareous skeletal soils that define this biome, even though the rainfall pattern matches.

Avocado, macadamia, litchi, banana, mango, papaya — all frost-sensitive summer-rainfall subtropicals. Avocado's -4°C floor with fatal exposure at August–September flowering, litchi's demand for >50% humidity, and banana's need for night minima above 18°C are each independently fatal here. SANBI horticultural zone and ARC subtropical guidance exclude the interior Karoo for all of them.

Apple and pear (commercial scale) — chill is actually adequate in the Roggeveld and higher Klein Karoo, but 92% of SA apples sit in five Western Cape/Langkloof mountain districts with the water and cool summers this biome lacks. Pear is the exception worth noting rather than excluding outright: the Klein Karoo already carries 984 ha, so a few pear trees on quince rootstock are defensible on a well-irrigated Klein Karoo site.

Pecan — needs 10 000–15 000 m3/ha/yr of irrigation (1 000–1 500 mm equivalent). Physiologically it would love the winter cold and hot dry summer, but 80–90% of SA pecans sit on Northern Cape irrigation schemes for a reason: the water bill, not the climate, is the gate.

Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) — tempting on paper (alkaline, saline, extreme heat tolerance) but the Succulent Karoo has the shortest summers of any SA biome (<198 days) and the small SA date industry sits on the Orange River and in Limpopo, not here. It would also need enormous irrigation. Reconsider only for the hottest low-altitude Gariep-margin sites.

Vetiver (Chrysopogon zizanioides) — the default erosion-control grass everywhere else in SA, but it needs reliable moisture to establish (Vetiver SA: plant in the rainy season, 3–6 weeks to establish) and will not take at 100–250 mm without irrigation. Use stone packs, brush packs, hand-dug basins and riplines planted with spekboom truncheons and mesembs instead — the documented Karoo method.

Comfrey, Jerusalem artichoke, moringa, pigeon pea, Sesbania sesban — none are NEMBA-listed and all are permaculture staples elsewhere in SA, but all are summer-growing and either frost-sensitive or water-hungry. In a winter-rainfall biome with a bone-dry summer and 15–30 frost days they invert the season and would run entirely on irrigation.
palettes.notes:
WATER IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. MAP 100–250 mm (biome average ~170 mm) against mean annual potential evaporation of ~2 400–2 550 mm is roughly a 15:1 deficit, with mean annual soil moisture stress around 81%. Only the spineless cactus pear, spekboom and the indigenous shrub/grass/groundcover layers on this palette will produce on rainfall alone. Every fruit tree here is an irrigated or heavily water-harvested crop. The compensating asset is unusual for an arid zone: Succulent Karoo rainfall has relatively high predictability and prolonged droughts are very rare, so a sized rainwater or run-on system actually behaves as designed.

THE SEASON IS INVERTED — THIS IS THE MOST COMMON PLANNING ERROR. The wild flora is winter-growing and summer-dormant, the opposite of the summer-cropping rhythm most South African farm advice assumes. Sow and plant in AUTUMN, immediately after the late-summer/autumn rain: Karoo restoration practice is explicit that "sowing seeds immediately after late summer-autumn rain is recommended for establishment of forage shrubs in the southern and western regions", and that autumn-germinating seed establishes far better than spring-sown seed. Vegetable production is a winter-season affair here — brassicas, alliums, broad beans, peas, carrots and beetroot — not a summer one.

FROST VARIES MORE WITHIN THIS BIOME THAN BETWEEN MANY OTHERS. Coastal Sandveld, western Richtersveld and the Knersvlakte are effectively frost-free; the Namaqualand escarpment runs 7–13 days; deep valleys surrounded by high ranges hit 15–30 days through thermal inversion; the continental plateau 20–25 days; and Roggeveld Karoo reaches almost 60 days. Drive the palette off the site's own frost-day figure, not the biome average. Practical consequences on this list: soft citrus and spekboom belong only in the warm frost-free pockets; almond flowers in late winter and must go on a slope with cold-air drainage, never a valley floor; fig, pomegranate, olive, apricot, plum, quince and karee will take anything this biome produces.

ALKALINE CALCAREOUS SKELETAL SOIL IS WHY THE MEDITERRANEAN LIST WORKS. Soils are lime-rich, weakly developed and shallow over rock. Do not lime. Expect iron and zinc chlorosis on sensitive species and correct with chelates rather than by trying to move pH. This is the reciprocal of the Fynbos problem: here the base status is fine and the constraints are water and rooting depth, so build depth and moisture (pits, riplines, basins, gypsum at 3–5 t/ha on capped saline patches) rather than chasing fertility. On brak and saline flats use the halophyte set — Tamarix usneoides, Salsola aphylla, Atriplex vestita, Tetragonia fruticosa, Trachyandra ciliata.

WIND, UV AND HEAT ARE STRUCTURAL, NOT COSMETIC. This biome has the highest summer incoming radiation of any in South Africa (270–280 J/m2/day) and autumn berg-wind events that push above 44°C and can persist for days. Windbreaks and shade are load-bearing infrastructure: layer them as an outer line (Eucalyptus cladocalyx or wild olive), an inner tree line (karee, tamarisk) and a low filter (sand olive, quince, kriedoring). Target roughly 40–60% porosity — a solid wall creates damaging turbulence downwind.

FIRE-FREE BIOME. There is not enough fuel to carry fire and the vegetation is succulent-dominated. Do not import fire as a management tool the way you would in Fynbos, Grassland or Savanna, and do not plan burn cycles into retained veld.

THE EUCALYPT EXEMPTION IS REAL AND WORTH USING CAREFULLY. Six listed Eucalyptus taxa (camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis) are expressly NOT LISTED within the Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes — so a sugar-gum wind-row or bee-forage block is lawful here without a permit, unlike almost everywhere else in the country. The exemption falls away inside riparian areas, Protected Areas, and Listed Ecosystems or ecosystems identified in a Bioregional or Biodiversity Management Plan, where they revert to Category 1b. The app should hard-block them near watercourses and in protected/listed ecosystems, and should still warn on water use.

SECTIONS DELIBERATELY UNDER-FILLED. Large trees stop at four and medium trees at three because this biome genuinely has almost no tree layer — the honest canopy set is karee, wild olive, sweet thorn (on run-on ground only) and, if you accept the water cost, sugar gum. Padding it would misrepresent the site. Conversely the shrub, groundcover and herbaceous layers are where the real diversity and function sit, which is the correct shape for a Succulent Karoo design.

EASY EXTENSIONS NOT LISTED SEPARATELY. The rosemary entry stands in for a whole Mediterranean culinary/medicinal block that performs here with no special treatment — thyme, oregano, sage, lavender, savory. Pear on quince rootstock is defensible on well-irrigated Klein Karoo sites (984 ha already planted there). Morus nigra (black mulberry) is unlisted and is the lawful substitute for the Category 3 white mulberry in chicken-forage designs.

LEGAL CAVEAT FOR THE APP. NEMBA category is a function of place as well as species — the Eucalyptus biome rule, the riparian override that turns any Category 3 plant into Category 1b, and cultivar carve-outs like "spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed" all mean a species-only lookup will be wrong a meaningful fraction of the time. The gazette PDFs (GN 1003, GG 43726, 18 Sept 2020) are the only authority on category; SANBI/POSA is the authority on identity and synonyms. Notice 1 also states that where a scientific name changes or is misspelled, the COMMON name determines whether a species is listed — so synonym matching on binomials alone is legally insufficient.

palettes.biome: Grassland (Highveld) — summer rainfall 500–900 mm, hard frost −5 to −10°C, hail, clay soils

entries.why: The one indigenous fruit tree unambiguously at home on the Highveld — SANBI records it in Free State, Gauteng, North West and Mpumalanga and says it 'withstands heat and cold equally well', while the flowers 'produce abundant nectar and often yield a good honey' and stock browse the leaves and pods.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ziziphus-mucronata

entries.why: A true Highveld grassland species (SANBI: 'grasslands and rocky outcrops from the Highveld southward') carrying deep-red berries with 'a pleasant sweetish taste', and it doubles as a hedging and screening shrub — the most reliable small indigenous fruit for a frost-hard site.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/diospyros-lycioides

entries.why: SANBI calls it explicitly 'frost- and drought-hardy', records it in the Free State and Gauteng, and it delivers three functions at once — fruit dried or boiled in milk, leaves browsed by cattle and goats, and it 'feeds honeybees' plus hosts butterfly larvae.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-occidentalis

entries.why: Fast (600–700 mm/yr), drought-resistant and present through the Free State and Gauteng; the fruit is 'edible but not tasty', so plant it for the bird and insect load and the tangled thorn-free hedge rather than for the harvest.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ehretia-rigida

entries.why: The classic stock-proof living fence that also fruits, but it is only half-hardy — it survives on Pretoria ridges yet is uncommon in Gauteng because of frost, so on the Highveld give it a north-facing wall or shelterbelt microclimate and protect it for its first three winters.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra

entries.why: The only temperate fruit with a genuinely national footprint and the best exotic bet here — ARC Infruitec's low-chill selections perform on as few as 200–500 chill units, and Hortgro's 2021 census records real plantings in Free State (74 ha), Mpumalanga (49 ha), North West (27 ha) and Gauteng (5 ha).
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.why: Fully dormant through a Highveld winter and lower-chill than apple or pear; Hortgro records small but real Free State and Northern Provinces blocks, and plums crop at a different point in the season from peaches so the two spread the harvest.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but WHITE mulberry (Morus alba) IS NEMBA Category 3 and may not be planted, propagated, moved, sold or given away
entries.why: The permaculture workhorse — fruit, high-protein leaf fodder (15–28% DM), poultry forage and summer shade — and critically it is the BLACK mulberry that is legal: only Morus alba appears on the 2020 NEMBA list (entry 215, Category 3). Buy Morus nigra by name and check the label.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, entry 215 lists only Morus alba; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: One of the few crops that actively WANTS the Highveld's winter frost for budbreak plus its hot summers — SAPPA's own central irrigation zone is Cullinan, Parys, Potchefstroom, Kroonstad and Bloemfontein — but budget 12,000 m³/ha/yr of irrigation and 460–800 litres/tree/day at peak before planting one.
entries.source: https://www.sappa.za.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/sappa-water-requirement-per-production-area.pdf

entries.why: Hardy to roughly −5°C and some cultivars to −10°C with only a modest chill need, so winter is no obstacle; the catch is that figs want dry weather at harvest and Highveld summer rain and hail split ripening fruit — site it against a warm wall and expect the early (breba) crop to be the reliable one.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/

entries.why: Mature trees shrug off about −10°C and it needs only ~200 chill hours — the lowest genuine chill requirement of any crop here — which is exactly why it works in both a Cape and a Highveld winter. Keep frost-protecting until year three, as young growth stays green and vulnerable.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/

entries.why: The Free State's 527 ha proves apples crop on the Highveld, but this is a managed workaround not a natural fit — SA apples run on 500 chill units against a 1,000–1,200 CU textbook need, using rest-breaking agents and central-leader training. Pick low-chill cultivars and the coldest site you have.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro-science.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/2022/09/CLIMATE-18-MIDGLEY-Guide-to-climate-change-and-pome-and-stone-fruit-production-extended-executive-summary.pdf

entries.why: More forgiving than apple of the Highveld's imperfect chill and its heavy clay, and it flowers slightly later so dodges some spring frost; national plantings are Western Cape-centred, so treat it as a homestead tree here rather than a commercial block.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.why: The one crop that exists BECAUSE of this biome's cold — roughly 500 ha around Ficksburg, Clocolan and Fouriesburg at 1,650 m. But sweet cherry wants >1,100 Utah chill units and even Ficksburg only exceeds ~900 DPCU, so restrict it to the high eastern Free State and expect late-spring-frost losses. Do not offer it in Gauteng.
entries.source: https://www.ishs.org/ishs-article/1235_33

entries.why: The default Highveld shade tree: SANBI says it 'can withstand frost', occurs to 2,100 m in every province, puts on 1–2 m a year and carries a dense semi-circular canopy — and its heavy autumn leaf drop is free mulch while the fruit feeds pigeons, bulbuls, mousebirds and barbets.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/celtis-africana

entries.why: SANBI records it specifically in 'bushveld and highveld grasslands', calls it frost and drought resistant, notes 700–900 mm annual growth and that it withstands fire — a legume that fixes nitrogen, feeds stock, and casts shade light enough for pasture to keep growing underneath.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/senegalia-caffra

entries.why: The indigenous answer to a collapsing Highveld stream bank — SANBI calls it 'surprisingly drought and frost resistant' with seedlings frost-resistant after two years, and it hits 4–6 m in three years, so it stabilises a watercourse faster than anything else legal to plant here.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/combretum-erythrophyllum

entries.why: The wide flat-crowned nitrogen fixer that gives a Highveld paddock genuine livestock shade over a 12 m spread, with pods relished by stock and game — but it is a fast grower whose young plants must be protected from cold, wind and frost for the first two or three winters.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-sieberiana-var-woodii

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — SANBI names it explicitly as an unlisted bee-forage eucalypt. Do NOT substitute E. grandis, camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor or tereticornis: those are Category 1b in the Grassland biome, Category 2 by permit only for plantations, woodlots, wind-rows and bee-forage areas, and never exempt in riparian areas or listed ecosystems.
entries.why: The legal eucalypt. SANBI's own bee-forage infosheet states E. sideroxylon is 'not listed in Alien and Invasive Species Regulations and… could be maintained or planted in non-riparian areas'; it takes about −10°C when dormant and is one of SA's two most important honey-bee eucalypts — so a beekeeping windbreak needs no permit if you plant this one. Keep it out of riparian zones.
entries.source: https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/infosheet-eucalyptus-trees-honey-bee-forage-19-11-2014.pdf

entries.why: The highest-value multifunction tree in the whole South African palette, and fully Highveld-hardy: SANBI notes its nitrogen fixation lets 'grasses and other plants thrive in its shade', stock feed on leaves, flowers and pods, and its unusually long flowering season makes it one of SANBI's named standout indigenous bee-forage trees.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo

entries.why: The Highveld windbreak of choice — evergreen, so it works in the July gales when everything else is bare; SANBI-rated for Zone 4 (summer-rainfall Highveld, winter frost), ~80 cm/yr growth, and a root system explicitly described as not aggressive, so it can go near buildings, paving and dam walls.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea

entries.why: SANBI gives a working range of about −5°C to 40°C and calls it 'frost, drought and wind-resistant'; it has been used specifically to stabilise erosion dongas, is an 'excellent fodder plant for stock and game', and its 12 m spread makes a single tree a serious windbreak. Accept that it is slow.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — no Salix of any species appears on the 2020 NEMBA plant list
entries.why: The indigenous streambank willow used in SA river-rehabilitation work; it strikes readily from truncheons so a bank can be planted with cuttings at no cost, and coppice regrowth gives repeated chop-and-drop mulch. Reserve it for wet feet — it is not a dryland tree.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, no Salix entry; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: The best biodiversity anchor on this list — SANBI records it in Gauteng and the Free State, describes an 11 x 13 m non-aggressive shade tree that 'feeds honeybees', hosts Acraea butterfly caterpillars and draws cuckoos in to hunt them. SANBI's stated tolerance is only about −2°C, so shelter it and protect young trees for two or three winters.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/kiggelaria-africana

entries.why: Highly frost-resistant, fast, evergreen and native to Gauteng, Mpumalanga and the eastern Free State — the natural pioneer for a gullied or overgrazed Highveld slope, and its posts last in permanently wet soil. Honest caveat: it 'forms dense thickets on overgrazed, eroded or otherwise disturbed areas', so plant it where you want thicket and manage the edge.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/leucosidea-sericea

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — the NEMBA-listed Buddlejas are the exotic B. davidii and B. madagascariensis, both Category 3
entries.why: SANBI places it directly in Zone 4, 'Summer rainfall Karoo and Highveld, Frost in winter'; it 'attracts many insects such as bees, butterflies and birds', makes an excellent clipped hedge, roots from cuttings in 3–4 weeks and the leaves give a herbal tea — the cheapest pollinator hedge you can propagate yourself.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/buddleja-salviifolia

entries.why: SANBI rates it hardy to about −7°C, records it through the eastern Free State, Gauteng and Mpumalanga, and it is fast — nectar-rich flowers pull in sunbirds and 'feed honeybees' when little else does. Note the berries are technically edible but 'sickly sweet' and mouth-drying: plant it for the pollinators, not the fruit bowl.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/halleria-lucida

entries.why: One of the practitioner staples on SANBI's Kirstenbosch honey-bee forage list and a mainstay of Highveld sunbird gardens; it flowers into late autumn when the veld has gone over, dies back to the crown in a hard frost and re-shoots in spring, and is a widely used traditional medicinal.
entries.source: https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — do not confuse with Tecoma stans (yellow bells), which is NEMBA Category 1b
entries.why: A named practitioner staple on the Kirstenbosch bee-forage list; it clips into a dense informal barrier hedge, roots from cuttings, and flowers over a very long season for sunbirds and bees. Frost cuts it back on the open Highveld but it recovers from the base, so hedge it against a wall or windbreak.
entries.source: https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.why: A fast, short-lived legume that fixes nitrogen at shrub level, where most Highveld N-fixers are either trees or annuals; SANBI puts it across horticultural zones 3–5, i.e. into winter-frost country, sunbirds pollinate it, and it is one of the most-used medicinal plants in the country. Treat it as a 3–5 year plant and let it self-seed.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lessertia-frutescens

entries.why: The single most important pollinator plant in this biome: the literature describes it as 'the most important indigenous South African bee plant'; it is a Grassland-and-Bushveld species, very common in Gauteng and the Free State, and it flowers in WINTER — filling the June–August forage gap that decides whether a colony survives to spring. Migratory beekeepers move hives for it.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-greatheadii-var-davyana

entries.why: Named on SANBI's Kirstenbosch bee-forage list and the most widely used indigenous medicinal in southern Africa; a genuine Highveld grassland and mountain species that cuts hard for mulch and regrows, and whose aromatic foliage earns it a place on bed edges as a pest-confusing companion.
entries.source: https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf

entries.why: A tough, thorny, frost- and drought-hardy Highveld native that self-establishes on disturbed veld — the indigenous stock barrier to reach for now that Mauritius thorn (Caesalpinia decapetala) is Category 1b and prickly pear and agave are listed or alien. Its mass of small cream flowers is heavily worked by insects.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/gymnosporia-buxifolia

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — the NEMBA-listed lookalike is Nicandra physalodes (apple-of-Peru), Category 1b
entries.why: The fastest route to fruit on a new Highveld plot — it crops in its first summer from seed and self-seeds thereafter, and although frost kills the top growth it behaves as a short-lived perennial that re-shoots or replaces itself. Verified absent from the 2020 NEMBA plant list.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, no Physalis entry; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: The one perennial nitrogen fixer that survives a −10°C Highveld winter and keeps producing for 4–6 years — deep-rooted enough to open Highveld clay, cut 5–8 times a season for fodder or chop-and-drop mulch, and a heavy bee plant if you let a cut flower. This is the biome's answer to the frost-tender tropical N-fixers.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/

entries.why: Frost kills it — which does not matter, because it is a summer annual that fits the Highveld's frost-free November-to-April window exactly. ECHO's South African trials measured over 100 kg N/ha in above-ground biomass, and you eat the leaves as morogo and the dry grain, so it earns its bed twice.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf

entries.why: The indigenous Highveld pasture and reclamation grass — the standard cover for mine dumps, road cuts and bare clay across Gauteng, the Free State and Mpumalanga because it establishes fast on poor soil, takes hard frost and gives baled hay. Use it as the nurse cover on any newly earthworked contour or swale.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eragrostis-curvula

entries.why: Top of ARC-VOPI's indigenous-crops list and the most eaten traditional green in the summer-rainfall interior; it volunteers in disturbed Highveld ground, so the practice is managed encouragement rather than sowing. Harvest at 4–6 weeks and 15–30 cm, about half adult height, and it re-shoots until frost.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — the NEMBA-listed Solanums are the exotic S. mauritianum, elaeagnifolium, pseudocapsicum, seaforthianum and sisymbriifolium, all Category 1b
entries.why: On ARC-VOPI's researched indigenous-crop set, and it gives both a cooked green and an edible ripe berry from the same plant; it self-seeds through Highveld gardens and croplands. Confirm the species at purchase — several exotic Solanums in the same genus are Category 1b invasives.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.why: ARC-VOPI counts traditional pumpkin among the indigenous crop set precisely because both the leaves (as morogo) and the fruit are eaten; a single plant's 4 m sprawl smothers weeds and shades soil through the hot half of the Highveld summer, and the fruit stores through winter without a cold room.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — the sterile cultivar used in SA does not set viable seed
entries.why: The practitioner default for gullies and contour hedges, already commercial in SA for mine rehabilitation in Mpumalanga and North West; roots 3–5 m deep and survives below freezing (top growth browns, then regrows). Vetiver SA's spec: slips 10–15 cm apart in a single row across the slope, trimmed to 20–30 cm at 3–4 months, cuttings used as mulch.
entries.source: https://www.vetiver.co.za/vetiver-grass-faq/

entries.why: The Highveld's practical substitute for Tithonia — the global chop-and-drop standard, which is Category 1b here and illegal to plant. Comfrey is fully frost-hardy, dies back and re-shoots, gives 4–5 cuts of potassium-rich mulch a season, and is absent from the 2020 NEMBA list. Use sterile Bocking cultivars and site it permanently: the taproot makes it very hard to move.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, no Symphytum entry; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — note that Crotalaria agatiflora IS Category 1b
entries.why: The fastest summer green manure for a worn-out Highveld clay field: southern African conservation-agriculture trials put the cover-crop group at 5–50 t/ha extra biomass and 50–350 kg/ha residual N, and sunn hemp also suppresses root-knot nematode. Sow after the first good rains, slash at flowering, and frost cleans up the residue.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf

entries.why: A frost-hardy indigenous bulb giving a garlic-flavoured leaf and flower all year; it clumps into a dense weed-suppressing edging, flowers over a long season for butterflies and bees, and is traditionally planted around beds and homesteads as a mole and insect deterrent — genuinely useful, not decorative.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tulbaghia-violacea

entries.why: Fully dormant and unharmed by −10°C, low chill demand, and on a pergola it delivers the classic permaculture double — deciduous summer shade over a west wall or eating area, then bare winter branches that let the sun back in. Choose loose-bunched table cultivars: Highveld summer rain and hail rot tight-bunched wine grapes.
entries.source: NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Lists 2020, GN 1003 GG 43726, no Vitis entry; https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf

entries.why: SANBI places it squarely in Zone 4 (summer-rainfall Highveld with winter frost) and records it in the Free State, Gauteng and North West; it scrambles up a fence or a thorn tree and carries edible, if sour, grape-like berries. Warning for app copy: the tuberous roots are reported to be poisonous if eaten — fruit only.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-tridentata

excluded: ALL SUBTROPICAL FRUIT — citrus, avocado, mango, macadamia, banana, litchi, papaya. ARC's Climate-Smart module and SANBI's horticultural zones agree that Zone 4 (summer-rainfall Karoo and Highveld, minimum below −5°C) rules out every subtropical crop. Citrus is the one users will ask for: production is confined to areas where temperature seldom drops below −2°C and almost never below −3°C, so at −5 to −10°C it is out. Citrus genuinely has broad reach across five other SA biomes — just not this one.

Guava (Psidium guajava) — the broadest-reach subtropical (fruits to 1,515 m, mature trees withstand rare cold, biggest national block is in the Western Cape) and therefore the most tempting mistake here. Hard Highveld frost at −5 to −10°C still kills or severely cuts back mature trees. Only offer it for a walled, north-facing, frost-drained microclimate, never as a field planting.

Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — NEMBA Category 1b. The most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture literature and flatly illegal to plant, propagate, move, sell or give away in South Africa. Comfrey and lucerne are the substitutes in this palette.
Leucaena leucocephala — NEMBA Category 2 nationwide (permit required; unpermitted it is treated as Category 1b under reg 4(4)). It is also frost-tender, so it fails this biome twice over.

Sesbania sesban and Cajanus cajan (pigeon pea) — the two woody legumes DFFE's own agroforestry guideline names for South African improved fallows, but both are frost-tender and the guideline's field examples are KwaZulu-Natal. Pigeon pea can still be grown here as a single-season summer annual; neither will persist as a hedgerow through a Highveld winter.
Portulacaria afra (spekboom) — the standout SA fodder and restoration shrub, but an Albany Thicket and Karoo species and frost-sensitive. Do not port it onto the Highveld.

Sclerocarya birrea (marula), Strychnos spinosa (monkey orange), Vangueria infausta (wild medlar), Carissa macrocarpa (num-num), Harpephyllum caffrum (wild plum) — the headline SA indigenous-fruit set, all frost-sensitive Savanna, Thicket or coastal species. This is why the Indigenous fruit section here has only five entries.

Mimusops zeyheri (Transvaal red milkwood) — genuinely good fruit and it does occur on Magaliesberg ridges, but SANBI states it 'will not survive any extreme degree of frost' and needs three years of protection at altitude. Too marginal to rank for a −5 to −10°C site.

Carissa bispinosa — SANBI describes it as 'rather frost-tender', with growth slowing considerably where winters are cold. Diospyros lycioides and Gymnosporia buxifolia do the same hedge-plus-fruit job here without the risk.

Morus alba (white mulberry) — NEMBA Category 3. Existing trees may stand, but planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving away another one is prohibited under s71A with no permit route, and any Category 3 plant in a riparian area is deemed Category 1b. Morus nigra (black mulberry) is unlisted and is what this palette recommends instead.

Eucalyptus grandis, camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor and tereticornis — all six are Category 1b in the Grassland biome, with a Category 2 permit route only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenue lines, and no exemption at all in riparian areas or listed ecosystems. E. sideroxylon is unlisted and is the substitute in this palette.

Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust) and Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust) — both NEMBA Category 1b. Frost-hardy nitrogen fixers that would otherwise be near-perfect Highveld choices, and both are illegal to plant.

Sambucus nigra (elder) — Category 1b, so no elderflower/elderberry hedgerow. Rubus fruticosus (European blackberry) — Category 2, permit required (the carve-out exempts the fruit, not the plant). Azolla — Category 1b, so it is not available as duck or fish feed in a Highveld dam.

Opuntia ficus-indica (prickly pear) and Agave americana — used as real live fences in the Eastern Cape but listed or alien here. Note the carve-out worth encoding: spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are NOT listed, so spineless fodder cactus remains lawful if a user asks.

Cultivated olive (Olea europaea subsp. europaea) — the eastern Free State is on record as a workable summer-rainfall olive pocket, but whole trees die at about −7°C, which overlaps this biome's frost range, and summer-rainfall humidity raises disease pressure. Left out of the ranked list; wild olive (subsp. africana, SANBI-rated to about −5°C and far tougher) carries the windbreak and erosion function instead.

Apricot (Prunus armeniaca) — hardy enough, but it flowers earlier than any other stone fruit and Highveld late-spring frost destroys the crop in a high proportion of years. 71% of national trees sit in the Klein Karoo for a reason. Peach and plum are the Highveld stone fruit.
Moringa oleifera — heavily promoted to Limpopo smallholders and frequently mis-recommended nationally; frost-tender and will not overwinter on the Highveld.

Chamaecytisus palmensis (tagasaste / tree lucerne) — circulates in SA regenerative circles as a frost-hardy N-fixing fodder tree, but I could not confirm it against any SA institutional source, and it is described as frost-tender when young against a −5 to −10°C winter. Lucerne and the indigenous acacias cover the same function with evidence behind them.
palettes.notes:
45 entries. Three things drive this palette and should shape the app's copy for this biome.

1. FROST IS THE WHOLE STORY. Strelitzia 19's Grassland chapter gives mean frost days of 11–158 across vegetation units, and SANBI Zone 4 is the only horticultural zone whose minimum drops below −5°C. That single fact deletes the entire subtropical fruit list (citrus, avocado, mango, macadamia, banana, litchi, guava) and makes this the one biome where temperate deciduous fruit is the RIGHT answer rather than a compromise. Frost also inverts the usual permaculture nitrogen-fixer canon: leucaena, sesbania, pigeon pea, tagasaste and spekboom all fail. The nitrogen work here is done by indigenous acacias (Vachellia karroo, V. sieberiana, Senegalia caffra), perennial lucerne, and summer-annual legumes that die at frost by design.

2. THE ~600 mm SOUR/SWEET LINE IS THE SECOND FILTER, and the app should ask which side of it the site is on. Strelitzia 19: above ~600 mm rainfall, sour andropogonoid grasses dominate on leached dystrophic soils and 'plant growth… is mostly macronutrient-limited'; below ~600 mm, sweet chloridoid grasses on eutrophic soils, and growth is 'mostly water-limited'. Practically: on the wet eastern Highveld (Mpumalanga escarpment, eastern Free State, 700–900 mm) budget for lime and phosphate before anything else; on the dry western Highveld (500–600 mm) the soil chemistry is fine and the constraint is water harvesting and rooting depth. Same biome, opposite prescriptions.

3. HAIL AND CLAY ARE DESIGN INPUTS, not footnotes. This biome has high lightning-flash density and near-annual hail — a direct argument for shelterbelts on the storm side (Searsia lancea and Eucalyptus sideroxylon here) and against tight-bunched or thin-skinned fruit. Heavy Highveld clay is why deep-rooted openers (lucerne, vetiver, pecan, Combretum) earn their place, and why anything wanting sharp drainage (fig, pomegranate) should go on a mound or slope.

TWO LEGAL POINTS THE APP MUST SURFACE HERE SPECIFICALLY. (a) The Eucalyptus rule is BIOME-SCOPED and Grassland is on the wrong side of it: the six listed eucalypts are Category 1b in this biome, with a Category 2 permit route only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenues, and no exemption at all in riparian areas or listed ecosystems. E. sideroxylon is unlisted — SANBI's own bee-forage infosheet says so in terms — so it is the safe recommendation, and the app should warn hard against species substitution at the nursery counter.
