(b) Mulberry is a name trap: Morus alba is Category 3 (plant/propagate/move/sell/give all prohibited), Morus nigra is unlisted. Since Notice 1 says the COMMON name determines listing where scientific names conflict, and both are sold simply as 'mulberry', this needs an explicit buying instruction, not just a status field.

INDIGENOUS FRUIT IS GENUINELY THIN HERE — five entries, not ten, and that is the honest finding rather than a gap in the research. South Africa's indigenous fruit flora is overwhelmingly Savanna, Thicket and coastal, and nearly all of it (marula, monkey orange, wild medlar, num-num, wild plum) is frost-sensitive. Do not pad this section; instead point Highveld users at the deciduous exotics, which are unusually strong in this biome, and at the fact that two of the five indigenous entries (Ziziphus, Grewia) are worth more as fodder and bee forage than as fruit.

CONFIDENCE AND METHOD. NEMBA status was checked against the parsed text of the 2020 gazette (GN 1003, GG 43726) rather than from memory. Directly verified as listed: Morus alba (Cat 3), the six Eucalyptus taxa, Solanum mauritianum/elaeagnifolium/pseudocapsicum/seaforthianum/sisymbriifolium, Prunus serotina, the alien Rubus set, Buddleja davidii/madagascariensis, Tecoma stans, Sesbania punicea, Nicandra physalodes. Directly verified as ABSENT from the list: Salix (all species), Vitis, Physalis, Symphytum, Punica, Malus, Pyrus, Cydonia, Carya, Juglans, Medicago, Ficus carica, Olea, Celtis africana, Chrysopogon, Eragrostis, Grewia, Diospyros, Ziziphus, Dovyalis, Searsia, Vachellia, Rhoicissus, Tulbaghia, Hypoxis, Leonotis, Artemisia, Aloe, Kiggelaria, Halleria, Lessertia, Amaranthus, Cleome, Corchorus, Vigna, Cucurbita, Cajanus, Chamaecytisus. Sizes and frost tolerances come from SANBI PlantZAfrica species pages where one exists (cited per entry); crop hectares and chill data from Hortgro's 2021 census, ARC and the ISHS cherry paper.

WEAKEST ENTRIES, flagged honestly: Kiggelaria africana (SANBI gives only ~−2°C, yet it is a standard Johannesburg and Pretoria street tree — marked 'moderate' and ranked last in its section); Dovyalis caffra (explicitly half-hardy, kept for its unmatched living-fence value with a microclimate caveat); Vachellia sieberiana (young plants need real frost protection). Gymnosporia buxifolia, Eragrostis curvula and Medicago sativa were assigned from SA practice literature rather than a fetched species page, so their sizes are conventional cultivation figures worth a second check before publication. Two further options deliberately left unranked but worth a mention in app copy: walnut (Juglans regia, unlisted, frost-hardy, good on the eastern Highveld but very large), and quince (Cydonia oblonga, unlisted, hardy, useful as a hedge and pear rootstock).

palettes.biome: Desert — Richtersveld / far NW Northern Cape, under ~100 mm MAP, fog-influenced on the coast, extreme heat inland (Gariep Desert is the hottest area in southern Africa)

entries.why: The only tree crop whose whole physiology matches this biome — it grows best at 26–45°C and tolerates 10–52°C, needs bone-dry air at ripening (rain at pollination and ripening causes cracking and rot), and takes saline soil and brackish groundwater; plant one male per six females and space ~9 m (about 120 palms/ha).
entries.source: https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Phoenix+dactylifera ; Palm Foundation Africa, Commercial Cultivation RSA (https://palmfoundation.co.za/?page_id=2995) — SA industry is centred on the Northern and Western Cape

entries.why: Roughly 200 chill hours (the lowest genuine chill requirement of any temperate fruit), mature hardiness near -10°C, and 38°C actively helps fruit development — it wants hot dry summers and mild winters, which is precisely what the Gariep delivers; the Northern Cape already carries about 7% of national plantings.
entries.source: ARC Climate-Smart Agriculture subtropical module (https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf); SA pomegranate industry hectare split WC 81% / LP 10% / NC 7%

entries.nembaStatus: Category 1b as a species — BUT GN 1003 of 2020 item 238 states 'Spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed' and 'The fruit of the sweet prickly pear is not listed if used for human consumption'. Plant NAMED SPINELESS CULTIVARS ONLY; seedlings revert to spiny and are then Category 1b.
entries.why: The most water-efficient fodder crop on earth and the proven answer to arid-zone feed shortages — Grootfontein Agricultural Development Institute imported 22 spineless Burbank cultivars in 1974 for exactly this purpose, and Cape livestock farmers have run cactus fodder banks since the 1910s; fruit plus year-round green fodder off almost no irrigation.
entries.source: GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020) item 238, verified in parsed gazette text; ISHS/Grootfontein cactus pear literature (https://ishs.org/ishs-article/1247_8/)

entries.why: Hardy to about -5°C (some cultivars to -10°C) with only a modest chill requirement, and it specifically needs warm DRY weather through the summer harvest because moisture cracks the ripening fruit — the exact reason it fails in the summer-rainfall east and succeeds here; the Klein Karoo is SA's commercial core.
entries.source: Hortgro / SA deciduous fruit industry data via Agribook (https://www.agribook.co.za/deciduous-fruit/); SA commercial fig area ~222 ha, Klein Karoo + Swartland

entries.why: ARC rates lemon as 'well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions' than any other citrus and it has no chill requirement, so it is the citrus that reaches furthest into hot arid country; the Northern Cape carries 240 ha of lemon on Orange River irrigation. River-corridor or borehole only, and whitewash trunks against 45–50°C sunburn.
entries.source: ARC CSA subtropical module (https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf); CGA Key Industry Statistics 2025 (https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf)

entries.why: The most cold-hardy citrus and the most evenly spread across SA's climates (27,479 ha in six provinces, incl. 285 ha Northern Cape) — worth a few trees beside the lemon for fresh eating, but like all citrus it is an irrigation-corridor crop here, not a dryland one.
entries.source: CGA Key Industry Statistics 2025 (https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf)

entries.why: ARC Infruitec has released peach selections that fruit on as few as 200–500 chill units, explicitly to reduce climatic risk for small-scale producers — worth trying only on the cooler winter-rainfall coastal side or higher ground; the hot-winter Gariep interior (MAT 23.3°C at Goodhouse) will not accumulate enough chill and the tree will simply not break dormancy properly.
entries.source: Hortgro chill-accumulation mapping and ARC Infruitec low-chill breeding programme (https://www.hortgro-science.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/2022/09/CLIMATE-18-MIDGLEY-Guide-to-climate-change-and-pome-and-stone-fruit-production-extended-executive-summary.pdf)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (SANBI Red List: Least Concern)
entries.why: SANBI calls it 'the largest and tallest indigenous tree from Namaqualand'; it follows the Orange River and its habitat is exclusively rock faces and granite domes, so it roots into crevices and reaches moisture no other tree can — the one indigenous shade-and-fruit canopy that will hold here unirrigated once established. Small speckled figs are edible (usually insect-infested).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ficus-cordata ; SANBI Red List (https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=1906-13)

entries.why: A genuine desert tree — SANBI describes it as 'happy with both winter and summer rainfall', occurring 'in harsh, stony and sandy desert and semi-desert areas, usually in low-lying areas along watercourses' with an extensive taproot; sweet edible fruit, leaves browsed by goats and sheep, twigs used as chewing sticks. Site it in a wash, not on a plain.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/euclea-pseudebenus

entries.why: SANBI records its 'ability to withstand intense heat, cold and drought' and it occurs naturally in the Northern Cape; edible berries, browse for stock, thorny branches are the traditional kraal fence, and the flowers 'produce abundant nectar and often yield a good honey' — four functions off one tree in a biome that offers very few.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ziziphus-mucronata

entries.why: SANBI records it growing on 'an annual rainfall of less than 40 mm to 900 mm' and tolerating 'hot summer temperatures and severe frosts' — no other nitrogen-fixing canopy tree in South Africa will hold at this rainfall. The pods are the premier arid fodder in southern Africa and the crown throws dense shade. Slow: allow 25–30 years and plant it where run-off concentrates.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-erioloba

entries.nembaStatus: NOT LISTED within the Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes (GN 1003 of 2020, item 133b) — BUT Category 1b (a) in riparian areas, (b) in a Protected Area under the Protected Areas Act, and (c) in a Listed Ecosystem or one identified in a Bioregional/Biodiversity Management Plan. The Gariep corridor IS riparian and much of the Richtersveld is a Protected Area / World Heritage landscape, so this is lawful only at inland borehole sites away from the river and outside the parks.
entries.why: Included because the biome exemption is real and almost always misread: this is the one place in South Africa where a river red gum windbreak, woodlot or bee-forage block is legal without a permit. It is also a heavy drinker — justify it only where a borehole already carries a homestead, and never within the riparian zone.
entries.source: GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020), item 133, verbatim from parsed gazette text (https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf)

entries.why: SANBI's own pick: 'an excellent shade tree especially in hot regions such as the Karoo and Kalahari since it is evergreen and drought resistant'. Grows up to 80 cm a year, dense enough to work as a wind screen, and 'does not have an aggressive root system' so it can sit beside buildings, paving and drip lines — the safest all-round shelter tree for a desert homestead.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lancea

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA — but it IS a Protected Tree under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998 (Schedule item 122). Planting your own is free; cutting, damaging, removing, transporting or selling one (or its products) requires a Ministerial licence under s15(1).
entries.why: The classic deep-rooted top-browse tree of the arid west — it holds green leaf through drought when everything else has dropped, and delivers three foods (fruit, caper-substitute flower buds, and the root that is 'commonly used as a substitute for coffee or chicory'). Dense round crown makes it a genuine shade tree for stock.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/boscia-albitrunca ; National Forests Act protected tree list, GN 155 GG 44204 (https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/201912/42887gen635.pdf)

entries.why: The fast nitrogen fixer — SANBI records growth 'up to 1 m per year' and a maximum near 12 m 'where there is good water' — so it buys you shade and fertility in five years while the camel thorn takes thirty. SANBI's named indigenous bee-forage tree (long flowering season), and stock feed on leaves, flowers and pods. In this biome it only holds in a wash, on a berm, or under irrigation.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo ; SANBI indigenous honey-bee forage infosheet (https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/infosheet-indigenous-plants-honey-bee-forage-19-11-2014.pdf)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — and the 2020 gazette explicitly flags it as the indigenous species 'not to be confused with' the four Category 1b alien tamarisks (T. aphylla, T. chinensis, T. gallica, T. ramosissima). Identify by cream-white flowers and vaginate scaly leaves; the invasives have pink flowers and sessile leaves.
entries.why: A halophyte with tap roots to 30 m that draws salt from deep groundwater and excretes it through leaf glands — the one windbreak, dune binder and riverbank fixer that will establish on brak soil and saline borehole water, which is exactly what most Richtersveld sites offer. Leaves are browsed; wood is firewood.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tamarix-usneoides ; GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020), items 353–356

entries.why: SANBI: tolerates 'about -5°C to 40°C', is 'frost-, drought- and wind-resistant' and once established 'virtually indestructable' — the safest evergreen shelterbelt tree for an exposed desert homestead, and it feeds honeybees. Slow-growing, so plant it early and behind a nurse. Note this is the indigenous subspecies, not the cultivated olive, which needs winter cold this biome does not have.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana

entries.why: Adapted to 25–35°C, tolerates extreme heat and short drought once well rooted, and coppices to 3 m for continuous leaf harvest — the fastest route to a dense protein-and-micronutrient green in country that grows almost no vegetables. The hard limit is frost: SA/Namibian accessions shed all foliage and desiccated stems through winter cold, so keep it out of cold-air pockets and off the higher eastern ground.
entries.source: North West DARD Moringa production guide (https://dard.nwpg.gov.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Moringa-production-for-food-security.pdf); SA Journal of Science review (https://scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0038-23532021000200013)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — DO NOT confuse with Parkinsonia aculeata (Jerusalem thorn), which is Category 1b. A genus-level lookup will wrongly flag this indigenous species.
entries.why: An indigenous Northern Cape and Richtersveld tree that photosynthesises through its green bark once the leaves drop, so it keeps working right through drought. Usually 3–4 m (to 8 m), leaves browsed by both game and livestock, and its light dappled shade is the right nurse cover for an understorey rather than the dense shade that kills it.
entries.source: Tree Atlas of Namibia (https://treeatlas.biodiversity.org.na/viewspec.php?nr=437); SANBI Red List Green-hair Thorn (http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=352-2)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA; SANBI Red List: Vulnerable (climate-driven die-back is most severe in the Richtersveld/Sperrgebiet).
entries.why: Flowers in mid-winter (June–July) with copious nectar that draws sunbirds, bees and insects — the single most important pollinator forage in the coldest, driest months, when almost nothing else is in flower. Young flower buds are edible. Because wild populations are declining, plant it and protect it rather than harvesting; site it where run-off concentrates on a rocky slope.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloidendron-dichotomum ; SANBI Red List Quiver Tree (https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=15461-2)

entries.why: A stiff, rigidly branched, very spiny indigenous shrub, widespread across South Africa, southern Namibia and Botswana — the practical stock-proof living fence in country where nothing grows fast enough to make one any other way. Small red berries feed birds, foliage is nibbled by goats, and the thicket is prime nesting habitat.
entries.source: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/532043-Lycium-cinereum ; SANBI PlantZAfrica Lycium accounts (https://pza.sanbi.org/lycium-ferocissimum) for the genus's hedging use

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only Salsola kali and S. tragus are listed, both Category 1b — a genus-level lookup on the old name Salsola aphylla will wrongly flag this)
entries.why: The drought-reserve browse of the arid west: a succulent halophyte that 'still retains its small fleshy grey foliage' when the rest of the veld is dry and black, browsed by all stock and game, and it naturally grows in exactly the brak dry watercourses and floodplains this biome offers. This is the indigenous, legal substitute for old man saltbush, which is Category 2 here. (Recently renamed from Salsola aphylla.)
entries.source: Feedipedia, Ganna bush (https://www.feedipedia.org/node/100); SANBI Red List Lye Ganna (https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3590-8)

entries.why: Its natural distribution is literally both banks of the Gariep from the river mouth to Kakamas, in rock crevices on steep slopes 'in the driest part of its course' — so it is already adapted to the exact site. Winter-flowering (June–August) with nectar for sunbirds and insects, it partners the quiver tree to carry pollinators through the cold season.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aloe-gariepensis

entries.why: Occurs naturally through to Namaqualand, with a taproot to 6 m and aromatic oils that 'help reduce water loss'; on SANBI's honeybee-forage list ('on warm days many bees are attracted to the flowers'), medicinal, and it recovers from grazing — one of very few useful understorey shrubs that will hold on an unirrigated slope.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eriocephalus-africanus ; SANBI Kirstenbosch bee-forage list (https://www.sanbi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/kirstenbosch-nbg-list-plants-provide-food-honey-bees.pdf)

entries.why: The actual fodder crop of the lower Orange irrigation schemes, and the highest-value thing you can grow here: Richtersveld herders currently truck lucerne in from Springbok (R60/bale plus R10 transport), so growing it on flood beds or under a pivot substitutes a bought input directly. Deep-rooted, heat-tolerant, fixes nitrogen, cut 8–10 times a year, and the surplus is the only reliable mulch source in the biome.
entries.source: Interdisciplinary drought risk assessment for communal farmers, Northern Cape (https://scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0301-603X2013000100005)

entries.why: The most drought-hardy legume in the SA smallholder set — ECHO trials in South Africa measured over 100 kg N/ha in above-ground biomass — and both the leaves (as morogo/imifino) and the dry grain are eaten, so one irrigated bed delivers nitrogen, a green vegetable, a pulse and living mulch that shades its own soil against 2,500 mm/yr evaporation.
entries.source: DFFE Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline (https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf); ARC-VOPI indigenous crops (https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx)

entries.why: Grows wild on coastal sand dunes from southern Namibia down the Northern Cape coast, so it belongs to the fog-influenced western strip specifically. SANBI calls it 'an extremely valuable plant for stabilizing moving sand… acts as a seed-trap and also provides organic matter that enables other species to grow' — a first coloniser that is also a leafy green (harvest new growth after rain).
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tetragonia-decumbens

entries.why: An indigenous Northern Cape annual halophyte that tolerates over 450 mM NaCl — so it will crop on the salt-crusted ground that flood irrigation inevitably leaves behind, which is the standard failure mode of desert irrigation. Leaves are eaten boiled like a salty spinach or pickled; self-seeds after rain and needs no establishment.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/mesembryanthemum-crystallinum

entries.why: Grows naturally 'from Namaqualand in the Northern Cape' southward, is 'drought-, and wind-resistant' and thrives in lime-rich and brackish sandy soil. SANBI lists it as 'a sand binder, groundcover, dune and embankment stabilizer, and fire-resistant barrier', the fruit has been eaten since ancient times, and the leaf juice is the standard first-aid remedy. Not frost-hardy — keep it coastal and low.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carpobrotus-edulis

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but check the name carefully: as Pennisetum, the genus contains P. purpureum (Category 2), P. setaceum and P. villosum (both 1b). Pearl millet itself (syn. Pennisetum glaucum) is not on the 2020 list.
entries.why: The most drought-tolerant cereal in cultivation and it matures in roughly 75–90 days, so it fits inside one irrigation cycle or a single good wash flood. Grain for the household plus a large straw crop — and straw is the scarcest input in this biome, because there is no other source of mulch.
entries.source: GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020) List 1, verified absent from parsed gazette text; Agribook field crops (https://www.agribook.co.za/)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (only Sorghum halepense, Johnson grass, is listed — Category 2)
entries.why: Far more heat- and drought-tolerant than maize and it goes dormant rather than dying when water runs out, which suits an intermittent flood-irrigation regime; grain, stover for fodder and stalks for mulch. Pair it with cowpea in the same bed for the nitrogen.
entries.source: GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020) List 1 item 342 (S. halepense only), verified in parsed gazette text

entries.why: African in origin, and the southern African tsamma/citron landraces (now often segregated as Citrullus amarus) were historically a desert water source as much as a food — flesh, seed and stock feed from one trailing crop whose own canopy shades the soil. Sow into a wash after rain or on the edge of irrigation.
entries.source: Agribook indigenous food crops (https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/); GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020) List 1 — Citrullus absent, verified in parsed gazette text

entries.why: ARC-VOPI's lead traditional leafy green: extremely heat-tolerant, nutrient-dense (vitamin A, iron), harvestable at 4–6 weeks, and it self-seeds so an irrigated bed keeps producing. In a biome that grows almost no vegetables this is the highest-return square metre you have. SA's indigenous A. thunbergii will volunteer in the same beds — let it.
entries.source: ARC-VOPI Indigenous Crops (https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx)

entries.why: The practitioner default for erosion in SA, and the desert failure mode is flash flooding, not slow sheet wash: hedgerows planted on contour above a gully head stop it advancing, and rows along irrigation berms and canal edges hold them. Slips 10–15 cm apart in a single row, plant with water available, hedge visible in 3 months, trim to 20–30 cm and use the cuttings as mulch. Sterile cultivars do not seed and will not escape.
entries.source: Vetiver SA (https://www.vetiver.co.za/vetiver-grass-faq/)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed; SANBI Red List: Least Concern, occurs in all nine provinces
entries.why: Already lines the Gariep, so it is free planting material: use it for bank stabilisation on the irrigation channel, as a cut windbreak screen and shade-cloth substitute, as thatch, and as a greywater reed bed. It is rhizomatous and aggressive — confine it to the channel edge and cut it hard, or it takes the wet ground you wanted for crops.
entries.source: SANBI Red List Phragmites australis (https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=1145-1)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed under NEMBA — but commercial trade triggers Bioprospecting/Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) permitting under NEM:BA Chapter 6 and the Bioprospecting Regulations.
entries.why: A Namaqualand succulent that grows on quartz patches at rainfall as low as 100 mm — one of the very few things here that will yield without irrigation, and it has a real commercial market with organic-certified Namaqualand producers already operating. Plant it under the light shade of a nurse shrub, which is how it grows wild.
entries.source: Mountain Herb Estate / SA growers (https://www.herbgarden.co.za/mountainherb/herbinfo.php?id=706); ABS Biotrade Sceletium (https://www.abs-biotrade.info/sceletium-tortuosum/)

entries.why: The proven flagship crop of exactly this landscape: Aussenkehr and Vioolsdrif on the lower Orange produce table grapes under 50 mm of rain, with summer river-valley temperatures reaching 50°C, and the extreme heat is an advantage — harvest comes three to five weeks earlier than anywhere else. Trellised over a walkway it is also the cheapest deep shade you can build.
entries.source: Aussenkehr / lower Orange table grape production (https://saiia.org.za/research/greening-the-namibian-desert-an-african-success-story/)

excluded: Prosopis glandulosa var. torreyana / P. velutina (mesquite) — the most-planted arid fodder tree in the Northern Cape and the first thing anyone will ask about. It is Category 3 in the Northern Cape (Category 1b in EC, FS, NW, WC). Category 3 means existing trees may stand and 'the utilisation of the pods for fodder is not listed', BUT growing, propagating, moving, selling, giving away and allowing spread are all PROHIBITED under s71A with no permit route — and reg 5(2) makes any Category 3 plant in a riparian area a Category 1b plant, which covers the entire Gariep corridor. Do not plant. Vachellia erioloba is the legal equivalent.

Atriplex nummularia subsp. nummularia (old man saltbush) — Category 2 nationally, so possession, growing, moving and selling all require a permit, and an unpermitted plant is treated as Category 1b (reg 4(4)). This is the default dryland fodder shrub in every international arid-zone permaculture list. Use indigenous Caroxylon aphyllum (gannabos) instead.
Leucaena leucocephala — Category 2 nationwide with no area qualifier. The canonical tropical permaculture nitrogen fixer and the single most likely legal trap in any imported species list.

Casuarina cunninghamiana (beefwood) — Category 2, and Category 1b within 100 m of riparian areas or untransformed land. In the Desert biome effectively everything is either riparian or untransformed, so despite being a commercial SA windbreak species it is unusable here.

Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican sunflower) — Category 1b, prohibited to plant. Also needs far more water than this biome has. The most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture literature.

Portulacaria afra (spekboom) — NOT a Desert-biome plant, despite being recommended for 'anywhere arid in South Africa'. SANBI gives its range as Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and Mozambique; it belongs to Albany Thicket and the eastern Succulent Karoo (the Baviaanskloof/Camdeboo riplines work at 350–500 mm) and it will not establish at 10–70 mm without permanent irrigation.

Olea europaea (cultivated olive) — hardy to -7°C and superficially a desert tree, but it is an obligate thermoperiodic species needing 10+ weeks below 12.2–13.3°C, 600 to 1,000+ cultivar chill hours, and June–July maximum temperatures below 21°C or it bears no fruit at all. The Gariep Desert's winters are far too warm (MAT 23.3°C at Goodhouse). Grow the indigenous subsp. africana for shelter; olives belong upstream at Upington/Prieska and in the Western Cape.

Mango (Mangifera indica) — physiologically the most tolerant subtropical (45°C, under 300 mm rainfall) and therefore tempting here, but SAMGA's 2024 tree census records ZERO hectares in the Northern Cape against 4,280 in Limpopo. The industry has already tested this. Cold at full bloom aborts fruit and the crop needs a frost-free wet-season flush this biome cannot supply.

Pecan (Carya illinoinensis) — grown just upstream at Kakamas, Upington and Augrabies, but SAPPA's own zoning puts the warm dry west at 15,000 m3/ha/yr (peak 460–800 litres per tree per day), the highest water requirement of any crop in South Africa. It also needs winter frost for budbreak, which the low Gariep does not reliably provide. Only viable with a very large secure water allocation.

Avocado, macadamia, litchi and banana — all excluded on water and humidity. Avocado wants over 1,000 mm evenly distributed; macadamia 750–850 mm/yr; litchi needs relative humidity above 50% from October to harvest; ARC states outright that optimum banana conditions 'do not exist' anywhere in South Africa. None of these survive 10–70 mm MAP against roughly 2,500 mm/yr evaporation, irrigated or not.

Acanthosicyos horridus (!nara melon) — genuinely the great indigenous food plant of the fog Namib (deep taproot to groundwater, dune-binding, 1 kg fruit and oil-rich seeds, a staple before maize). Excluded because it has not been recorded in South Africa since 1925 and its SA range lies inside closed diamond-mining ground. Not a plantable recommendation, however good the story.

Salvadora persica (mustard/toothbrush tree) — occurs in South Africa, but the arid-west population reaches only as far south as the Kuiseb in Namibia; it is a Limpopo/Kruger species in SA, not a lower-Gariep one.

Salix mucronata (Cape silver willow) — not NEMBA-listed and an excellent riverbank binder, but its documented range is the Cape river systems (Kei, Bashee, Sundays, Fish, Breede, Berg), not the Orange. Left out rather than guessed at; use Tamarix usneoides and Phragmites australis for Gariep bank work.

Sambucus nigra (elder), Robinia pseudoacacia (black locust), Gleditsia triacanthos (honey locust) and Azolla spp. — all Category 1b and all standard in imported permaculture designs. Prohibited to plant anywhere in South Africa.

Agave americana and Agave sisalana — A. sisalana is Category 2; A. americana subsp. americana var. expansa is Category 3 in the Western Cape only and technically unlisted in the Northern Cape, but it is an aggressive arid-zone escapee with no function that Opuntia (spineless) and Lycium do not fill legally and better.
palettes.notes:
HONEST FRAMING FIRST. Strelitzia 19 Ch.6 is blunt: this is 'an area of extreme aridity with a MAP generally below 70 mm' — roughly 10 mm on the coast to 70–80 mm on the inland margin, 'highly variable from year to year'. There is NO rain-fed food palette here. Every entry above assumes one of three siting decisions: (a) the Gariep/Orange River irrigation corridor, (b) a borehole or spring at a homestead/stock post, or (c) a wash, drainage line or micro-catchment where run-off concentrates. Plant on the plains and it dies. This is an irrigation-and-microcatchment design problem before it is a species-selection problem.

THE BIOME SPLITS IN TWO AND THE PALETTE FOLLOWS. Strelitzia 19 separates the western Southern Namib (winter cyclonic rain, Alexander Bay ~50 mm, MAT 17.2°C, Benguela fog felt up to 100 km inland, 'the softer rain and drizzle… much more effective for plant growth') from the eastern Gariep Desert (late-summer convective rain, Goodhouse MAT 23.3°C, CV over 65%, 'the hottest area within the whole of southern Africa', roughly 15°C hotter in summer). Coastal/fog side: Tetragonia decumbens, Carpobrotus edulis, Mesembryanthemum crystallinum, Sceletium, Eriocephalus, and the only place low-chill peach has any chance. Gariep/hot side: date palm, grape, pomegranate, fig, citrus, Ficus cordata, Euclea pseudebenus, Aloe gariepensis — all on the river. Frost is 'not of any importance' near the coast and at low altitude inland; it only appears on higher eastern peaks, so frost tolerance is a minor filter here compared with every other SA biome.

WHY 'LARGE TREES' HAS ONLY TWO ENTRIES. At 10–70 mm of rain against roughly 2,400–2,600 mm potential evaporation, almost nothing reaches canopy size. Vachellia erioloba is the only indigenous nitrogen-fixing canopy tree that will hold (SANBI records it at 'less than 40 mm' annual rainfall). Ficus cordata is genuinely canopy-sized and is filed under Indigenous fruit because that is where a farmer will look for it, as is the date palm under Exotic fruit — check the stratum field, not the section, for structure. Padding this section would have meant recommending trees that die.

INDIGENOUS FRUIT IS THIN, AND THAT IS THE TRUTH. Three entries, not ten. The Richtersveld's 1,077 indigenous taxa are overwhelmingly Aizoaceae and Asteraceae dwarf succulents — magnificent botanically, near-useless as crops. The indigenous productivity here is browse and pollinator forage, not fruit, which is why the Shrubs and Small trees sections carry the ecosystem-service load.

FOUR NEMBA TRAPS SPECIFIC TO THIS BIOME, all verified against the parsed text of GN 1003, GG 43726 (2020): (1) Eucalyptus camaldulensis and five other eucalypts are expressly 'Not listed within Nama-Karoo, Succulent Karoo and Desert biomes' — but Category 1b in riparian areas, Protected Areas and Listed Ecosystems. Since the Orange corridor is riparian and much of the Richtersveld is a Protected Area/World Heritage landscape, the app must apply a spatial test, not a species test. (2) Opuntia ficus-indica is Category 1b as a species but 'spineless cactus pear cultivars and selections are not listed' — a cultivar-blind lookup will wrongly block the single best fodder plant available here. (3) Parkinsonia africana (indigenous, unlisted) versus Parkinsonia aculeata (1b), and Tamarix usneoides (indigenous, unlisted, and named in the gazette as the species 'not to be confused with' the four 1b alien tamarisks) — both will be false-flagged by genus matching. (4) Prosopis is Category 3 in the Northern Cape, which people read as 'allowed'. It is not: planting, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are all prohibited under s71A, and reg 5(2) converts any Category 3 plant in a riparian area to Category 1b.

TWO NON-NEMBA LEGAL FLAGS. Boscia albitrunca is a Protected Tree under the National Forests Act 84 of 1998 (item 122) — you may plant it freely, but cutting, damaging, transporting or selling one needs a Ministerial licence. Sceletium tortuosum triggers Bioprospecting/ABS permitting if traded commercially.

GROUND TRUTH ON HOW PEOPLE ACTUALLY FARM HERE. Richtersveld Nama pastoralism is transhumant: herds base in the Orange River riparian zone through the dry season and move onto the plains in the wet season, at very low stocking density. Farmers currently buy lucerne at R60/bale plus R10/bale transport from Springbok. That single fact is why Medicago sativa is rank 1 in the herbaceous layer — the highest-value intervention available is substituting a bought feed input, not growing a novel crop.

CITRUS, SINCE IT WAS SPECIFICALLY FLAGGED. Citrus does reach here, but only as an irrigation-corridor crop and only at the tolerant end of the genus. Lemon is the most climatically adaptable citrus and soft citrus the most cold-hardy; the Northern Cape carries 240 ha of lemon and 285 ha of soft citrus, versus 5,005 ha of grapefruit in Limpopo and none in the Western Cape. Navel is explicitly wrong for hot country (ARC: 'much of South Africa's subtropical area is unsuited'). Do not let a broad-reach 'citrus' tag imply the whole genus works — it does not, and 45–50°C summers mean trunk whitewashing and shade netting are part of the design, not extras.

DESIGN RULES THAT MATTER MORE THAN SPECIES CHOICE HERE. Evaporation-to-rainfall runs about 30:1 to 100:1, so shade, mulch and windbreak are structural, not optional — and mulch is the scarcest input in the biome, which is why lucerne, sorghum stover and pearl millet straw earn their place. Flood irrigation on lime-rich desert soil salinises fast, which is why three halophytes (Caroxylon, Mesembryanthemum, Tamarix) are in the palette as a deliberate salt-management layer. Fire is absent from this biome — do not import fire management. And build the shelterbelt (Searsia lancea, Tamarix usneoides, wild olive) before the fruit, because unsheltered fruit trees in berg-wind conditions above 44°C will not establish.

entries.why: The flagship crop of this biome and the clearest climate match on the list — olive is an obligate thermoperiodic species needing 10+ weeks below ~13C and June-July maxima under 21C to flower, which is precisely a fynbos winter, and 93-95% of SA's olives sit in the Western Cape as a result.
entries.source: https://www.saolive.co.za/olive-growing/ ; https://olivessa.co.za/climatic-regions/ ; Agribook olives (WC = 95% of national production, ~3,700 ha)

entries.why: Figs need warm DRY weather through summer harvest or the fruit splits — the exact condition fynbos gives and summer-rainfall biomes cannot; hardy to about -5C (some cultivars -10C), tolerant of stony infertile ground, and strikes readily from hardwood truncheons so a whole hedge costs nothing.
entries.source: Hortgro / Agribook deciduous fruit (SA fig core = Klein Karoo, Swartland, Overberg, ~222 ha); frost tolerance -5 to -10C per exotic-range brief

entries.why: The Western Cape carries 10,202 ha of soft citrus — more than any other province — and mandarin is the most cold-hardy citrus with no chill requirement, so it works from Citrusdal to the Overberg; but the frost floor is about -2C and rainfall here is 'insufficient' per ARC, so treat it as an irrigated tree, never a dryland one.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf ; https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: ARC Infruitec's low-chill selections crop on as few as 200-500 chill units, and every fynbos district clears that easily; Ceres (213 ha) and Citrusdal (202 ha) are two of SA's four largest dessert-peach blocks, and unlike apple it needs no rest-breaking chemistry.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf ; ARC Infruitec low-chill breeding programme

entries.why: 81% of SA's pomegranates are in the Western Cape, and the reason is a perfect fit: ~200 chill hours (the lowest real chill requirement of any temperate fruit), mature hardiness near -10C, 38C tolerance, and a demand for hot dry summers — plant at 5-6 m in an orchard or 2.5 m as a fruiting security hedge.
entries.source: SA pomegranate industry data (1,167 ha; WC 81% / LP 10% / NC 7%); size and spacing per https://greenharvest.com.au/blogs/growing-information/pomegranate-growing-information

entries.why: 300-600 chill hours and a Mediterranean summer put almond squarely in the Olifants, Breede and Klein Karoo valleys, and its very early bloom is the first big bee-forage event of the year — that same early bloom is the risk, so keep it off frost-pocket sites and out of cold valley bottoms.
entries.source: https://journals.co.za/doi/pdf/10.10520/EJC181721 (AgriProbe: almond as a possible crop for Western Cape province); IDC/OABS almond market study 2017

entries.nembaStatus: not listed in Western Cape (Category 2 for plantations / Category 3 elsewhere in EC, KZN, LP, MP and NW only — GN 1003, GG 43726, 2020)
entries.why: The Western Cape is SA's largest guava province (~547 ha, ahead of Limpopo) and — critically — guava is NOT NEMBA-listed here, unlike in the five summer-rainfall provinces where it is Category 2/3; ARC notes yield and quality actually improve with a distinct winter. Protect young trees from frost; wilt disease makes rootstock choice matter more than climate.
entries.source: NEMBA List 1 item 292, GN 1003 GG 43726 (verified: 'Not listed elsewhere'); https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: SA's 10.6 million plum trees are overwhelmingly Western Cape — Klein Karoo, Wolseley/Tulbagh, Franschhoek, Wellington, Paarl, Ceres — because Japanese-type plums have modest chill needs and crop across almost every fynbos district; plant two cultivars, most are poor self-pollinators.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf

entries.why: ARC rates lemon as suited to a broader range of climatic conditions than any other citrus, 2,371 ha are already planted in the Western Cape, and one tree covers a household year-round — the single highest-value fruit tree per square metre in a zone-1 built bed, provided it gets summer water.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf ; https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: Only worth planting on the high-chill fynbos uplands: Ceres, Elgin/Grabouw, Villiersdorp/Vyeboom and the Langkloof hold 92% of SA's 24,956 ha, and even there poor-chill seasons drop to 200-350 chill units and the crop leans on rest-breaking agents. Below about 500 units, plant a low-chill peach instead — that is the honest cut-off.
entries.source: https://www.hortgro.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/dlm_uploads/2022/08/KEY-DECIDUOUS-FRUIT-STATSISTICS-2021.pdf ; https://www.hortgro-science.co.za/wp-content/uploads/docs/2022/09/CLIMATE-18-MIDGLEY-Guide-to-climate-change-and-pome-and-stone-fruit-production-extended-executive-summary.pdf

entries.why: A true 250-500 mm Mediterranean dryland tree — evergreen shade, human food and high-energy stock fodder from the pods with no summer irrigation once established, which nothing else in this section can claim. It is dioecious, so plant a male for every 8-10 females, and note it is a legume that does NOT nodulate — do not count it as a nitrogen fixer.
entries.source: https://www.feedipedia.org/node/320 ; https://plantinfo.co.za/plant/ceratonia-siliqua/ (6-12 m); WC is the main SA planting area

entries.why: The one genuinely fynbos indigenous fruit that also does real work — 35 mm figs for konfyt, leaf juice that is the standard Cape remedy for stings and sore throats, and a proven binder of loose acid dune sand where nothing else roots. C. acinaciformis and C. deliciosus have sweeter fruit if food is the priority.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carpobrotus-edulis

entries.why: The only indigenous staple vegetable native to the winter-rainfall Cape, and it runs on exactly the inverted calendar this biome demands — it fills a farm dam or seasonal vlei from autumn through spring and goes dormant as tubers precisely when summer water disappears. Zero irrigation cost, and it is the only entry that turns a seasonal wet spot into a cash crop.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aponogeton-distachyos

entries.why: The best-evidenced stock-proof living fence in South Africa — thorny, drought- AND frost-resistant, growing about 600 mm a year — and it pays a second time with heavy 60 mm fruit for jam. Indigenous to SA but not to fynbos; it takes the sandy soil and the dry summer without complaint. Dioecious: plant males with females for fruit.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra

entries.why: The Cape's hardest-working coastal shelter shrub — SANBI notes it tolerates poor soil, salt, wind, drought and frost simultaneously and makes an excellent coastal hedge or screen. Edible (sour) berries for fermented drinks, heavy bird and honeybee traffic, and it is the species to put on the outer, seaward row of any fynbos windbreak.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/searsia-lucida

entries.why: Not a fynbos native but long established in Cape coastal horticulture — Y-shaped thorns, wind- and salt-resistant, and planted 1 m apart it forms an impenetrable edible security hedge with vitamin-C-rich fruit. Frost-tender: this is a coastal-lowland and sheltered-courtyard call only, not for Ceres or the Koue Bokkeveld.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carissa-macrocarpa

entries.why: THE fynbos permaculture tree: a nitrogen-fixing legume that puts on up to 1.3 m a year on poor acid sand, shelters and feeds a young food forest, then obligingly dies at 12-20 years leaving fertility and a canopy gap for the fruit trees planted beneath it. One caution — it is a documented forest precursor that invades fynbos even without fire, so keep it on the cultivated side of the line, never in retained veld.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/virgilia ; Coetsee & Wigley, Bothalia 2013 (V. divaricata and afrotemperate forest expansion)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (indigenous; often cited as subsp. africana)
entries.why: SANBI calls it virtually indestructible once established, tolerating -5C to 40C — the only large evergreen here that needs no summer water at all. Excellent stock and game fodder, dense enough for a genuine windbreak, used to stabilise erosion gullies, and it is the traditional rootstock for grafting cultivated olives onto a drought-proof root system.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/olea-europaea-subsp-africana

entries.why: The fastest indigenous shade canopy for a Cape smallholding — flowers at two years, tolerates -2C to 36C, sandy through clay soil, acid through alkaline — and it is the single most important wildlife tree in the palette: Acraea horta host plant, hornbills and woodpeckers on the fruit, honeybees on the flowers. Fruit is not edible for people; this one earns its place on habitat and shade.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/kiggelaria-africana

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (indigenous; no Salix species appears on the 2020 NEMBA plant list)
entries.why: The indigenous, unlisted answer for a Cape streambank where people default to invasive poplars or exotic willows. Plants straight from truncheons, holds banks against winter flood, withstands both frost and drought, gives cut fodder that livestock eat, and yields the single biggest annual mulch/biomass crop available in a biome where mulch material is the scarcest input.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/salix-mucronata

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (indigenous) — but a nationally Protected Tree under the National Forests Act
entries.why: The definitive Cape coastal shelter tree: 10-15 m of dense evergreen crown, edible purple-black berries, and heavy bird, bat and honeybee value. It burns in direct salt wind, so plant it BEHIND a Searsia or Morella front line rather than on it. Hard constraint: it is a Protected Tree, so once planted it may never legally be felled, moved or damaged — site it deliberately and away from future buildings.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/sideroxylon-inerme

entries.why: The one yellowwood that actually belongs in the winter-rainfall Cape — SANBI rates it tougher and more drought-resistant than the other SA yellowwoods, it holds at about 6 m and as broad as it is high, and the fruit on female trees is a serious bird resource. Use it as the permanent evergreen spine of a shelterbelt, behind the fast pioneer row.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/podocarpus-elongatus

entries.why: South Africa's most multi-functional indigenous tree and its range starts in the Western Cape — fixes nitrogen so grasses thrive in its shade, gives non-toxic browse of leaves, flowers and pods, has an unusually long bee-forage season, grows up to 1 m a year, and supplies thorn brush for fencing. On a fynbos farm put it on the heavier renosterveld or clay soils rather than on deep leached sand.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/vachellia-karroo ; SANBI indigenous honeybee forage infosheet

entries.why: The fynbos streambank tree — Van Riebeeck's 1660 living hedge is still partly standing, which tells you everything about its performance as a permanent barrier. Multi-stemmed, coppices hard, binds banks, shelters everything behind it, and it is a true fynbos-biome species that wants the acid sand. Do NOT list the nut as food: it is cyanogenic and needs days of soaking then boiling and roasting.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/brabejum-stellatifolium

entries.why: The nitrogen answer on deep coastal sand: it is actinorhizal, carrying root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen where rhizobial legumes struggle at pH 4. Horizontal branches cover about 7 square metres, it binds moving dune sand (the old Department of Forestry used it for exactly that and it is being reintroduced for the purpose), it takes salt spray, and the berries are edible and yield candle and polish wax.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/morella-cordifolia

entries.why: A fast nitrogen-fixing legume that specifically wants well-drained acidic soil and does not thrive in alkaline ground — i.e. it is built for this biome — and SANBI rates it frost-hardy to roughly -7C, which covers the coldest fynbos uplands. Clips into an informal hedge and is a carpenter-bee magnet, which then improves fruit set across the whole planting.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/podalyria-calyptrata

entries.why: The nitrogen fixer for the wet end of the farm — seeps, swale bottoms, spring lines and stream margins where the drier fynbos legumes rot. It feeds honeybees, draws insectivorous white-eyes, and herbarium records show it persisting even under pine and wattle, so it is the species to establish while you are still clearing invasives.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/psoralea-pinnata

entries.why: The biggest nectar producer in the biome — historically boiled down into bossiestroop — and the anchor for Cape sugarbirds, sunbirds, protea beetles and honeybees; it takes everything from heavy clay to deep white sand and is damaged only below about -4C. CRITICAL: its cluster (proteoid) roots are killed by the phosphate your vegetable beds need, so it must sit on the unimproved side of a hard line, upslope of no fertiliser runoff.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/protea-repens ; Mucina & Rutherford, Strelitzia 19 ch.4 (proteoid roots, fertiliser runoff)

entries.why: The longest-flowering nectar shrub you can plant here — sunbirds, honeybees and butterflies work it through autumn and into winter when almost nothing else is out — and SANBI rates it tolerant of moderate to severe frost, cutting to the ground and reshooting. Traditional medicinal for coughs, fever and headache; note toxicology work flags organ damage at high doses, so treat dosing cautiously.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/leonotis-leonurus

entries.why: The only commercial crop in the world that actively requires this biome's worst agronomic liabilities — sandy, acid, nutrient-poor soil and only 300-350 mm of winter rain — so it converts the unimprovable part of a fynbos farm into income. A legume, so it also puts nitrogen back into the sand, and it feeds honeybees. Grows to 2 m wild; commercial rows are kept lower by annual harvest.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/aspalathus-linearis

entries.why: A second indigenous tea crop for acid sand — it needs pH 3.5-5 and good drainage, resprouts vigorously from a storage rootstock after fire (so it survives the biome's fire cycle), and carpenter bees do the pollination. Plant C. genistoides or C. subternata, which are the cultivable species; C. intermedia is harvested almost entirely from the wild and can only be cut every second or third year, so it should never be a planting recommendation.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/cyclopia-genistoides ; Karsen et al., Crop Science 2022 (propagation and cultivation of Cyclopia spp.)

entries.why: The Cape's highest-value medicinal crop per hectare, grown on the same acid mountain sand as rooibos, and the whole shrub flowers over with bees. A. betulina is commercially preferred for its lower pulegone but is restricted to Cederberg/Piketberg/Tulbagh-type mountain slopes; if you want bulk rather than premium oil, A. crenulata reaches 1.5-2.5 m, withstands a fair amount of frost and long drought, and is easier to grow.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/agathosma-crenulata (gives A. betulina 2 m and A. crenulata 1.5-2.5 m)

entries.why: A 6 m taproot and 2 m of lateral roots on a 1 m shrub — that root-to-shoot ratio is why it holds dry banks and terrace edges and is effectively unkillable by a Cape summer. Culinary and medicinal leaf, reliable bee forage, browsed by stock, and it clips into a low hedge or bed edging on the poorest sand.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/eriocephalus-africanus

entries.nembaStatus: not listed (indigenous; long known as Salvia africana-lutea)
entries.why: The coastal front-line shrub — a natural component of Cape dune vegetation, so it takes strong salt-laden wind, is drought resistant, and resprouts after frost damage. Heavy sweet nectar for sunbirds, bees and moths, and the leaves make a genuinely good tea for coughs and bronchitis. Use it as the low, sacrificial outer layer of a coastal windbreak.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/salvia-aurea

entries.why: A short-lived nitrogen-fixing legume that self-seeds into gaps — the right way to use it is as a living green manure and gap-filler that happens to also be the best-known medicinal plant in the region and a sunbird-pollinated nectar source. Hardy across the fynbos frost range and drought resistant once established.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/lessertia-frutescens

entries.why: The single most useful exotic herb for this biome and the one exception to a mostly indigenous shrub layer: Mediterranean-native so it needs no summer water at all, it flowers right through the Cape winter when bee forage is scarcest, and it clips into a low hedge or terrace-edge stabiliser on the poorest sand. (Renamed from Rosmarinus officinalis, which is still the name on most nursery labels.)
entries.source: Verified absent from NEMBA List 1, GN 1003 GG 43726 (2020); Mediterranean climatic origin per standard horticultural references

entries.why: The soil-building engine for fynbos sand and the highest-leverage plant on this whole list. Lupins prefer LOW soil pH and tolerate aluminium toxicity — the exact condition (pH 3.5-4.5) that defeats most legumes — they have become the standard cover crop on Western Cape coastal sands, and field measurements record 195-255 kg N/ha fixed in a single winter season. Sow with the first autumn rains, roll or slash at flowering.
entries.source: https://www.grainsa.co.za/conservation-agriculture:-part-17 ; Nitrogen fixation and accretion of soil N by field-grown lupins, Field Crops Research 1987; PMC8766672 (lupin adaptation to acid, Al-toxic soils)

entries.why: The living nitrogen-fixing floor for under fruit trees, running from autumn to spring while the trees are dormant. Serradella is adapted to soils down to pH 4.0 with exchangeable aluminium up to 30% CEC and improves phosphorus-use efficiency by about 30% relative to subterranean clover — which matters enormously on P-fixing fynbos sand. On the less acid renosterveld and shale soils, substitute subterranean clover (Trifolium subterraneum) instead.
entries.source: https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/pastures/Html/French_serradella_-_soft_seeded.htm ; Crop & Pasture Science (serradella vs subclover on deep acid sands, P-use efficiency)

entries.why: Edible leaves and flowers for salads, a decoction for coughs and colds, and — the reason to plant it in quantity — crushed on skin it genuinely repels fleas, ticks and mosquitoes, and it is reputed as a snake repellent. Grows in almost any soil, survives prolonged drought, hardy across the fynbos frost range: use it as the permanent edging of every vegetable bed and path.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tulbaghia-violacea

entries.why: An indigenous perennial leafy green that grows on pure salt-blown sand — harvest the new growth and leafy stem tips through the winter rains, and meanwhile it acts as a seed trap, builds organic matter and stabilises the most hostile ground on the farm. Stems run horizontally and root at intervals, ascending to about 50 cm, one plant covering several square metres. Frost-free coastal sites only.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tetragonia-decumbens ; https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Tetragonia+decumbens (stems ascending to 50 cm, branches to 1 m)

entries.why: The one deep-acid-sand crop that needs no soil improvement whatsoever — a long-lived restio harvested for thatch on a five-year cycle (a well-thatched roof lasts 30 years on the coast and up to 70 inland), producing abundant honeybee pollen and holding sand in the years between cuts. Prefers deep, slightly acidic sandy soil and needs very little water once growing. Like the proteas, keep it off fertilised ground.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/thamnochortus-insignis

entries.why: A Mediterranean perennial vegetable that runs on the fynbos calendar — vegetative through the wet winter, cropping in spring, dormant through the dry summer — so it produces food in the season when the biome actually has water. The huge leaf mass is a serious chop-and-drop mulch source, and any heads left to flower are among the best bee plants in a zone-1 bed.
entries.source: Verified absent from NEMBA List 1, GN 1003 GG 43726 (2020); Mediterranean-climate perennial vegetable, standard Cape kitchen-garden crop

entries.why: The farm first-aid plant: the fresh leaf yields a jelly-like juice for burns, rashes, blisters, insect bites, cracked lips and mouth ulcers — worth having within arm's reach of the work areas. A vigorous clump-forming succulent that flowers year-round for bees, needs almost no water, and is the standard tough groundcover where you need bare acid sand covered fast.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/bulbine-frutescens ; https://plantinfo.co.za/plant/bulbine-frutescens/ (listed 300 x 300 mm; clumps spread wider with age)

entries.why: The Cape's defining crop for 350 years and the near-perfect fynbos climber — deep-rooted, tolerant of poor stony soil, and it actively needs the dry summer that rots table grapes in summer-rainfall biomes. On a pergola it gives dense summer shade over a patio, kitchen or animal pen and then drops its leaves for winter sun, and the annual prunings are a reliable mulch and cutting-wood source.
entries.source: Verified absent from NEMBA List 1, GN 1003 GG 43726 (2020); Western Cape wine and table grape industry, Mediterranean-climate crop

entries.why: The indigenous edible vine for shaded kloof and forest-margin corners where table grapes mildew — 20 mm purple-black berries described by SANBI as edible and pleasant, used for jam, jelly, wine and vinegar. Its range starts on the Cape Peninsula, it grows in low light (forest floor to forest edge), and it will run up a tree, over a shade structure or across the ground as a cover.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-tomentosa

excluded: Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica) — NEMBA Category 1b IN THE WESTERN CAPE and in the Forest biome (not listed elsewhere in SA; not listed in WC urban areas). A staple of global permaculture fruit lists and outright illegal to plant on a Western Cape farm — no permit route exists for Category 1b. Verified at List 1 item 132, GN 1003 GG 43726.

Eucalyptus (E. camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis) — Category 1b IN THE FYNBOS BIOME by default. There is a Category 2 carve-out for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenues (permit required), and non-listing within cultivated land 50 m from untransformed land or within 50 m of the main farmhouse — but it is 1b unconditionally in riparian areas, Protected Areas and Listed Ecosystems. Too conditional to put in a farmer-facing palette, and it is the wrong tree for a fire-prone, water-scarce biome anyway.

Cluster pine and Monterey pine (Pinus pinaster, P. radiata) — Category 2 for plantations and wind-rows only, Category 1b everywhere else, which is where a smallholder would plant them. These are the Cape's principal water-thieves and the main fuel load behind catastrophic fynbos fires. P. halepensis is Category 3 in the Western Cape.

Australian wattles — Acacia saligna (Port Jackson) 1b, A. cyclops (rooikrans) 1b, A. longifolia 1b, A. pycnantha 1b, A. mearnsii and A. dealbata Category 2. The classic 'free nitrogen fixer and firewood' trap in the Cape; almost all are 1b with no permit route. Note the Notice 1 general exemption: DEAD specimens and listed invasive plant material used as BIOMASS are exempt from permits for transport and sale — so clearing wattle for firewood, charcoal, biochar or mulch is lawful. Planting is not.

Leucaena leucocephala — NEMBA Category 2 nationwide (permit required for possession, growing, moving or selling; without a permit it is treated as Category 1b under reg 4(4)). It is also a tropical summer-growing species that performs poorly in a cool wet winter / dry summer regime, so it fails on climate as well as law.

Mexican sunflower (Tithonia diversifolia) — Category 1b. The single most-recommended chop-and-drop species in international permaculture writing, and illegal to grow, move, sell or give away in South Africa. It also needs summer rain. Use Virgilia, Podalyria, Salix mucronata prunings and artichoke leaf for biomass instead.
Elder (Sambucus nigra) — Category 1b. Elderflower and elderberry hedgerows are a European permaculture staple and cannot be planted here.

Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia) 1b and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos) 1b — the two default temperate nitrogen-fixing support trees in Northern Hemisphere designs; both compulsory-control species in SA.

White mulberry (Morus alba) — Category 3. Not 'allowed': planting, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are all prohibited under s71A; only keeping a tree that already stands is exempt, and in a riparian area reg 5(2) makes it 1b outright. The fruit-for-human-consumption carve-out exempts the fruit, never the tree. Australian silky oak (Grevillea robusta) is also Category 3.

Sweet prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica) — Category 1b, though SPINELESS cactus pear cultivars and selections are expressly not listed and are legal. Left out on climate rather than law: it is a Karoo and thicket fodder crop, not a fynbos one.

Century plant (Agave americana subsp. americana var. expansa) — Category 3 IN THE WESTERN CAPE only (not listed elsewhere). Genuinely used as a live fence in the Eastern Cape, and specifically restricted here. Use Dovyalis caffra, Carissa macrocarpa or pomegranate for a thorny edible barrier instead.

Hakea sericea / gibbosa / drupacea, Leptospermum laevigatum (Australian myrtle), Pittosporum undulatum, Metrosideros excelsa (1a in Overstrand) — all major Cape invaders, all 1a/1b, and all frequently suggested as coastal windbreaks. Use Searsia lucida, Morella cordifolia, wild olive and Podocarpus elongatus.

Pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan) and Sesbania sesban — the two woody legumes the DFFE national Agroforestry Best-Practice Guideline names for improved fallows and alley cropping in South Africa. Both are warm-season, summer-rainfall, largely photoperiod-sensitive species documented in KwaZulu-Natal; they are the wrong hemisphere of the calendar for a winter-rainfall Cape farm. Replaced here by lupin, serradella, Virgilia, Podalyria and Psoralea.

Vetiver (Chrysopogon zizanioides) — not NEMBA-listed and the SA practitioner default for erosion control, but it is a C4 warm-season grass that grows through summer; in a winter-rainfall biome it establishes slowly and needs irrigation in the very season it should be growing. Fynbos erosion work is better done with Morella cordifolia, restios, Carpobrotus, Tetragonia and Salix mucronata on the banks.

Spekboom (Portulacaria afra) — an Albany Thicket and Karoo species adapted to non-seasonal or summer rain, frost-sensitive, and not part of fynbos practice despite being the SA restoration poster plant.

Mango, banana, litchi, macadamia, pecan and papaya — excluded on climate. All require frost-free, warm, summer-humid conditions; ARC states outright that optimum banana conditions exist nowhere in SA, litchi needs winter minima above 6C AND below 14C with summer humidity above 50%, and macadamia is not frost resistant and needs 750-850 mm/yr. Avocado is a partial exception: about 972 ha exist in the Western Cape and clonal rootstocks are pushing it further, but the -4C floor combined with August-September flowering frost and a >1,000 mm evenly-distributed water preference makes it a sheltered, irrigated, site-specific call rather than a palette recommendation.
Moringa oleifera and Erythrina lysistemon — both promoted in SA permaculture and both frost-tender summer-rainfall subtropicals that will not carry a Cape winter.

The ARC traditional-greens set (Amaranthus, Cleome gynandra, Corchorus, Solanum retroflexum, Bidens pilosa) — genuinely important indigenous SA vegetables, but warm-season summer-rainfall crops. In the Cape they need full summer irrigation and are out of phase with the rain; the winter-rainfall equivalents are brassicas, alliums, broad beans, peas and the entries above.

English oak (Quercus robur) — not NEMBA-listed and historically the Cape's signature shade and acorn-pannage tree, but DFFE's October 2025 briefing flags it as a primary Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer amplifier host, and PSHB is killing mature oaks across the Western Cape now. Not worth a 60-year investment.
palettes.notes:
FYNBOS IS THE HARDEST BIOME IN SOUTH AFRICA FOR FOOD, AND THE REASON IS SOIL, NOT CLIMATE. The climate is superb — a Mediterranean winter-rainfall regime that grows the best deciduous and Mediterranean fruit in Africa. The soil is the problem. Strelitzia 19 states it flatly: "the low nutrient status of fynbos makes the soils unsuitable for agriculture." Mountain sandstone weathers to soils with under 5% clay; podzol B-horizons run pH 3.5-4.0; Witfontein-form soils sit below pH 4.0 with base saturation at or under 20%. So zones 1-2 here are a soil-CONSTRUCTION job, not a plant-selection job: built beds, imported topsoil, compost, lime and rock phosphate, on a defined footprint you can afford to maintain. Renosterveld and strandveld soils are the exception — granite, shale and dolerite-derived, clay-richer and far more base-rich — and they are exactly where Cape agriculture historically went (vineyards and orchards). If your site has them, put the annuals and the fruit sections there and leave the deep acid sand to the rooibos / honeybush / buchu / restio layer, which wants it.

THE PHOSPHATE RULE — the single most important design constraint. Proteaceae, Restionaceae, Ericaceae and Cyclopia carry cluster (proteoid) roots evolved for extreme phosphorus scarcity, and phosphate fertilisation kills them. Retained fynbos and fertilised production beds must be physically separated, with fertiliser runoff kept off the veld (Strelitzia 19 flags runoff explicitly). In practice: Protea repens, Thamnochortus, buchu, rooibos and honeybush go on the unimproved side of a hard line and preferably upslope; everything in the fruit sections goes on the built-soil side. A permaculture design here has two soil regimes on one farm, not one.

SEASON INVERSION. Rain falls May-August; December-March is hot, dry and windy. Every "low" water rating above means "survives on winter rain alone once established" — it does NOT mean it will fruit without summer irrigation. Every entry in the exotic fruit section is an irrigated tree for its first 3-5 years and most stay irrigated permanently (SA Olive calls drip or micro-sprinkler "a prerequisite" even for olives). Note also that fynbos has almost no annual plants at all, which Wisheu et al. attribute to soils too infertile for an annual to complete a life cycle and set seed in one season — read that as a direct warning about rain-fed annual vegetables on unimproved ground.

FIRE IS A DESIGN INPUT, NOT A HAZARD TO IGNORE. Fynbos burns on a 5-50 year rotation, usually 15-25 years; renosterveld burns every 2-10 years. Put the irrigated, high-moisture, low-resin plantings — the fruit sections, artichoke, the willow and wild-almond streambank line — on the windward side as a living green firebreak, and keep resinous species away from buildings. This is a second, independent reason the pine and eucalypt windbreaks people default to are the wrong answer here.

FROST IS SITE-SPECIFIC, NOT BIOME-SPECIFIC. Mean frost days across fynbos vegetation units run 1-62. Paarl averages 0.3 heavy-frost days a year, Grabouw 12, Ceres 14, Sutherland 93. Coastal lowlands are effectively frost-free. So the frost-tender entries (sour fig, dune spinach, num-num, honeybush, granadilla) are coastal and lowland calls, while apple only makes sense in the high-chill uplands. Drive the palette off the site's own frost-day figure, not off "Fynbos".

FOG IS UNMEASURED WATER. Over 500 mm/yr can be precipitated from wet stratus without registering in a rain gauge, and Schulze reports above 600 mm/yr of orographic fog moisture in the Jonkershoek mountains. On a mountain-slope site the effective water budget is materially better than the rainfall figure suggests — and fog-drip fences and canopy interception are worth designing for.

WIND. The south-easter is usually the dominant stress on a Cape smallholding. The sequence that works on sand is: Searsia lucida or Morella cordifolia on the outer, seaward row; wild olive or Podocarpus elongatus behind it; then the fruit. Target roughly 40-60% porosity, not a solid wall — the macadamia industry's published windbreak spec, and it applies equally here.

NITROGEN. Fynbos legumes are the engine of this design and they are unusually good: Virgilia (canopy), Podalyria and Psoralea (shrub), rooibos, honeybush and Lessertia (crop plus understorey), and Morella cordifolia, which is actinorhizal (Frankia, not rhizobia) and therefore fixes nitrogen on deep sand where rhizobial legumes struggle. On the annual side, lupin and serradella are the two that actually perform at pH 4-5 — lupin measurably at 195-255 kg N/ha in a winter season. This is why the SA agroforestry defaults (pigeon pea, Sesbania) are in the excluded list: better options exist here and they are indigenous.

ONE HONEST GAP: INDIGENOUS FRUIT. Fynbos has very little. Sour fig and waterblommetjie are the two genuine winter-rainfall indigenous foods; kei apple, num-num and Searsia berries are indigenous to South Africa but not to this biome. That section is deliberately five entries rather than padded to ten. If you want more depth, worth adding: quince (Cydonia oblonga — classic Cape hedge, pear rootstock and preserve fruit, unlisted); pear (Pyrus communis — Ceres 4,734 ha, essentially the same envelope as apple); Elegia tectorum for wet seeps (1-1.5 m x 2-3 m); Artemisia afra (wilde-als, the most-used indigenous medicinal in SA); and purple granadilla (Passiflora edulis), which is Category 2 in six provinces but is NOT LISTED in the Western Cape — verified at List 1 item 256.

LEGAL BASIS. Every NEMBA status above was checked against the parsed text of the Alien and Invasive Species Lists, 2020 (GN 1003, GG 43726, 18 September 2020), read with the AIS Regulations 2020 (GN R.1020, GG 43735), both in force since 1 March 2021 and unamended as of DFFE's October 2025 briefing. Two Western-Cape-specific traps to encode in the app: loquat is Category 1b in the Western Cape and the Forest biome but unlisted elsewhere in SA, and Agave americana var. expansa is Category 3 in the Western Cape only. And the general warning: Category 3 does not mean "allowed" — growing, propagating, moving, selling and giving away are all prohibited under s71A; only keeping what already stands is exempt, and in a riparian area a Category 3 plant is treated as 1b. Category 2 without a permit is treated as Category 1b under reg 4(4). Beyond NEMBA, a fynbos farm also sits under the National Water Act (s21 water use and stream-flow-reduction authorisation for any significant tree planting or irrigation) and CARA, neither of which this palette addresses.

palettes.biome: Forest — Afromontane and coastal forest patches (Southern Afrotemperate, Southern/Northern Mistbelt, Scarp and Coastal Dune forest). MAP ~860–1 030 mm+ in the named Strelitzia 19 units, heavily supplemented by mist; APCV 19–22% (very reliable); MAT 15.7–16.7°C; MAPE ~1 650–1 675 mm (low); frost-free by definition; fire-free; shaded, high humidity. Persists above ~525 mm under strong winter rainfall and ~725 mm under strong summer rainfall, and kloof/riverine forest breaks that envelope entirely on groundwater.

entries.why: The one indigenous fruit tree that actively wants the wet seep or streambank every forest farm has and cannot crop otherwise — SANBI records it 'near streams, on forest margins or in swampy spots', it 'feeds honeybees', and the fruit is eaten fresh or fermented.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/syzygium-cordatum (height '8-15 m'; habitat, bee and fruit uses)

entries.why: A riverine-forest native that gives a real jam-and-wine crop plus the heaviest bird load of any tree here (Cape parrots, louries, green pigeons) — but it is dioecious, so plant several seedlings or buy sexed stock or you get no fruit.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/harpephyllum-caffrum ('up to 15 m tall'; 'popular tree in frost-free areas'; riverine forest; fruit for jams, jellies, rosé wine)

entries.why: Ranked in SA indigenous-fruit prioritisation work as a domestication candidate and the sweetest, highest-vitamin-C indigenous fruit in this palette; it fruits April–September, filling the gap when nothing exotic is ready.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/mimusops-zeyheri ('up to 15 m under ideal conditions', crown 'as wide as the tree is high'; fruit 'sweet and high in vitamin C'; 'tolerant only of a moderate degree of frost') + https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: The best value-per-square-metre plant in the whole palette: stock-proof thorn hedge, fruit for jam, leaf fodder and bee forage from one row — and it is frost-hardy and drought-resistant, so it holds the cold, exposed forest margin the tender species cannot.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dovyalis-caffra ('usually 3-5 m in height, but sometimes reaches 8 m'; growth 'about 600 mm per year'; 'impenetrable hedge'; 'leaves are used as fodder')

entries.why: The coastal and scarp-forest hedge plant — salt- and wind-resistant, thorny enough to turn animals, and the fruit is high in vitamin C and eaten raw or as jam; plant 1 m apart for an impenetrable line.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/carissa-macrocarpa ('small tree up to 4 m high'; 'Plant 1 m apart to form a dense, impenetrable hedge'; 'wind resistant and can grow in coastal areas'; 'frost tender')

entries.why: One of very few edible-fruit shrubs SANBI says grows 'often in the shade of trees' and may be planted 'in either full sun or shade', so it actually crops under a canopy; it also browses well and feeds honeybees.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/grewia-occidentalis ('reaching up to 3m in height'; 'frost-hardy'; 'browsed by cattle, goats and game'; 'Feeds honeybees')

entries.why: The single biggest wildlife-food event on a forest farm — figs are eaten by people and turn the tree into a bird and fruit-bat table — but allow a full 18 m and keep it far from buildings, paving and sewer lines because the roots are genuinely destructive.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ficus-sur ('up to 35 m high'; 'inadvisable to plant... near buildings, paving, sewer lines or walls'; 'will not tolerate moderate or severe frost'; figs 'readily eaten by local people')

entries.why: The crop this biome exists for: ARC wants >1 000 mm evenly distributed with only June–July dry and humidity above 50%, which is the mistbelt description, and SAAGA 2024 censused 3 925 ha in Mpumalanga and 3 429 ha in KZN — but plant on a slope, never a cold-air bottom, because the killing exposure is frost at August–September flowering, not the -4°C survival floor.
entries.source: https://avocado.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/SAAGA-Industry-Census-Report-2024.pdf + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf + https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Persea+americana ('Grafted trees generally tend to be 8 - 10 metres tall')

entries.why: SA's biggest tree-nut crop sits almost entirely in this biome and the neighbouring coastal belt (~29 000 ha Mpumalanga, ~23 800 ha KZN) precisely because macadamia is 'easily damaged by strong winds' and needs a sheltered, humid, 1 000 mm+ site — forest shelter is the asset, not an obstacle; note it is NOT frost resistant despite surviving 3°C.
entries.source: https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Macadamia+integrifolia ('up to 15 metres tall'; rainfall '1,000 - 3,000mm'; 'require a sheltered position and are easily damaged by strong winds') + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: The rare high-value crop that actually wants to be under other trees — it 'prefers a position in light shade' and 1 400–2 300 mm — so it monetises the shaded understorey that would otherwise carry nothing, and SA has a real if small mistbelt coffee sector (Port Edward, Sabie).
entries.source: https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Coffea+arabica ('compact shrub 1.5 - 3 metres tall'; 'Prefers a position in light shade'; rainfall '1,400 - 2,300mm'; subtropics 'sea level to 1,000 metres')

entries.why: The cold-insurance fruit for high mistbelt margins where avocado and banana get burnt — hardy to about -10°C dormant, clips into a shelter hedge, and is the legal substitute for guava, which is Category 3 across most of this biome's provinces.
entries.source: https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Acca+sellowiana ('3 - 7.5 metres tall'; 'can survive temperatures down to about -10°c'; 'grown as a shelter hedge... responds well to trimming'; rainfall '750 - 1,500mm')

entries.why: Fastest exotic fruit to first harvest in warm coastal and scarp forest — bearing inside 12–18 months, occupying almost no ground area, so it fills the years while avocado and macadamia are still establishing; strictly frost-free, low-altitude sites.
entries.source: https://www.agribook.co.za/subtropical-fruit/ + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

entries.why: Worth planting in warm low-altitude scarp and coastal forest for fruit plus enormous pseudostem and leaf biomass for mulch, but be honest about the ceiling: ARC states optimum banana conditions 'do not exist elsewhere in the nation' and mean night temperatures below 10°C wreck flower initiation, so cool high mistbelt sites will grow leaves and little fruit.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf ('climate significantly limits banana cultivation'; 'nearly all bananas are irrigated'; night minima and choke-throat effects)

entries.why: Citrus genuinely has the broadest reach of any SA fruit crop and lemon is its most climatically adaptable type, so it belongs here — but this is citrus's weakest warm biome, not its best: ARC's citrus districts are chosen for dry air, and forest humidity that 'may reach saturation point' means real fungal pressure, so site it on an open, well-drained, airy margin and expect to manage disease.
entries.source: https://www.cga.co.za/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CGA-Key-Industry-Statistics-2025.pdf (lemon 17 970 ha across all six citrus provinces) + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf ('lemon is well suited to a broader variety of climatic conditions')

entries.why: The indigenous nitrogen-fixing canopy tree for this biome — a natural pioneer of forest clearings that nodulates with Bradyrhizobium and puts on ~2 m a year, and its flat crown throws filtered rather than dense shade, so coffee and understorey crops still perform beneath it. Note three other Albizia (A. lebbeck, A. procera, A. lophantha) are Category 1b — this one is indigenous and unlisted.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/albizia-adianthifolia-var-adianthifolia + https://apps.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Albizia_adianthifolia.PDF (6–15 m, flat wide-spreading crown; N-fixing nodules; ~2 m/yr)

entries.why: The best all-round indigenous shade tree of this biome, working from sea level to 1 500 m in both high-altitude evergreen and riverine forest, and feeding honeybees, butterflies and at least five fruit-eating bird families — the anchor tree for a homestead or livestock shade point.
