entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ekebergia-capensis ('grows to about 15 m in height'; 'high altitude evergreen forests to riverine forests, and from the sea level to about 1500 m'; 'Feeds honeybees'; 'tolerate light drought conditions and very light frost')

entries.why: Fast (1–2 m a year), frost-hardy and deciduous, so it shades a house or kraal in summer and lets winter sun through — the one canopy tree here that will take a cold, exposed upper-mistbelt margin, and cattle and goats browse the leaves. Do not confuse with Celtis australis and C. occidentalis, both Category 3.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/celtis-africana ('up to 25 m tall' in forest, 'up to 12 m' in a garden; '1 to 2 m per year'; 'Can withstand frost'; 'Leaves are browsed by cattle and goats')

entries.why: A mass nectar event for honeybees and butterflies from a single tree, hardy to about -7°C once established and growing nearly a metre a year; on an open margin it stays around 7 m and spreads wide, which is the shape you actually want over a working yard.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/calodendrum-capense ('up to 20 m' in forest, 'approx. 7 m, with a more spreading canopy' at the margin; 'feeds honeybees'; 'survive in Zone 9 (-7°C)'; 'nearly 1 m in a year')

entries.why: The legal and ecological answer to 'I need a tall shelterbelt' in a biome where every listed Eucalyptus is Category 1b — evergreen, narrow, frost-tolerant, long-lived, with valuable timber and fleshy cones that feed pigeons, turacos and bushpig; slow, so plant it once and early.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/podocarpus-latifolius ('between 20 and 30 m in height'; 'slow-growing'; 'able to withstand some frost'; 'shelter from strong winds'; timber uses)

entries.why: A fast indigenous pioneer for closing a canopy gap quickly and pulling in forest specialists (Forest Weavers, Cinnamon Doves, Green Pigeons, Charaxes butterflies); the fruit is poisonous to people, so plant it as habitat and shade, never as food.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/croton-sylvaticus ('up to 21 m, high'; 'fast-growing'; 'coastal and inland forests, in scrub, often along streams'; 'fruits are poisonous, but are eaten by birds')

entries.why: The nurse tree of Southern Afrotemperate forest and the fastest legitimate way to build a forest system from bare ground: 5–7 m in a few years, and peer-reviewed work shows soils under Virgilia stands carry higher nitrogen AND phosphorus than adjacent fynbos, with the species acting as a documented forest precursor. Short-lived by design — it hands the site to the slow canopy trees.
entries.source: https://scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0075-64582013000100007 ('fast-growing nitrogen-fixing tree... found on the margins of forest'; higher N and P under stands; 'forest precursor') + https://pza.sanbi.org/virgilia

entries.why: The cheapest fence on any SA farm: whole branch sections are cut as truncheons and planted straight into the ground, so the post becomes the tree — SANBI confirms the traditional use as living fences around kraals and homesteads — and the winter nectar flush feeds every sunbird for a kilometre.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/erythrina-lysistemon ('up to 10 m in height, occasionally reaching 12 m'; 'planted as living fences around kraals, homesteads and waterholes'; truncheon propagation; 'winter minimum of -7 to -1 °C... provided it is planted in a sheltered position')

entries.why: Plant this as pest control, not decoration — it is the larval host for Acraea butterflies, and the resulting caterpillar flush is what pulls insectivorous cuckoos and robins into an orchard; it is also the most frost-tolerant tree in this section (-2°C to 36°C) with a non-aggressive root system, so it can go near buildings.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/kiggelaria-africana ('11 m high x 13 m wide'; 'Reasonably frost-hardy... about -2°C to 36°C'; Acraea larvae attracting insectivorous cuckoos; 'non-aggressive root system')

entries.why: The indigenous chop-and-drop tree that replaces the illegal Tithonia — a fast forest-margin pioneer whose young leaves are eaten as a spinach, whose foliage is browsed by game and stock, and which hosts 14 butterfly species; coppice it for mulch on a system that has no other biomass source.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/trema-orientalis ('up to 18 m on forest margins'; 'a common pioneer tree'; 'young leaves are eaten as a spinach by the Zulus'; 'Kudu and giraffe browse the foliage'; '14 species of butterfly use Trema orientalis as a larval food plant')

entries.why: The Pondoland scarp-forest legume — fast for a hardwood at 0.8–1 m a year, feeds honeybees, and produces genuinely valuable dark heartwood, so it is the timber-plus-nitrogen option on high-rainfall KZN and Eastern Cape sites.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/millettia-grandis ('up to 25 m tall with a spreading crown in good conditions, but much smaller in shallow soils'; 'fast growing (0.8 to 1 m per year)'; 'Feeds honeybees'; KZN and Eastern Cape, most common in Pondoland)

entries.why: The DFFE national agroforestry guideline names it as one of only two woody legumes actually used as improved fallows in South Africa, with maize established directly into its prunings — 4–5 m in six months and 4–12 t/ha of dry matter a year makes it the fastest fertility engine available here. Do not confuse with Sesbania punicea, which is Category 1b.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf + https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Sesbania+sesban ('1 - 7 metres tall'; '4 - 5 metres in only 6 months'; '4 to 12 tonnes/hectare dry matter per year'; rainfall '800 - 2,000mm')

entries.why: The best sunbird plant in the biome — nectar-rich flowers borne on the old wood keep nectar-feeding birds and bees resident year-round — and it is fast and hardy to about -7°C once established. Berries are technically edible but 'sickly sweet' and drying, so treat it as habitat, not fruit.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/halleria-lucida ('2-5 m' exposed, 'up to 12 m' protected; 'Relatively hardy to frost (zone 9: minimum -7 °C)'; 'nectar-rich flowers attract sunbirds'; berries 'have a sickly sweet taste')

entries.why: An indigenous legume of forest margins and clearings that earns its place twice — fast nitrogen-fixing shrub-layer biomass, and a working farm remedy, with leaves and powdered root used against lice, itch and maggots in wounds; carpenter bees work the flowers heavily.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/calpurnia-aurea ('2-4 m tall with a light, open crown'; 'Forest, on forest margins and in clearings'; 'fast-growing'; lice/maggot/insecticidal uses; 'withstand a climate with a winter minimum of -5 °C')

entries.why: A genuinely frost-resistant evergreen for the shaded understorey and stream banks, carrying bee-worked flowers and berries 'favoured by many bird species'; long used medicinally and as the bittering herb in traditional brewing, so it has a household yield beyond habitat.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhamnus-prinoides ('up to 4,5 m high'; 'forests, stream banks'; 'full sun or semi-shade'; 'tough and frost resistant'; 'flowers are loved by the bees')

entries.why: One of the very few plants here that SANBI says grows 'equally well in sun or shade', which makes it the default filler for the difficult dark band directly under a big canopy tree where nothing else will hold; bulbuls, starlings, robins and barbets strip the berries.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/psychotria-capensis ('3-8 m tall'; 'Evergreen forests, forest margins... sea level to 1,500 m'; 'growing equally well in sun or shade')

entries.why: Frost-hardy, reaches full size in 4–5 years and flowers from year two, so it delivers bee forage faster than anything else in this section — and its bark is reputedly the strongest natural fibre of any tree in KwaZulu-Natal, a real cordage crop from prunings.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/dais-cotinifolia ('only to 6 metres'; 'full height within 4 to 5 years, flowering from about their second year'; 'frost hardy'; 'Feeds honeybees'; 'strongest fibre of any tree in KwaZulu-Natal')

entries.why: The other woody legume the DFFE guideline documents in actual South African use, photographed as an improved fallow in KwaZulu-Natal and grown as hedgerows cut at 90 cm — it gives grain, leaf fodder, nitrogen and mulch from the shrub layer in the same season. Short-lived (1–5 years), so treat it as a rotating crop, and give it drainage because forest-biome rainfall exceeds its comfort range.
entries.source: https://www.dffe.gov.za/sites/default/files/docs/strategy.framework/forestry/agroforestryguideline_english.pdf ('Pigeon pea being grown as an improved fallow in KwaZulu-Natal'; hedgerows cut at 90 cm) + https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Cajanus+cajan ('4 metres tall'; 'rainfall in the region of 500 - 1,000mm'; 'dying after 1 - 5 years')

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but note Tecoma stans in the same genus is Category 1b
entries.why: A fast multi-stemmed scrambler that takes clipping into a formal hedge or bushes out to bind a cut bank, works in semi-shade to full sun, and is the reliable sunbird-and-honeybee nectar shrub at eye level. Widely sold as Tecomaria capensis; flag it carefully in an app because the congener Tecoma stans is Category 1b.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/tecomaria-capensis ('may grow up to 2-3 m high and spread more than 2.5 m'; 'fast growing, scrambling, multi-stemmed shrub'; 'withstands clipping and can be trained into a neat hedge'; 'semi-shade to full sun'; sunbird pollination)

entries.nembaStatus: not listed — but note Plectranthus barbatus var. grandis is Category 1b
entries.why: A soft, fast shrub confined in the wild to exactly this habitat — 'moist coastal subtropical and afrotemperate Forest and forest margins' — that is pruned back hard every midwinter, which is precisely a chop-and-drop cycle producing shade-grown mulch where sun-loving biomass crops fail.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/plectranthus-ecklonii ('soft, erect, fast growing shrub to 3 m tall'; 'moist coastal subtropical and afrotemperate Forest and forest margins'; 'best grown in partial shade'; 'Prune back hard after flowering during midwinter')

entries.why: Fills the hungry gap: it flowers from May right through winter into early spring, in shade, when almost nothing else in a forest garden is feeding bees — a deliberate winter-forage planting under the canopy rather than an ornamental.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/hypoestes-aristata ('grows up to 1.5 m high'; 'from May right through winter till early spring'; 'Full Sun, Shade, Morning Sun'; 'Feeds honeybees')

entries.why: The staple starch of this biome and the only major food crop that treats a waterlogged seep as an asset — some varieties grow in standing water — so it crops the wet ground that would otherwise be a drainage problem, and it tolerates light shade under a canopy.
entries.source: https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Colocasia+esculenta ('40 - 200cm tall'; 'some varieties will even grow in shallow water'; 'tolerating light shade') + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx

entries.why: An indigenous tuber crop of forest margins and dry woodland that Zulu communities have cultivated on the KZN coast since prehistory — 80% starch with 13% essential amino acids plus calcium and iron — and its storage organ lets it sit out a bad season. Widely listed as Plectranthus esculentus.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/coleus-esculentus ('600–1 200 mm tall'; 'high level of starch (80%)' plus '13% essential amino acids'; 'forest margins'; 'in coastal areas such as KwaZulu-Natal, the Zulu speaking people have been cultivating... since prehistoric times')

entries.why: A high-value crop that wants exactly what this biome oversupplies — partial shade and 1 400–3 000 mm — so it turns dappled understorey into income; plant on a raised or mounded bed because it will not take waterlogging. Turmeric (Curcuma longa, also unlisted) grows in the same niche and can be interplanted.
entries.source: https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Zingiber+officinale ('1.50 m'; 'full sun or partial shade'; rainfall '1,400 - 3,000mm'; 'prefers a well-drained, humus-rich' soil)

entries.why: The living-mulch layer for moist shade: a creeping indigenous mat that holds bare soil under trees without competing for canopy space, occurring naturally in SA forests, marshy ground and riverbanks, and carrying real medicinal value (asiaticoside, madecassic acid) as a saleable understorey crop.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/ + https://weedopedia.co.za/plant.php?name=pennywort (SA distribution 'from the Cape Peninsula towards the damp eastern areas'; 'forests, marshy areas and riverbanks'; creeping groundcover of moist shade)

entries.why: One of ARC-VOPI's core researched indigenous leafy vegetables and a staple imifino green — it volunteers in disturbed ground, so in a forest system the practice is managed encouragement in canopy gaps and bed edges rather than sowing; harvest at 4–6 weeks and 15–30 cm.
entries.source: https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-vopi/Pages/Crop%20Science/Indigenous-Crops.aspx + https://www.agribook.co.za/indigenous-food-crops/

entries.why: A true forest-floor plant needing 'a warm, but shady position' — the deepest-shade niche in the design — and the highest-value medicinal here; it is Red Data listed and thought extinct in the wild in KwaZulu-Natal, so cultivating it both earns money and takes pressure off wild harvesting.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/siphonochilus-aethiopicus ('up to 400mm'; 'a warm, but shady position'; 'Listed in the Red Data book of South African plants'; 'thought to be extinct in KwaZulu-Natal')

entries.why: The indigenous, legal, edible climber for this biome and the only entry that crops the vertical space between understorey and canopy — pleasant acidic 20 mm berries, and it 'grows in low light', so it fruits where a granadilla would sulk; it also doubles as a shade groundcover if left unsupported.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/rhoicissus-tomentosa ('reaching the tops of 20 m high trees'; 'fruits are edible and pleasant tasting but acidic', 'up to 20 mm in diameter'; 'grows in low light'; forest and riverine fringes)

entries.why: A thorny evergreen scrambler that makes a genuine security and stock barrier where a hedge cannot be planted — up a fence line or over a bank — while feeding honeybees and giving small birds protected nesting cover; it thrives in shade, so it works inside the forest edge.
entries.source: https://pza.sanbi.org/asparagus-falcatus ('up to 7 m high'; 'climber, scrambler'; 'planted to serve as a protective hedge'; 'grows well in shade'; 'attracts birds'; 'feeds honeybees')

entries.nembaStatus: Category 2 in Eastern Cape, Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and North-West — PERMIT REQUIRED to grow, move, sell or possess. NOT listed in urban areas in those provinces. NOT listed elsewhere (so unrestricted in Western Cape forest patches). The fruit is not listed if used for human consumption — that exempts the fruit, never the vine.
entries.why: Included only because it is genuinely universal practice in KZN and Eastern Cape homesteads and crops heavily in this warm, humid, high-rainfall climate — but the app must warn, because on most Forest-biome farms it is a Category 2 species and an unpermitted vine is treated as Category 1b under regulation 4(4), converting a normal garden plant into a compulsory-control obligation.
entries.source: https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/202009/43726gon1003.pdf (Notice 3, List 1 item 256) + https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-iscw/CSA-Toolbox/Pages/assets/modules/6.pdf

excluded: LOQUAT (Eriobotrya japonica) — THE headline exclusion. Category 1b **in the Forest biome by name**: List 1 item 132 reads '1b in Western Cape and Forest biome... Not listed elsewhere.' It is the ONLY taxon in the entire 383-species 2020 plant list scoped to the Forest biome, and loquat is a classic mistbelt homestead tree, so this is the single most likely illegal planting a forest-garden list would cause. There is no permit route: planting or propagating is a s71A offence. The fruit-for-human-consumption carve-out exempts the fruit, not the tree.

GUAVA (Psidium guajava) — excluded here despite being the broadest-reach exotic fruit in South Africa. It is Category 2 only 'for plantations' in Eastern Cape, KZN, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North-West, and **Category 3 elsewhere in those same provinces** — i.e. a homestead guava in a KZN, EC, MP or LP forest patch may not be planted, propagated, moved or given away. It is genuinely unlisted in the Western Cape, so Southern Afrotemperate (Knysna/Tsitsikamma) forest sites may plant it freely. Feijoa is the substitute in the listed provinces.

TREE TOMATO / TAMARILLO (Solanum betaceum) — Category 3 in Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Mpumalanga, which is most of this biome. Thrives in mistbelt conditions, which is exactly why it is a trap. Unlisted in the Western Cape.

WHITE MULBERRY (Morus alba) — Category 3 nationally. Standing trees may be kept, but planting, propagating, moving, selling or giving away another one is prohibited under s71A. A staple of chicken-forage and silvopasture designs and therefore a common error.
SILKY OAK (Grevillea robusta) — Category 3. Very widely used as a mistbelt shade and windbreak tree; no new planting permitted. Use Podocarpus latifolius or Calodendrum capense.

TITHONIA / MEXICAN SUNFLOWER (Tithonia diversifolia) — Category 1b, and already invading coastal KZN, Lowveld Mpumalanga and Limpopo. The most-recommended chop-and-drop species in global permaculture literature and flatly illegal here. Replaced in this palette by Trema orientalis, Plectranthus ecklonii and Sesbania sesban.

LEUCAENA (Leucaena leucocephala) — Category 2 nationally (Category 1a in the Western Cape). The default tropical nitrogen-fixer of international permaculture; needs a permit and a paid risk-assessment practitioner. Replaced by Albizia adianthifolia, Virgilia divaricata, Millettia grandis, Sesbania sesban and Cajanus cajan.
ELDER (Sambucus nigra) — Category 1b. The cool, moist mistbelt climate suits elderflower/elderberry hedgerows perfectly, which is precisely why it gets recommended and why it is dangerous.
CAMPHOR TREE (Cinnamomum camphora) — Category 1b in Eastern Cape, KZN, Limpopo and Mpumalanga; Category 3 in Western Cape. A big shade tree of exactly this climate.
ROSE APPLE (Syzygium jambos) — Category 3; JAMBOLAN (S. cumini) — Category 1b. Both are moist-forest fruit trees. The indigenous S. cordatum in this palette fills the same niche legally.

EUCALYPTUS (all six listed taxa: E. camaldulensis, cladocalyx, conferruminata, diversicolor, grandis, tereticornis) — **Category 1b in the Forest biome**, with a Category 2 carve-out only for plantations, woodlots, bee-forage areas, wind-rows and avenue lining, and hard 1b inside riparian areas, Protected Areas and Listed Ecosystems. Not a casual windbreak or firewood choice on a forest farm. Podocarpus latifolius is the shelterbelt substitute.

BRAMBLES (Rubus spp.) — omitted deliberately. Indigenous forest brambles do exist (R. pinnatus, R. rigidus, R. ludwigii) and are unlisted, but seven alien Rubus are Category 1a/1b (R. ellipticus 1a; R. cuneifolius, flagellaris, immixtus, niveus 1b; R. fruticosus agg. Cat 2) and field identification between them is unreliable. The mis-ID risk of putting 'wild bramble' in a farmer-facing app outweighs the yield.

PECAN (Carya illinoinensis) — not NEMBA-listed, wrong climate. ARC requires humidity below 55% for most of the growing season and warns that scab punishes humid river valleys; Strelitzia 19 records Forest/IOCB humidity that 'may reach saturation point'. Also needs winter frost this biome does not get, and 10 000–15 000 m3/ha/yr of irrigation.

MANGO — physiologically tough (45°C, <300 mm) but ARC requires relative humidity of 55% or LESS from October to harvest and caps monthly rainfall (140 mm Dec–Feb) for disease-free fruit. Forest-biome rainfall and humidity guarantee failure. Also economically capped above ~600 m.

OLIVE and FIG — cold-hardy (-7°C and -5 to -10°C) but excluded for the opposite reason to the subtropicals: olive is an obligate thermoperiodic species needing June–July maxima below 21°C plus 600–1 000+ chill hours and dry air, and fig needs warm DRY weather during summer harvest or the fruit cracks and rots. Humid summer forest is wrong for both.

APPLE, PEAR, APRICOT and other high-chill deciduous fruit — the Forest biome is frost-free by definition, so it cannot accumulate the chill units these need (SA apples require ~500 CU even with rest-breaking agents; 92% of national apple hectares sit in five Western Cape/Langkloof districts). Low-chill peach is borderline on cold high-mistbelt margins only and was not strong enough to include.

LITCHI — too narrow to recommend on general principles. Needs frost-free AND winter minima above 6°C but below 14°C AND summer maxima below 32°C AND humidity above 50%, qualifying only the Mpumalanga Lowveld, Soutpansberg and KZN coast (~1 300–1 700 ha nationally). It can work on warm northern scarp-forest margins, but that is a site call, not a biome call.

TEA (Camellia sinensis) — unlisted and climatically excellent in the mistbelt (Magoebaskloof, Ntingwe), but excluded on usefulness rather than legality: leaf tea needs industrial withering, rolling, oxidising and firing to be worth anything, so it delivers almost no smallholder yield. Coffee was included instead because a farmer can pulp, dry and sell or drink it.

VACHELLIA KARROO, PORTULACARIA AFRA and VETIVER (Chrysopogon zizanioides) — South Africa's three great multi-function permaculture workhorses, all wrong here. Sweet thorn is an open sunny savanna/grassland pioneer, spekboom is fire-free semi-arid thicket, and vetiver is a full-sun contour grass. None will establish under or beside a closed forest canopy, and in this biome erosion control is done by keeping the litter layer and canopy intact, not by planting hedgerows.

OPUNTIA FICUS-INDICA and AGAVE AMERICANA — genuinely used as living fences in the Eastern Cape but alien and listed (Opuntia 1b except spineless cultivars; Agave americana subsp. americana var. expansa Cat 3 in Western Cape). Dovyalis caffra and Carissa macrocarpa do the same job legally and better in this rainfall.
palettes.notes:
HOW TO READ THIS PALETTE. The Forest biome's binding constraint is not rainfall and not frost — it is frost-free by definition, MAP runs ~863 mm (Southern Afrotemperate) to ~1 030 mm (Scarp Forest) with mist adding substantially more, rainfall variability is among the country's lowest (APCV 19–22%) and evaporation among the lowest (MAPE ~1 650 mm). The constraint is that the fertility is not in the soil. Strelitzia 19 is explicit: high rainfall leaches the profile and waterlogs clays, so forest trees keep roots in the top 30 cm with a dense fine feeder-root mat in the upper 10 cm, and "Disturbance of the root and litter layers will have significant negative effects on forest nutrition"; the trees are also "particularly sensitive to poor soil aeration caused by standing water resulting from disturbance of the natural drainage patterns and from soil compaction." A forest site READS as the most fertile land on the farm and is not — clearing or ploughing destroys the whole nutrient capital in one pass. So this is a plant-through-the-mulch palette: do not till, do not compact (vehicle and livestock traffic are direct threats), do not alter drainage, and build production on top of the existing litter layer. That is also why the list is deliberately heavy on shade-tolerant understorey (coffee, ginger, wild ginger, Centella, Psychotria, Plectranthus, Rhoicissus) rather than on annual beds.

MARGIN VS INTERIOR. Forest is the smallest biome in southern Africa (<0.25% of the surface), few patches exceed 1 km², and it has the third-longest boundary with other biomes relative to its area. Almost every real farm here is on the MARGIN, not inside. Use the strata accordingly: nurse and pioneer species (Virgilia, Trema, Croton, Albizia, Sesbania, Cajanus) on the margin and in gaps to build the system; shade species under an existing canopy; and the exotic orchard block (avocado, macadamia) on the sheltered open ground the forest protects from wind.

THE ONE SPLIT THAT MATTERS MOST — this biome is two different farms. (a) SOUTHERN AFROTEMPERATE (Knysna, Tsitsikamma, southern/eastern Cape; winter-to-even rainfall, cooler, MAT ~16.7°C): Virgilia divaricata, Podocarpus, Calodendrum, Halleria, Celtis, Dais, feijoa. Critically, guava, tamarillo and granadilla are NOT NEMBA-listed in the Western Cape, so those three exclusions do not apply there. (b) MISTBELT / SCARP / COASTAL (KZN, Eastern Cape, Mpumalanga, Limpopo; summer rainfall, warmer): Albizia adianthifolia, Millettia grandis, Trema, Croton, Harpephyllum, avocado, macadamia, banana, papaya, amadumbe — and this is where the Category 2/3 listings bite hardest. Any app should apply the province filter before the biome filter for the fruit sections.

FROST — READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING THE "none" ENTRIES. PlantZAfrica says forests are "restricted to frost-free areas", and Strelitzia 19's forest climate diagrams report MAP, APCV, MAT and MAPE but NOT mean frost days, so there is no published MFD figure for this biome. In practice high-altitude mistbelt margins above ~1 400 m and any valley bottom DO get radiation frost, and MFD is a screen-temperature statistic that always understates ground frost in a cold-air pool. Treat every frostTolerance:"none" entry (Ficus sur, coffee, banana, papaya, amadumbe, ginger) as a site-specific gamble: put them upslope on a thermal belt, never in the bottom. Avocado's real exposure is not its -4°C floor but frost during August–September flowering and fruit set.

FIRE. Forest is a fire-free system — it "rarely burns, mainly due to the high humidity", and disturbance is gap dynamics at 0.005–0.5 ha. Unlike Fynbos and Grassland, do NOT plan burns or import fire as a management tool here; it is actively destructive. The corollary is a design bonus: no burn cycle to work around.

RAINFALL FLOOR / KLOOF EXCEPTION. Forest persists above ~525 mm under strong winter rainfall and ~725 mm under strong summer rainfall (the summer figure is higher because summer rain is lost to evaporation), and Strelitzia 19 notes a summer aridity index predicts forest better than rainfall does. Riverine and kloof forest break the envelope entirely using groundwater, flood water and low-irradiation gorges. So a sheltered kloof or a groundwater-fed site several hundred millimetres below the nominal 1 200 mm can carry this whole palette — worth encoding as an override rather than hard-gating on MAP.

PRACTICAL PLANTING NOTES. Harpephyllum caffrum and Dovyalis caffra are dioecious — plant several seedlings or buy sexed stock or you get no fruit. Ficus sur has genuinely destructive roots; keep it well away from buildings, paving and sewer lines. Croton sylvaticus fruit is poisonous to people (habitat tree only) and Halleria lucida berries are edible but unpalatable (bird tree only). Virgilia divaricata, Sesbania sesban and Cajanus cajan are all short-lived by design (roughly 20, <10 and 1–5 years) — they are scaffolding, not permanent structure, and the plan should show what replaces them.

FOUR GENUS-LEVEL TRAPS AN APP MUST HANDLE. A species-only lookup will get these wrong: Tecoma capensis (indigenous, unlisted) vs Tecoma stans (1b); Celtis africana (indigenous) vs C. australis and C. occidentalis (both Cat 3); Plectranthus ecklonii (indigenous) vs P. barbatus var. grandis (1b); Syzygium cordatum (indigenous) vs S. jambos (Cat 3) and S. cumini (1b); and Sesbania sesban (unlisted) vs S. punicea (1b). Note also Notice 1's own naming rule — where a scientific name changes or is misspelt, "the common name of the species takes precedence and determines whether a particular species is listed or not" — so matching on binomials alone is legally insufficient.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY THIN. There is no separate fodder/pasture section: this is a shaded, closed-canopy system with low herbaceous production, and Strelitzia 19 warns that forest and thicket biomass badly overstates carrying capacity. Browse here is incidental (Celtis, Trema, Grewia, Dovyalis leaves) rather than a designed pasture. Likewise the imifino/leafy-green layer is short — those species need sun, so in a forest system the honest practice is managed encouragement in canopy gaps and bed edges, not a vegetable block under trees.

SOURCES CHECKED, NOT RECALLED. NEMBA status for every entry was grepped against the parsed 383-taxon List 1 of the Alien and Invasive Species Lists, 2020 (GN 1003, GG 43726, 18 Sept 2020, in force 1 March 2021 per GN 115, GG 44182 — no amendment gazetted since). Sizes come from SANBI PlantZAfrica species pages, Useful Tropical Plants, and industry censuses (SAAGA 2024, CGA 2025); climate envelopes from Strelitzia 19 Ch.12 and the ARC Climate-Smart Agriculture subtropical module. Two caveats on my own data: Virgilia divaricata has no live PlantZAfrica species page (I used the peer-reviewed Bothalia/SAJB forest-expansion study plus the genus page), and Centella asiatica's indigenous status is occasionally reported as "naturalised" by nursery sources though SA botanical sources treat it as native from the Cape Peninsula through the damp east — flag it as native-with-a-note if the app displays provenance.
